Must retrieve the publication venue and event information indicating that the work appeared at NAACL SRW 2019 in Minneapolis.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and present the data scarcity and rare-word translation issues in multimodal machine translation as illustrated by the Multi30k example in the paper?

requirements.description: Must state that the Multi30k dataset [Elliott et al., 2016] is small in size and is explicitly cited in the paper as a limitation for multimodal machine translation training data.
Must reference the paper's statistics or discussion of the training data size (e.g., number of examples or explicit mention of 'small amount of data') that motivate the data scarcity issue.
Must explicitly mention that the paper identifies difficulty in training rare word translation as a consequence of limited multimodal training data.

Must describe the paper's observation that the NMT model tends to output more frequent synonyms guided by the language model when rare words appear, rather than correctly translating the rare word itself.

Must reproduce or accurately describe the concrete translation example from the paper showing the French source sentence with 'mais', the reference translation containing 'corn', and the NMT output where 'corn' is replaced by the synonym 'food'.

decisions: What previous data-based solutions for multimodal machine translation does the paper describe as alternatives to their proposed method?

requirements.description: Must identify that one prior solution is using a parallel text-only corpus (parallel corpus without images) as discussed in the paper's background/related work on multimodal MT.

Must state that another prior solution is generating pseudo in-domain data by filtering general-domain parallel data, as described in the paper's discussion of data augmentation or domain adaptation approaches.
Must state that a further prior solution is back-translation of caption or other monolingual data, as described in the paper's section on leveraging monolingual or caption data for multimodal MT.

Must correctly retrieve and list the cited works associated with the parallel corpus without images approach, specifically Elliott and Kadar (2017) and Gronroos et al. (2018), as they appear in the paper's text or references.

Must locate and use the part of the paper that explicitly summarizes 'previous solutions' or prior data strategies for multimodal MT (typically in the Related Work or Background section), rather than inferring methods not mentioned there.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the paper’s motivation for introducing pretrained word embeddings into multimodal machine translation, including prior text-only NMT approaches it builds on?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper’s main motivation is to introduce pretrained word embeddings into multimodal machine translation (MMT) to improve rare word translation performance in this setting.
Must explicitly connect the motivation to the rare word problem in multimodal NMT, i.e., that multimodal NMT suffers from poor performance on rare words due to limited training data.
Must describe the use of pretrained word embeddings in text-only NMT as initializing the encoder and decoder embedding layers, and attribute this approach to Qi et al. (2018).
Must state that the Qi et al. (2018) pretrained embedding initialization improves overall performance in low-resource domains in text-only NMT.
Must mention a search-based decoder with continuous output for handling rare words, and attribute this method to Kumar and Tsvetkov (2019).

decisions: What baseline IMAGINATION setup from Bahdanau et al. (2015) is used during validation and testing, and how are the MT and shared-space learning tasks trained to improve the shared encoder in this NAACL SRW 2019 work?

requirements.description: Must identify that the baseline referred to as IMAGINATION is based on the Bahdanau et al. (2015) attention-based neural machine translation model used as the MT component.

Must state that the model is trained jointly on two tasks: (1) the machine translation (MT) task and (2) a shared-space learning task (e.g., mapping text and visual features into a shared embedding space).
Must explicitly mention that the purpose of the joint training of MT and shared-space learning tasks is to improve or refine a shared encoder.

Must locate and use the part of the paper that describes the baseline IMAGINATION model or baseline system setup (typically in the experimental setup or baseline/architecture description section) rather than unrelated sections such as introduction or related work.
Must correctly associate the work with its venue and time frame by identifying that it is presented as part of NAACL SRW 2019 in Minneapolis.

decisions: What specific training and inference techniques does the paper propose for multimodal machine translation with embedding prediction?

requirements.description: Must state that the model uses an embedding prediction approach in the decoder specifically during validation and testing (inference), as opposed to standard softmax over the vocabulary.

Must specify that during training, the encoder and decoder word embedding layers are initialized with pretrained word embeddings (e.g., from an external embedding model) rather than random initialization.
Must describe the preprocessing step applied to visual features where the visual feature vectors are shifted so that their mean vector becomes zero (mean-centering of visual features).

Must extract these three elements (embedding prediction usage at validation/testing, pretrained embedding initialization at training, and mean-centering of visual features) from the paper's description of the proposed model or training procedure, not from unrelated background or related work sections.

Must connect the use of pretrained word embeddings and embedding prediction explicitly to the multimodal machine translation setting (i.e., indicate that these techniques are applied within an NMT system that also uses visual features).

decisions: How does the embedding prediction (continuous output) approach generate the next word in multimodal machine translation using pretrained word embeddings?

requirements.description: Must state that the model predicts a continuous word embedding vector for the next word instead of directly predicting a discrete word index (embedding prediction / continuous output).
Must describe the first step of the procedure as predicting the embedding of the next word from the model (e.g., decoder) output.
Must describe that cosine similarity is computed between the predicted embedding and each vector in the pretrained word embedding matrix.
Must specify that the final output word is chosen by selecting the vocabulary item whose pretrained embedding is most similar (nearest) to the predicted embedding.
Must explicitly state that the pretrained word embeddings used for the nearest-neighbor search are kept fixed and are not updated during training.

decisions: How does the proposed multimodal NMT model initialize and train the word embedding layers in the encoder and decoder?

requirements.description: Must state that the model initializes its word embedding layer using pretrained word embeddings, as explicitly described in the paper's model or implementation section.
Must specify that the encoder-side embedding layer is fine-tuned (updated during training), following the training strategy described for the encoder in the paper.
Must specify that the decoder-side embedding layer is kept fixed (not updated during training), as stated in the training or optimization description for the decoder.

Must extract the embedding initialization and update policy from the section that details model architecture or training setup (e.g., 'Model', 'Implementation Details', or 'Training'), not infer it from unrelated sections such as 'Abstract' or 'Introduction'.
Must identify that the described embedding initialization and update scheme is applied to the multimodal NMT system proposed in the paper, not to a baseline or unrelated model.

decisions: How does the paper define and structure the overall loss function for its multimodal machine translation model, including the specific loss types and their sources?

requirements.description: Must state that the model loss is an interpolation (i.e., weighted combination) of multiple loss terms, explicitly using the notion of 'interpolation of each loss' as described in the loss/objective function section.
Must identify that the machine translation (MT) task uses a max-margin loss with negative sampling, and explicitly attribute this formulation to Lazaridou et al. (2015) as cited in the paper.

Must identify that the shared space learning task (aligning text and visual representations) uses a max-margin loss, and explicitly attribute this formulation to Elliot and Kadaar (2017) as cited in the paper.

Must extract the description of the combined objective from the paper's loss/objective function subsection (or equivalent), including both the MT task loss and the shared space learning task loss as jointly optimized components.

Must recognize and state that the overall training objective is based on prior work by Elliot and Kadaar (2017) for the interpolation scheme of losses, as referenced in the paper's description of the model loss.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and explain the hubness problem as it affects the embedding prediction model in this multimodal machine translation paper?

requirements.description: Must define 'hubness' as the phenomenon where certain words (hubs) appear frequently in the nearest neighbors of many other word embeddings.
Must state that hub words can appear as neighbors even for words that have no semantic relationship with those hubs.
Must explain that the paper uses an embedding prediction model that searches in the word embedding space to select output words, and that hubness interferes with this search process.
Must state that due to hubness, the model can incorrectly output the hub word instead of the correct translation word.

Must locate and draw from the specific part of the paper where the hubness problem is introduced and discussed in the context of embedding prediction (e.g., a subsection on hubness or limitations of embedding prediction), rather than from unrelated sections such as general multimodal NMT background.

decisions: How does the paper debias pretrained word embeddings to address the hubness problem when used in the multimodal NMT encoder and decoder?

requirements.description: Must identify that the motivation is to address the hubness problem in NLP tasks by debiasing pretrained word embeddings based on their global bias.
Must state that the debiasing method first shifts all word embeddings so that their mean vector becomes the zero vector (centering step).
Must state that after centering, the method subtracts the top 5 principal component analysis (PCA) components from each shifted word embedding.
Must specify that this debiasing procedure is applied to pretrained word embeddings used in both the encoder and the decoder of the NMT system.

Must retrieve the part of the paper that references the 'All but the Top' style debiasing or hubness-mitigation technique (e.g., in the word embedding preprocessing or training setup description), not from unrelated sections such as results or discussion.

decisions: What implementation details and dataset information does the paper provide for the multimodal machine translation experiments?

requirements.description: Must identify that the primary dataset used is the Multi30k corpus and that the translation direction is specifically from French to English.
Must state that a pretrained ResNet50 model is used as the visual encoder in the multimodal machine translation system.
Must report that the textual word embeddings (or language-related pretrained components) are trained on both Common Crawl and Wikipedia, as specified in the implementation or dataset description.
Must extract the implementation detail that the authors provide a public code repository and give its URL exactly as https://github.com/toshohirasawa/nmtpytorch-emb-pred.
Must retrieve the publication venue and event information indicating that the work was presented at NAACL SRW 2019 in Minneapolis.

decisions: Did the system correctly retrieve and summarize the model hyperparameters used in the multimodal NMT experiments?

requirements.description: Must state that the dimension of the hidden state is 256, as specified in the hyperparameter description (e.g., model configuration or experimental setup section).

Must report that the dimension of the word embedding is 300, taken from the hyperparameter or embedding configuration description.
Must report that the dimension of the shared space (multimodal shared representation) is 2048, as given in the model or multimodal fusion hyperparameter specification.
Must attribute these values to the experimental setup or hyperparameters section that describes the NAACL SRW 2019 multimodal NMT model configuration.

decisions: How does the paper present word-level F1 scores as a function of word frequency in the training data?

requirements.description: Must identify that the slide refers specifically to word-level F1 scores (not BLEU, METEOR, or other metrics) as the evaluation measure being discussed.

Must locate and reference the figure or plot in the paper that shows word-level F1 score as a function of frequency in the training data (e.g., a graph with x-axis as word frequency bins and y-axis as F1).
Must extract that the x-axis or grouping variable in the relevant figure/table is word frequency in the training data, explicitly tied to the phrase 'Frequency in training data'.
Must identify the section of the paper where word-level F1 by frequency is analyzed (typically in the experiments or analysis subsection on rare words) and base the slide content on that section.
Must recognize that the word-level F1 by frequency analysis is presented as an experimental result (not as part of the method description), and treat it as such when summarizing for the slide.

decisions: How does the choice and fixing of encoder/decoder embedding layers affect multimodal machine translation performance in this paper?

requirements.description: Must state that the experiment compares encoder and decoder embedding initialization using either random values or pretrained FastText word embeddings, explicitly mentioning both options for both encoder and decoder.
Must explain the 'Fixed (Yes/No)' setting as defined in the paper: whether the decoder embedding layer is kept fixed (not updated) or fine-tuned during training.

Must mention the requirement from the paper that word embeddings in the input (encoder) and output (decoder) layers be kept consistent (i.e., aligned or shared in some way).

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the paper’s overall performance comparison between the proposed multimodal NMT model (with pretrained embeddings and debiasing) and baseline models?

requirements.description: Must state that the evaluated model uses pretrained word embeddings via embedding layer initialization, as explicitly described in the experimental setup or model description section.

Must state that the evaluated model applies the 'All-but-the-Top' debiasing (or 'All-but-the-Top' post-processing) to the pretrained embeddings, as described in the methodology or implementation details.
Must explicitly state that the proposed model outperforms baseline models in overall translation performance, as reported in the main results section (e.g., higher BLEU or related metrics).

Must explicitly state that the proposed model also outperforms baselines that themselves use embedding layer initialization with pretrained embeddings, as indicated in the comparative results table or discussion.
Must identify that the performance comparison is part of the main experimental results section that reports 'overall performance' or equivalent aggregate metrics across models.

decisions: How does the use and centering of visual features affect the multimodal NMT model’s performance compared to a text-only embedding prediction baseline?

Must state that 'No' visual features corresponds to a text-only NMT system using the embedding prediction model, as defined in the paper’s experimental setup or ablation description.

Must draw from the section of the paper that reports the ablation study on visual features (e.g., an 'Ablation Study' or 'Effect of Visual Features' subsection in the experiments/results section), not from unrelated parts such as introduction or related work.

decisions: What conclusions and future work directions about multimodal machine translation with embedding prediction does the paper present?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper concludes multimodal machine translation (MMT) with embedding prediction improves translation performance, specifically in the low-resource or rare-word setting, as described in the paper's conclusion or discussion section.
Must identify the design choice that the decoder-side word embeddings are fixed (not updated) during training in the embedding prediction model, as described in the model or training setup section.

Must describe the debiasing of pretrained word embeddings as a distinct step or component (e.g., normalization, mean-centering, or bias-removal procedure) applied before or during training, as specified in the paper's method or implementation details.

Must mention that the paper proposes future work on (a) obtaining better training corpora for embedding learning in the MMT domain and (b) incorporating visual features into contextualized word embeddings, as listed in the conclusion or future work section.

decisions: How does the paper define and use a Basque–English training dictionary entry involving the arg min notation in its cross-lingual embedding mapping formulation?

decisions: What specific optimization objective, initialization details, and iterative procedure from Artetxe et al. (ACL 2017) are needed to reproduce the slide showing the '= arg min min' formulation, '25 word pairs', 'num. * none 0 a | Iteration', and 'Numeral list A'?

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the components of the fully unsupervised initialization step of the proposed cross-lingual mapping method?

decisions: How does the paper evaluate and compare the robustness of different cross-lingual mapping methods across multiple language pairs using repeated runs and a success-rate criterion?

requirements.description: Must identify and use the specific experiments section that reports repeated-run evaluations (10 runs for each method) of cross-lingual mapping methods.

decisions: Does the system correctly summarize the paper’s overall conclusions about robustness, remaining challenges, and future multilingual extensions?

Must report that the proposed method is concluded to be more robust and more accurate than previous unsupervised cross-lingual mapping methods, as supported by the paper’s comparative evaluation sections (e.g., experiments against prior adversarial approaches).

Must identify that the method’s robustness stems from a fully unsupervised initialization exploiting structural similarity of monolingual embeddings combined with a robust self-learning algorithm that iteratively improves the mapping.

Must extract the paper’s explicit future work statement that extends the approach from bilingual cross-lingual mappings to multilingual settings, as described in the conclusions or future work discussion section.

Must reference at least one concrete empirical comparison (e.g., a table or set of reported scores) where the proposed method outperforms prior unsupervised adversarial approaches, to justify the claim of being more robust and accurate than previous methods.

decisions: What key properties of UCCA and the main definition of the SemEval-2019 Task 1 must be retrieved from the paper to generate this slide?

requirements.description: Must state that UCCA is a cross-linguistically applicable framework for semantic representation, explicitly using the notion of cross-linguistic applicability or cross-linguistically applicable semantic representation as described in the paper.
Must identify that UCCA builds on Basic Linguistic Theory and attribute this to R. M. W. Dixon, matching the paper's description of its theoretical foundation.
Must retrieve the claim that UCCA representations are stable in translation and attribute this property to Sulem et al. (2015) or an equivalent citation given in the paper.

Must extract or reconstruct the example sentence "After graduation John moved to Paris" together with its UCCA annotation labels in sequence "P D L A A" (or an equivalent figure/diagram in the paper that shows this mapping).

decisions: What applications of UCCA-based semantic parsing are presented in the paper, and how is grammatical error correction illustrated?

requirements.description: Must list UCCA-based machine translation as an application and explicitly attribute it to Birch et al. (2016).
Must list sentence splitting for text simplification as an application and explicitly attribute it to Sulem et al. (2018b).

Must reproduce or closely paraphrase the corrected example sentence used to illustrate grammatical error correction: 'He gave John an apple'.

decisions: How does the paper define and illustrate the graph-structural properties of UCCA representations, including reentrancy via remote edges?

requirements.description: Must state that UCCA structures are represented as labeled directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), explicitly using the terms 'labeled' and 'directed acyclic graphs (DAGs)'.
Must specify that complex semantic units in UCCA correspond to non-terminal nodes in the graph structure, using the phrase 'complex units' or 'complex semantic units' and 'non-terminal nodes'.
Must mention that UCCA allows discontinuous phrases or units, explicitly indicating that 'phrases may be discontinuous' or that units can be discontinuous in the graph.

Must reference or reconstruct the example illustrating remote edges with the sentence 'They thought ... taking a short break', including the presence of a 'remote edge' and role labels abbreviated as 'R', 'P', 'D', and 'A' attached to nodes or units in that example.

decisions: What baseline UCCA parsing model and illustrative example does the paper present for the SemEval-2019 Task 1 shared task?

requirements.description: Must identify TUPA as the baseline system and explicitly state that it is a transition-based UCCA parser.
Must attribute TUPA to Hershcovich et al. (2017), including both the author name 'Hershcovich' and the year '2017'.
Must describe or reproduce the example sentence 'They thought about taking a short break' used in the paper to illustrate the baseline parser.
Must mention that the example includes multiple LSTM units (a sequence of repeated 'LSTM' blocks) representing the model architecture for the baseline.
Must indicate that the phrase 'taking a short break' is treated as a single semantic unit or node (referred to as 'NodeC') in the UCCA structure for the example.

decisions: What datasets are used as the data sources for the SemEval-2019 Task 1 on cross-lingual UCCA parsing?

requirements.description: Must state that one data source consists of English Wikipedia articles, explicitly identifying it as 'English Wikipedia' or 'Wikipedia' in English.
Must state that another data source is an English-French-German parallel corpus derived from the book 'Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea'.

Must extract the dataset information from the part of the paper that describes the data/resources for the shared task (e.g., data, corpus, or resources section), not from unrelated background or results sections.
Must indicate that the 'Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea' corpus is multilingual by explicitly mentioning all three languages: English, French, and German.

Must retrieve and mention that the paper provides sentence and/or token counts for the datasets (e.g., number of sentences or tokens), even if the exact numeric values are not reproduced in the slide text.

decisions: How does the paper define and characterize the French low-resource track in terms of available training data?

requirements.description: Must identify that the paper defines a specific 'French low-resource' track or setting distinct from other language/track configurations.
Must state that the French low-resource track has only 15 training sentences, using the exact quantity '15' as given in the paper.
Must locate and use the description of task tracks or data settings (e.g., the section describing tracks, datasets, or experimental setups) where the French low-resource condition is specified.
Must indicate that the French low-resource configuration is part of the shared task design (i.e., an intentional experimental track or condition rather than an incidental data artifact).

decisions: How does the paper illustrate the conversion between CoNLL-U dependency format and SDP/UCCA-style semantic representations using the example sentence 'After graduation, John moved to Paris'?

requirements.description: Must identify that the example illustrates a conversion between a syntactic dependency representation (CoNLL-U) and a semantic representation (SDP/UCCA) for the same sentence.
Must describe that the conversion example uses the sentence 'After graduation, John moved to Paris' as the running example for demonstrating the mapping procedure.

Must reference the figure or diagram in the paper that shows both the CoNLL-U dependency structure (with relations such as 'root', 'obl', 'nsubj', 'case', 'punct') and the corresponding semantic/SDP layer (with roles such as 'ARG1', 'ARG2', 'G1', 'head') aligned for this sentence.
Must retrieve and reproduce the specific predicate label 'graduate-01' and its associated semantic roles (e.g., 'ARG1', 'ARG2', 'G1', 'op1') as shown in the conversion example for the sentence.

Must draw from the section that explains the conversion or preprocessing pipeline from CoNLL-U (or syntactic dependencies) to the target semantic representation used in the shared task, including any example-based illustration with 'After graduation, John moved to Paris'.

decisions: How does the paper define and compute the evaluation metrics for UCCA parsing, including the matching procedure for primary and remote edges between true and predicted graphs?

requirements.description: Must state that evaluation is performed by comparing a true (human-annotated) UCCA graph with an automatically predicted UCCA graph for the same text.

Must describe the example evaluation figure/diagram that shows parallel rows of labels (e.g., 'L H U H L H U A' and 'A P A S A') aligned with tokens such as 'graduation John moved to Paris', illustrating true vs. predicted graph structures.
Must explain that primary edges are matched based on their terminal yield (the set or span of terminal tokens they dominate) together with the edge label.
Must specify that precision, recall, and F1 scores are calculated from the matched and unmatched edges as the core evaluation metrics.
Must state that the same matching and metric computation procedure is repeated separately for remote edges, in addition to primary edges.

decisions: Which systems and affiliated institutions participated in the SemEval-2019 Task 1 on UCCA parsing, and how many groups were there in total?

requirements.description: Must state that there were exactly 8 participating groups in the SemEval-2019 Task 1 on UCCA parsing.
Must list the system name "MaskParse@Deskin" together with its affiliation "Orange Labs, Aix-Marseille University" as they appear in the participating systems list.
Must list the system name "TuPa" together with its affiliation "University of Tubingen" as they appear in the participating systems list.

Must list the system names "UC Davis", "GCN-Sem", "CUNY-PekingU", and "DANGNT@UIT.VNU-HCM" each paired with their respective university affiliations exactly as given in the participating systems list.

Must extract all participating system names and affiliations from the specific section or subsection of the paper that enumerates the shared task participating systems (e.g., a 'Participating Systems' or 'Systems' section), not infer them from other contexts.

decisions: Which systems achieved 1st, 2nd, 3rd place and what were the baseline scores for each track in the SemEval-2019 Task 1 UCCA parsing leaderboard?

requirements.description: Must retrieve, for the 'English-Wiki closed' track, that HLT@SUDA is 1st place, 'baseline' is 2nd place, and 'Davis' is 3rd place, with no numeric baseline score shown.
Must retrieve, for the 'English-Wiki open' track, that HLT@SUDA is 1st place, CUNY-PekingU is 2nd place, '0.800' is the baseline score, and 'TuPa' is the baseline system.

Must retrieve, for both 'English-20K closed' and 'English-20K open' tracks, that HLT@SUDA is 1st place, 'baseline' is 2nd place for closed, CUNY-PekingU is 2nd place for open, CUNY-PekingU is 3rd place for closed, '0.669' is the baseline score for closed, and '0.739' is the baseline score for open, with 'TuPa' as the baseline system for the open track.

Must retrieve, for both 'German-20K closed' and 'German-20K open' tracks, that HLT@SUDA is 1st place, CUNY-PekingU is 2nd place, '0.797' is the baseline score for closed, and '0.841' is the baseline score for open, with 'baseline' listed as the baseline system for both tracks.
