decisions: According to the SemEval-2019 Task 1 paper, what were the main empirical findings about system rankings and cross-lingual performance in UCCA parsing, particularly for French compared to English and German?

requirements.description: Must state that the HLT@SUDA system is reported in the paper as winning 6 out of 7 tracks in the shared task results section (or equivalent results summary).
Must describe HLT@SUDA's approach as a neural constituency parser augmented with multi-task learning and BERT, as characterized in the system description/results discussion for that team.
Must identify that for the French track, HLT@SUDA trained a model on all available languages with an explicit language embedding, as specified in the paper's description of their cross-lingual setup.

Must report that the CUNY-PekingU system is described as winning the French open track and that it used a TUPA ensemble combined with synthetic training data created via machine translation, as detailed in the system/results section.

Must note that the paper explicitly observes that French results are close to English and German results and interprets this as evidence for the viability of cross-lingual UCCA parsing, raising the question of whether this is due to UCCA's stability under translation.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the paper’s main conclusions, acknowledgments, and follow-up shared task invitation as presented in the conclusion slide?

requirements.description: Must state that the shared task led to substantial improvements in UCCA parsing performance, using wording that clearly reflects an overall positive advancement (e.g., 'substantial improvements to UCCA parsing').
Must mention that the participating systems employed a high variety of methods or approaches, explicitly indicating methodological diversity among systems.
Must extract from the paper’s conclusion or acknowledgments the fact that thanks are given to three distinct groups: annotators, organizers, and participants.

Must correctly identify and list the named individuals associated with organizing or authoring the shared task as: Daniel Hershcovich, Leshem Choshen, Elior Sulem, Zohar Aizenbud, Ari Rappoport, and Omri Abend, without adding or omitting names.

Must identify the follow-up CoNLL 2019 shared task on Cross-Framework Meaning Representation Parsing and list all four frameworks explicitly as SDP, EDS, AMR, and UCCA, along with the participation URL or identifier 'mrp.nlpl.eu'.

decisions: Does the system correctly retrieve and reproduce the slide’s definitions and characterizations of leadership as presented in the source content?

requirements.description: Must state that leadership is defined as a process of social influence in which a person can enlist the aid and support of others in the accomplishment of a common task.
Must include the idea that leadership involves getting others to do something significant (or equivalent wording that clearly conveys "Get them to do something significant").
Must describe leadership as energizing people toward a goal (or equivalent wording that clearly conveys "Energizing people toward a goal").
Must attribute the social influence definition of leadership specifically to Chemers (2014).
Must attribute the "energizing people toward a goal" characterization of leadership specifically to Mills (2005).

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and extract the paper’s core concept of categorizing monarchs’ ruling (leadership) styles from the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty to support a slide about different leadership styles and their application to kings in old times?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper defines three categories of monarchial ruling styles based on the written records in the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty, as described in the abstract.

Must explicitly connect the notion of "ruling styles" of kings to the modern concept of "leadership styles" implied by the slide (i.e., treating monarchial ruling styles as leadership styles of kings).
Must describe that the ruling (leadership) styles are inferred from a quantitative text-mining analysis of the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty, not from secondary historical summaries.

Must reference the part of the paper where the authors introduce and define the categories of monarchial ruling styles (e.g., the section following the corpus introduction where three ruling-style categories are formally defined).

Must mention that the paper compares the twenty-five kings in terms of these defined ruling (leadership) style categories, enabling a question like "How about the kings in the old times?" to be grounded in the results.

decisions: According to the paper’s categorization of monarchial ruling styles, how is the 'Autocratic' ruling style characterized?

requirements.description: Must identify that 'Autocratic' is one of the three defined categories of monarchial ruling styles in the paper.
Must state that the 'Autocratic' ruling style is characterized by the monarch having control over all decisions (or equivalent wording indicating complete decision-making control by the king).

Must retrieve the definition of 'Autocratic' from the specific section where the three monarchial ruling style categories are introduced and defined (e.g., the methodology or categorization subsection), not infer it from unrelated narrative text.

Must link the 'Autocratic' definition explicitly to the paper’s formal categorization scheme used to compare the twenty-five kings, rather than to any anecdotal or historical description outside that scheme.

decisions: Does the paper explicitly investigate whether different Joseon kings exhibit different kinds of leadership or ruling styles, and is this framed as a core research question?

requirements.description: Must identify that the paper defines multiple categories (specifically three) of monarchial ruling or leadership styles based on the written records in the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty.
Must state that a central aim of the study is to compare the ruling or leadership styles of the twenty-five kings in the Joseon monarchy.
Must extract or infer from the paper's problem statement or introduction that one of the main research questions concerns whether kings show different kinds of leadership or ruling styles.

Must mention that the categorization of leadership or ruling styles is derived quantitatively from the text of the Annals corpus (i.e., based on written records rather than external biographical sources).
Must indicate that the study investigates variation in ruling or leadership styles across different kings, not just describing a single, uniform style for the dynasty as a whole.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and describe the dataset requirements and the chosen dataset (the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty) as the source of records of kings’ official duty activities for a long, large-scale study of monarchy in Korea?

requirements.description: Must identify that the primary dataset is the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty, explicitly naming it as the corpus used in the study.
Must state that the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty are daily written records covering approximately five hundred years of a Korean monarchy.
Must describe that the corpus consists of written records of kings' official duties or activities (i.e., daily records of monarchial ruling and governmental affairs).

Must cover the paper's introductory description of the corpus (where the Annals are introduced as a series of books describing historical facts during the Joseon dynasty) rather than only later analytical sections (e.g., ruling style categories or topic analyses).
Must characterize the dataset as long and large-scale, referencing its extensive temporal span (entire Joseon dynasty) as a justification for being a 'long and large dataset'.

decisions: What key properties and annotations of the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty corpus, as prepared and published by the National Institute of Korean History, are described in the paper?

requirements.description: Must identify that the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty corpus is maintained or provided by the National Institute of Korean History and include the institute’s official website URL as given in the paper (http://www.history.go.kr or equivalent).
Must state that the original historical text of the Annals has been translated into modern Korean, as explicitly described in the corpus introduction or data description section.

Must report that each document or record in the corpus is annotated with topical categories including at least the four types: political, economic, social, and cultural, as specified in the paper’s corpus annotation or preprocessing description.

Must report that the corpus includes named entity annotations for at least the following entity types: person, location, and nation (or country), as described in the paper’s data or annotation scheme section.
Must mention that the corpus is publicly accessible or published on the web, as stated in the paper’s corpus description, data availability, or implementation section.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize how the king’s governing role and decision-making with officials are described in the paper when introducing the Joseon monarchy?

requirements.description: Must state that the Joseon king is the central figure who governs or rules the nation, reflecting the monarchy’s structure as described in the corpus introduction.
Must state that the king is responsible for deciding or making official decisions on state or governmental issues, as characterized in the paper’s description of monarchial ruling styles or roles.

Must state that the king discusses or consults on official issues with government officials (e.g., ministers, bureaucrats), indicating a deliberative process between king and officials mentioned in the corpus description.

Must draw these role descriptions (governing the nation, deciding official issues, discussing with officials) from the paper’s introductory or corpus-description content about the Joseon monarchy, not from external historical sources.

Must mention the presence of a visual or illustrative element related to a historical drama depiction of the Joseon king (e.g., a screenshot from a drama like 'Yi San') used to visually represent the monarch’s role.

decisions: Does the system correctly extract and summarize the methodological steps used to analyze kings’ decisions, topics, and speakers in the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty?

requirements.description: Must state that the method focuses specifically on the king’s own words and final decisions, including the constraint to avoid non-governmental affairs such as observational content.

Must describe the procedure for identifying kings’ final decisions in each article by using a set of approximately sixty candidate verbs and examining the verbs in the king’s last sentence and the article title.

Must explain that topic discovery is performed at the article level using LDA, including that LDA outputs (1) a topic proportion vector for each article and (2) a multinomial word distribution for each topic.
Must describe the step for identifying who said what in quoted speech by analyzing subjects and person tags that appear immediately in front of the sentence of each quote.

Must cover all three methodological components in a single coherent description: (a) extracting kings’ decisions, (b) discovering topics with LDA, and (c) attributing quotes to participants using subject and person tags.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and extract the three defined ruling style categories and their distinguishing characteristics needed to describe the 'Ruling styles' examples slide?

requirements.description: Must identify that the paper defines three distinct monarchial ruling style categories named 'Discussion and Order (DO)', 'Discussion and Follow (DF)', and 'Arbitrary Decision (AD)'.
Must extract that 'Discussion and Order (DO)' involves discussion with officials followed by the king issuing an order, approval, or rejection at the end.
Must extract that 'Discussion and Follow (DF)' is a ruling style where the king follows the outcome of discussion with officials rather than issuing an arbitrary decision.
Must extract that 'Arbitrary Decision (AD)' is characterized by no discussion with officials before the king orders, approves, or rejects a matter.

Must locate and use the section (or subsection) where the three ruling style categories are formally defined and exemplified, rather than inferring the categories from other parts of the paper such as results or corpus description sections.

decisions: Does the paper investigate whether different Joseon kings exhibit different kinds of leadership (ruling) styles based on the Annals corpus?

requirements.description: Must identify that the paper defines and analyzes 'ruling styles' or 'leadership styles' of kings as a primary research focus, as stated in the abstract.
Must state that the study compares multiple kings' ruling styles, explicitly referencing that twenty-five kings are compared, as mentioned in the abstract.
Must indicate that leadership or ruling styles are inferred from the written records in the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty corpus, not from external biographical sources.
Must reference the part of the paper where three categories of monarchial ruling styles are defined, as described in the abstract, as the conceptual basis for 'different kinds of leadership styles'.

Must connect the research question about different kinds of leadership styles to variation across topics within the corpus, as indicated by the investigation of how kings show different ruling styles for various topics.

decisions: According to the paper’s results comparing kings, how are the tyrant kings Yeonsangun and Gwanghaegun characterized in terms of their AD metric values?

requirements.description: Must identify that Yeonsangun and Gwanghaegun are explicitly categorized as 'tyrants' among the Joseon kings in the paper.
Must retrieve from the relevant results figure or table that the AD metric is reported per king and that Yeonsangun and Gwanghaegun have higher AD values than most or all other kings.

Must correctly interpret AD as one of the quantitative ruling-style measures defined in the paper (e.g., an index or score derived from the Annals text) rather than introducing a different or new meaning for AD.
Must use information from the results or analysis section that compares ruling-style metrics across the twenty-five kings, rather than from introductory or background text.

Must explicitly state that the key empirical finding is that the tyrant kings (Yeonsangun, Gwanghaegun) show a high value of AD, matching the wording or quantitative implication of the paper’s reported results.

decisions: What factors are related to kings' leadership styles in the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty corpus?

requirements.description: Must identify that the paper defines and analyzes different 'ruling styles' or 'leadership styles' of Joseon kings based on the written records in the Annals corpus.

Must state that the leadership styles are inferred from textual features or topics extracted from the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty (i.e., leadership is operationalized via text analysis of the corpus).
Must indicate that the study compares multiple kings (specifically the twenty-five kings of the Joseon monarchy) in terms of their ruling or leadership styles.
Must mention that the analysis examines how kings' ruling or leadership styles vary across different topics within the corpus (i.e., leadership is related to topical dimensions of the records).

Must reference or implicitly rely on the part of the paper that formulates research questions about factors related to kings' leadership or ruling styles (e.g., a 'Research Questions' or 'Introduction' section where this question is posed).

decisions: How does the paper’s topic-based analysis of the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty show differences between overall ruling styles and ruling styles within specific topics, particularly for King Injo and Sejong the Great in the ‘remission of sins’ topic?

requirements.description: Must identify that the paper explicitly compares monarchs’ overall ruling styles with their ruling styles conditioned on specific topics (i.e., a topic-based deviation from overall behavior).
Must retrieve that the paper defines and uses at least three ruling style categories (including DO and DF) and applies these categories both at the overall level and within individual topics.
Must state that in the 'remission of sins' topic, kings in general exhibit more DO-style actions compared to their overall ruling style distribution.

Must report that King Injo is characterized as a weak king overall and, within the 'remission of sins' topic, tends to show more DF-style behavior and to give more grants to servants than in his overall ruling style profile.
Must report that Sejong the Great is found to act in a DF style within the 'remission of sins' topic, as contrasted with the general trend of kings acting more DO in that topic.

decisions: How does the paper analyze the effects of different discussion participants, including agency officials who remonstrate to the king, by computing mutual information among monarchs’ ruling styles?

requirements.description: Must identify that the paper analyzes the effects of different participants in royal discussions (e.g., king, officials, remonstrating agencies) on the characterization of monarchial ruling styles.
Must state that the paper computes mutual information among the defined ruling styles as a quantitative measure of their relationships or dependencies.
Must specify that one focal group of participants are agency officials whose role is to remonstrate or offer corrective advice to the king.

Must reference the specific results or analysis section where the effects of discussion participants on ruling styles are examined (e.g., a subsection devoted to discussion participants or remonstrating officials).
Must retrieve any figure, table, or quantitative summary (if present) that reports mutual information values or comparisons among ruling styles in the context of different discussion participants.

decisions: How does the paper characterize and compare the temporal evolution of ruling styles for the kings Yeonsangun and Injo in its results?

requirements.description: Must identify that Yeonsangun and Injo are explicitly contrasted as example kings representing different ruling styles, with Yeonsangun labeled as a 'tyrant' and Injo labeled as a 'weak king' in the paper's results or discussion of ruling styles.

Must state that the analysis involves examining temporal changes in a single king's ruling style over time (i.e., a 'temporal difference of a king'), rather than only static, aggregate comparisons across all kings.
Must report the directional temporal trend for Yeonsangun specifically as becoming more arbitrary in his ruling style over time, as described in the results section or corresponding analysis.
Must report that Injo's ruling style is characterized as remaining consistent over time, with no major temporal shift in style, as described in the results section or corresponding analysis.

Must draw these characterizations (Yeonsangun as increasingly arbitrary, Injo as consistent, and their labels 'tyrant' and 'weak king') from the paper's results/analysis portion where temporal ruling-style patterns are discussed, not from unrelated background or corpus-introduction text.

decisions: Does the system correctly summarize the paper’s main conclusions about the Annals corpus and the analysis of kings’ leadership styles and their relationships to other factors?

requirements.description: Must state that the study introduces or presents the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty as the central corpus being analyzed.
Must describe the Annals corpus as a long, large-scale set of historical documents (e.g., multi-century, extensive daily records), not just a generic text collection.
Must indicate that the Annals corpus used in the study is a translated and annotated version of the original records (i.e., explicitly mention both translation and annotation).
Must mention that the authors quantitatively measure or define kings’ leadership or ruling styles based on the corpus (e.g., three categories of monarchial ruling styles or similar formalization).

Must report that the study analyzes or investigates relationships between kings’ ruling/leadership styles and at least two of the following factors: topics, members (e.g., officials or actors), and time.

decisions: What research problem does the paper define regarding mental illness detection on Twitter and the role of demographic and personality-based features?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper frames mental illnesses (specifically including depression and PTSD) as being highly underdiagnosed globally, as described in the abstract.

Must identify that the paper's central goal is to explore the predictive power of language-derived demographic and personality features for distinguishing users disclosing a mental illness diagnosis from random controls, as specified in the abstract.

Must explicitly mention that demographic and personality information is not self-reported but estimated from language use ("language-derived personality and demographic estimates") as described in the abstract.

Must reference that these language-derived demographic and personality estimates achieve an AUC of around 0.8 in distinguishing diagnosed users from controls, as reported in the abstract, to justify that these features have meaningful predictive power.

Must extract the problem formulation elements from the paper's introductory/problem motivation content (e.g., the abstract and introduction) that jointly describe underdiagnosis, the use of Twitter data, and the focus on demographic and personality-based features.

decisions: What key dataset characteristics does the paper report about Twitter users who disclose a diagnosis of depression?

requirements.description: Must identify that the dataset includes Twitter users who explicitly self-disclose a mental illness diagnosis using first-person statements such as 'I have been diagnosed with depression'.
Must state that the target group in the dataset specifically consists of users diagnosed with depression (not only PTSD or other conditions).
Must report the average number of messages (tweets) per user in the dataset as approximately 3,400 messages per user, using the numeric value given in the paper.
Must extract these details from the paper's dataset or data collection description (e.g., the section describing how Twitter users and their tweets were collected and filtered).

decisions: How does the study use age, gender, and personality information in relation to mental illness indication on Twitter?

requirements.description: Must state that the study investigates mental illness indication (e.g., depression or PTSD diagnosis disclosure) using Twitter data.
Must specify that age is treated as a language-derived demographic estimate used as a feature in distinguishing users with disclosed mental illness from controls.
Must specify that gender is treated as a language-derived demographic estimate used as a feature in distinguishing users with disclosed mental illness from controls.
Must specify that personality traits are inferred from language (language-derived personality estimates) and used as features in distinguishing users with disclosed mental illness from controls.
Must identify and draw from the part of the paper that describes the study setup or experimental design where age, gender, and personality are introduced as predictors of mental illness indication.

decisions: Does the paper describe using an age and gender prediction model trained on Facebook and Twitter data for analyzing users who tweet about mental illnesses?

requirements.description: Must state that age and gender are not self-reported in the Twitter dataset and therefore must be inferred or estimated automatically from text or profile information.
Must identify that the paper uses a pre-existing or externally trained predictive model to infer age and gender, rather than training a new model solely on the mental-illness Twitter data.
Must explicitly mention that this age/gender prediction model was trained (or developed) using both Facebook and Twitter data, or a combined social media corpus that includes Facebook and Twitter.

Must locate and use information from the section that describes demographic inference or user attribute prediction (e.g., a section detailing how age and gender are estimated), not just from the abstract.

Must, if present, reference any figure or table that summarizes the performance or description of the age/gender prediction model (e.g., a table of accuracy or AUC for age/gender classification), and connect it to the use of a model trained on Facebook and Twitter data.

decisions: According to the paper, how do the personality traits of Twitter users disclosing depression or PTSD differ from controls, after controlling for age and gender?

requirements.description: Must state that users disclosing a mental illness (depression or PTSD) are characterized as higher on neuroticism compared to control users.
Must state that users disclosing a mental illness are characterized as more introverted (i.e., lower on extraversion) compared to control users.
Must state that users disclosing a mental illness are characterized as less agreeable compared to control users.
Must explicitly mention that these personality differences are reported after statistically controlling for (or holding constant) age and gender.

Must extract these personality trait findings from the specific part of the paper that reports language-derived personality estimates for mental-illness-disclosing users versus controls (e.g., the results or analysis section discussing Big Five traits).

decisions: According to the paper, what does the affective analysis reveal about arousal and positivity levels in tweets from mentally ill users compared to controls, based on a model trained on 3000 users?

requirements.description: Must state that the affective model or analysis was trained on approximately 3000 mentally ill Twitter users (e.g., a sample size of 3000 users disclosing mental illness).
Must explicitly state that mentally ill users are characterized as less aroused in their language compared to a control or reference group, based on the paper's affective analysis.

Must explicitly state that mentally ill users are characterized as less positive (lower positivity or valence) in their language compared to a control or reference group, based on the paper's affective analysis.

Must identify that the affective conclusions (less aroused and less positive) are derived from an affect or emotion/valence-arousal modeling approach applied to users' tweets, not from personality or demographic models alone.
Must attribute the findings about lower arousal and positivity specifically to the group of users disclosing mental illness (e.g., depression or PTSD) rather than to the random control users.

decisions: How does the paper describe the LIWC resource used in the analysis of Twitter language about mental illnesses?

requirements.description: Must identify LIWC as a set of standard, psychologically inspired dictionaries used for linguistic analysis in the paper.
Must state that LIWC consists of 64 categories, matching the number explicitly given in the paper.
Must specify that LIWC categories include parts-of-speech, topical categories, and emotion-related categories, as described in the paper.
Must describe LIWC's role as a standard baseline feature set for open-vocabulary or open-vocabulary-style approaches in the study's methodology.

decisions: How does the paper describe the topic modeling features (number of topics and feature dimensionalities) derived from social media status updates for use alongside the personality model?

requirements.description: Must identify that Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) is the topic modeling method used to derive topic features from social media status updates.
Must state that the LDA model is trained on the same underlying set of Facebook status updates as the data used for the personality model.
Must report that the total number of LDA topics used in the paper is 2000.
Must specify that the paper considers three different topic-based feature dimensionalities: 7 features, 64 features, and 2000 features.

Must extract the above LDA and feature-dimension details from the section where the paper describes its feature representation or topic modeling setup (e.g., data, features, or methodology section), not infer them from unrelated parts.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify that the paper’s topic analysis of depression tweets is performed while statistically controlling for users’ age and gender?

requirements.description: Must state that the topic analysis related to depression is conducted with age and gender treated as control variables (i.e., topics are analyzed net of age and gender effects).
Must identify the specific methodological step or model specification in which age and gender are included as covariates or control variables in the topic analysis of depression-related tweets.
Must reference the section or subsection where the paper describes controlling for demographic variables (age and gender) in the topic modeling or topic-based analysis of depression users.
Must retrieve any table, figure, or reported result where depression-related topics are presented with an explicit note that age and gender have been controlled for in the analysis.
Must indicate that the reported depression topic findings are interpreted as effects or patterns after adjusting for age and gender, not raw unadjusted topic distributions.

decisions: How does the paper describe the topic modeling analysis for PTSD when controlling for age and gender?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper includes a topic analysis or topic modeling specifically for PTSD-related tweets (as distinct from depression or controls).
Must explain that the topic analysis for PTSD is conducted while statistically controlling for, or conditioning on, user age and gender.

Must reference the specific part of the paper where PTSD topics are presented (e.g., a subsection on 'PTSD topics', 'Topic modeling for PTSD', or similar) rather than a general or combined topic analysis.

Must identify any figure or table (e.g., 'Figure X' or 'Table Y') that presents PTSD topics with age and gender controlled, if such a visual element exists, and explicitly link it to the PTSD topic analysis.

Must retrieve and report that the PTSD topic results are derived from a model or analysis where age and gender are included as covariates or controlled variables, not from a raw, uncontrolled topic distribution.

decisions: How does the paper operationalize and compare classification tasks using demographic and personality-derived features (gender, age, and related traits) for distinguishing depressed, PTSD, and control Twitter users, as reflected in the '1–3 grams' slide?

requirements.description: Must identify that the study involves three distinct user-group comparison tasks: (1) Depressed vs. Control, (2) PTSD vs. Control, and (3) Depressed vs. PTSD, as explicitly defined in the paper when setting up classification experiments.

Must retrieve from the methods or experimental setup section that language-derived demographic and personality estimates (including at least gender and age) are used as predictive features for the classification tasks.

Must extract from the results (e.g., a table or reported metrics) that these language-derived demographic/personality features achieve an AUC of approximately 0.8 for distinguishing users who disclose depression or PTSD from random controls.

Must cover the part of the paper that describes how demographic variables (specifically gender and age) are inferred from Twitter language, including any referenced model or resource (e.g., the World Well-Being Project or similar) used to derive these estimates.

Must identify and describe any figure or table that jointly presents the three classification comparisons (Depressed vs. Control, PTSD vs. Control, Depressed vs. PTSD) alongside demographic/personality features (including gender and age), which the slide text summarizes.

decisions: What additional feature types and modeling approach does the paper describe for mental illness detection in the CLPsych 2015 Shared Task?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper uses multiple types of word cluster features, explicitly mentioning that they are 'different word clusters' used as features for mental illness detection.
Must identify all four specific clustering/embedding approaches used for word clusters as listed in the paper: Brown clustering, NPMI Spectral clustering, Word2Vec embeddings, and GloVe embeddings.

Must describe the classification model as a linear ensemble of logistic regression classifiers, using the same terminology ('linear ensemble of logistic regression classifiers') that appears in the paper.

Must correctly associate these features and model with the system built for the CLPsych 2015 Shared Task on mental illness detection, explicitly referencing the CLPsych 2015 Shared Task or its mental illness detection task as named in the paper.
Must retrieve and list the four authors' names exactly as given in the paper for this system description: D. Preotiuc-Pietro, M. Sap, H.A. Schwartz, and L. Ungar.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the paper’s main take-home findings about controlling for demographics, the role of personality, and the linguistic signals of depression/PTSD on Twitter?

requirements.description: Must state that the analysis explicitly controls for (or accounts for) both age and gender when examining mental illness–related tweeting behavior.
Must state that personality characteristics (e.g., language-derived personality traits) play an important or significant role in distinguishing users with depression/PTSD from controls.
Must indicate that personality, age, and gender are derived or estimated from users' language use on Twitter rather than from self-reported survey data.
Must state that the language use of users with depression or PTSD reveals or reflects symptoms, emotions, and cognitive processes associated with these mental illnesses.

Must mention that language-derived personality and demographic estimates achieve strong predictive performance (around AUC ≈ 0.8) in distinguishing diagnosed depression/PTSD users from random controls.

decisions: Does the slide correctly illustrate a machine reading comprehension example and enumerate common MRC task types as described in the paper?

requirements.description: Must state that the example is about machine reading comprehension (MRC) on a passage, explicitly indicating that a system reads a passage and answers a question based on it.
Must include a concrete question-answer pair derived from the passage, where the question asks what Tesla blamed for the loss of the initial money and the answer is 'Panic of 1901'.

Must reproduce or closely paraphrase the example passage text mentioning Tesla approaching Morgan for more funds, the query about where the money had gone, and Tesla's response that he was affected by the Panic of 1901.
Must explicitly connect the question to the passage by indicating that the answer span 'Panic of 1901' is taken directly from the passage text (i.e., a span-extraction style example).
Must list the different MRC task types as given in the slide: cloze test, entity extraction, span extraction, and multiple-choice, in a single grouped enumeration.

decisions: Does the system correctly retrieve and present the multi-passage web snippets needed to answer the question 'how many teams will be in the 2022 world cup?' including the key 'Teams: 32' fact and related contextual passages?

requirements.description: Must include the user question text about the 2022 World Cup team count, specifically the string 'how many teams will be in the 2022 world cup?'.
Must retrieve from the '2022 FIFA World Cup - Wikipedia' passage the line containing the team count, specifically the substring 'Teams: 32 (from 5 or 6 confederations)'.

Must include at least one additional passage beyond the main 2022 World Cup article, specifically a snippet from '2018 FIFA World Cup qualification - Wikipedia' mentioning 'Teams: 210 (from 6 confederations)'.
Must preserve the source titles for each passage, explicitly including the strings '2022 FIFA World Cup - Wikipedia' and '2018 FIFA World Cup qualification - Wikipedia'.
Must include the third source mentioning the alternative team-count scenario, specifically a snippet whose title begins with 'Qataris considering a 48-team option for 2022 World Cup - The'.

decisions: How does the paper’s multi-passage MRC model use cross-passage answer verification to identify and label correct, partially correct, and incorrect answer candidates for the MS MARCO question 'What is the difference between a mixed and pure culture?'

requirements.description: Must state that the example comes from the MS MARCO dataset and is used to illustrate multi-passage machine reading comprehension with cross-passage answer verification, explicitly linking the example question to the paper’s main task setting (multi-passage MRC).

Must describe that multiple answer candidates (e.g., options 1, 2, 4, 5, 6) are extracted from different passages and then compared against each other using their content representations in a cross-passage answer verification module, as defined in the paper’s model description.

Must explain that the model assigns correctness labels to each candidate answer (e.g., '@ Incorrect', '= Partially Correct', '= Correct') based on the cross-passage verification scores or predictions, as described in the paper’s answer verification or prediction component.

Must draw on the section of the paper that presents the MS MARCO case study or qualitative example (where the question 'What is the difference between a mixed and pure culture?' appears) rather than only using abstract or general model descriptions.

Must indicate that the model leverages semantic similarity or agreement between passages to identify that candidates explicitly defining 'pure culture' as a single species/strain and 'mixed culture' as multiple species/strains are treated as correct or verifiable answers, in contrast to off-topic candidates (e.g., about acculture or mixed economy).

decisions: How does the proposed multi-passage MRC model perform end-to-end answer prediction and cross-passage answer verification to produce a final answer?

requirements.description: Must state that the model is an end-to-end neural architecture for multi-passage machine reading comprehension that jointly handles answer extraction from each passage and cross-passage answer verification.
Must describe that for each passage, the model predicts start and end positions of answer spans (e.g., probabilities P(start) and P(end) per passage) as the basis for generating candidate answers.
Must explain that the model constructs content representations for each candidate answer ("Answer Content Modeling") that are used to compare and verify candidates across different passages.
Must state that the verified candidates are combined via a learned weighting or scoring mechanism across passages to produce a single final prediction ("weighted Final Answer" or equivalent).

Must reference the model overview figure/diagram that shows multiple passages (Passage 1, Passage 2, ..., Passage n), their associated answer candidates, per-passage start/end predictions, and the final aggregation into one final answer.

decisions: What does the paper define as the basic input structure for its multi-passage machine reading comprehension model?

requirements.description: Must state that the model input consists of a natural language question together with multiple passages, not a single passage.
Must identify and use the part of the paper where the input or problem formulation for multi-passage MRC is defined (e.g., the formal task definition or model input description section).
Must describe that individual passages are treated as separate input units (e.g., Passage 1, Passage 2, ...), rather than concatenated into one long text segment.

Must reference any figure or diagram in the paper that explicitly depicts the input as a combination of a question and multiple passages (e.g., a schematic showing 'Question' alongside 'Passage 1', 'Passage 2').
Must indicate that multiple passages are retrieved (e.g., by a search engine) and then fed as separate inputs to the model for answer prediction or verification.

decisions: How does the model in 'Multi-Passage Machine Reading Comprehension with Cross-Passage Answer Verification' encode the question and multiple passages before answer verification?

requirements.description: Must state that both the question and each passage (including multiple passages such as Passage 1, Passage 2, …, Passage n) are encoded into vector representations as the first step of the model.
Must specify that a Bi-LSTM (bidirectional LSTM) is the neural architecture used to encode the question and passages into contextual representations.
Must draw from the model description / encoding subsection (the part of the paper that explains question encoding and passage encoding) rather than from training, loss, or experimental sections.

Must reflect any figure or diagram (if present) that depicts the question and multiple passages being fed into a shared Bi-LSTM encoder, including the notion of multiple passages (1…n) arranged in parallel.

Must mention that the encoding step produces hidden states or vectors (e.g., Y, v, or similar notation used in the paper) that serve as inputs to later answer prediction or cross-passage verification modules.

decisions: How does the paper model question–passage matching across multiple passages using bi-directional attention flow representations?

requirements.description: Must identify that the paper defines a question–passage matching component that computes representations for each passage conditioned on the question (often denoted as u^P or similar notation in the text/equations).
Must state that the question–passage matching is implemented using a Bi-directional Attention Flow mechanism (or equivalent term explicitly used in the paper) between the question and each passage.

Must reference the specific figure or diagram in the paper that illustrates the question and multiple passages (Passage 1, Passage 2, ..., Passage n) being processed with bi-directional attention flow to produce passage-level representations (e.g., u^P).

Must explain that the same question–passage matching / Bi-directional Attention Flow module is applied to each of the n passages independently (i.e., Passage 1 through Passage n all use the same mechanism to obtain u^P representations).

Must draw the description of question–passage matching and Bi-directional Attention Flow from the model architecture / methodology section where the paper formally defines the passage representation u^P (or its equivalent notation) and its computation.

decisions: How does the proposed multi-passage MRC model perform answer boundary prediction over multiple passages using start and end pointers?

requirements.description: Must state that the model predicts answer boundaries in each passage using start and end pointers (i.e., a pointer-based span prediction mechanism for answer extraction).
Must describe that answer boundary prediction is applied independently to each of multiple passages (e.g., Passage 1, Passage 2, ..., Passage n) given the same question.

Must reference the architectural component or figure in the paper that depicts the question together with multiple passages (Passage 1 to Passage n) feeding into a start/end pointer module for span selection.
Must cover the part of the model description section that formally defines the computation of start and end scores (or probabilities) over token positions for answer boundary prediction.

Must mention how the content representations of question and passages are used as input to the start and end pointer mechanism (e.g., via encoded contextual representations over which boundary scores are computed).

decisions: How does the paper define and compute content-based scores for candidate answers across multiple passages in its answer content modeling component?

requirements.description: Must identify that the paper introduces an 'answer content modeling' (or equivalently named) component/module that assigns a content-based score to each candidate answer aggregated over multiple passages.

Must describe that the content score for each candidate answer is computed using its content representation derived from all supporting passages (e.g., by encoding answer spans from Passage 1, Passage 2, ... Passage n and aggregating them).

Must reference the specific figure or diagram in the paper that visually depicts the question with multiple passages (Passage 1, Passage 2, ... Passage n) and arrows or connections leading to content scores for each candidate answer (e.g., Answer A, Answer A2).

Must state that the model jointly considers multiple answer candidates from different passages and uses their content representations to verify or compare them when computing the final content scores.

Must draw from the section that formally defines the answer content modeling or answer verification module (e.g., the subsection describing cross-passage answer verification or content-based scoring), not from unrelated background or experimental sections.

decisions: What is the role and mechanism of cross-passage answer verification in the proposed multi-passage machine reading comprehension model?

requirements.description: Must state that the model introduces a cross-passage answer verification mechanism where answer candidates from different passages verify each other based on their content representations, as described in the abstract and main model description section.

Must describe that the approach is an end-to-end neural model jointly training three modules (including an answer verification module) to predict the final answer, referencing the main methodology/model architecture section where these modules are defined.

Must explain that the verification operates over multiple passages retrieved by a search engine for a single question, explicitly contrasting this multi-passage setting with single-passage MRC as discussed in the problem formulation/introduction section.

Must retrieve at least one quantitative result (e.g., EM/F1 or similar metric) from the experiments section showing that adding cross-passage answer verification improves performance over a baseline without verification.

Must reference the specific subsection (e.g., 'Cross-Passage Answer Verification' or equivalent) that formally defines the verification module, including how answer candidates are represented and compared across passages (e.g., via learned representations or attention-based scoring).

decisions: How does the proposed multi-passage MRC model jointly train its components and compute the final answer score during joint prediction?

requirements.description: Must state that the model performs three joint prediction subtasks: (1) finding the boundary of the answer span, (2) predicting whether each word should be included in the answer (content prediction), and (3) selecting the best answer from all candidate answers across passages (answer verification/selection).

Must describe that the training objective is a joint loss composed as a sum of three components corresponding to the three modules, i.e., a boundary loss term, a content loss term, and a verification/selection loss term (e.g., L_joint = L_boundary + L_content + L_verify, possibly with scalar weights).

Must explain that the final answer score for each candidate is computed by combining three scores from the respective modules—boundary score, content score, and verification score—using a multiplicative formulation (e.g., Score = S_boundary × S_content × S_verify or an equivalent product of three module scores).

Must draw from the specific section of the paper that describes joint training and prediction (the part where the authors define the combined loss function and the final scoring function for candidate answers), not from unrelated sections such as dataset description or related work.

Must indicate that the answer selection step operates over multiple passages by comparing or verifying candidate answers across passages, rather than selecting from candidates within a single passage only.

decisions: How does the paper describe the experimental setup, specifically the datasets used and the hyper-parameter configuration?

requirements.description: Must cover the dedicated 'Experiments' or 'Experimental Setup' section where the authors describe datasets and training configurations.
Must identify that the experimental evaluation is conducted on two multi-passage MRC datasets: MS-MARCO and DuReader, as explicitly named in the experiments section.

Must retrieve from the experiments section the characterization of MS-MARCO as a search-based question answering dataset with multiple passages per question and multiple annotated answers or answer spans (as described in the paper).

Must retrieve from the experiments section the characterization of DuReader as a Chinese search-based MRC dataset with multiple passages per question and multiple annotated answers or answer spans (as described in the paper).

Must extract the subsection or paragraph in the experiments section that lists hyper-parameters, including the use of GloVe word embeddings and the initialization scheme for other parameters (e.g., random initialization), and state that these hyper-parameters are tuned on the development set.

decisions: What does Table 1 report about the model’s performance on the MS-MARCO test set in the paper 'Multi-Passage Machine Reading Comprehension with Cross-Passage Answer Verification'?

requirements.description: Must identify and use the specific table explicitly titled or captioned as 'Table 1' in the paper.
Must confirm from the table caption that Table 1 reports 'Performance on MS-MARCO test set' (or an exact equivalent phrase indicating MS-MARCO test-set performance).
Must recognize that the metrics in Table 1 evaluate the proposed multi-passage MRC model with cross-passage answer verification on the MS-MARCO dataset, not a different dataset.
Must retrieve Table 1 from the paper’s Results/Experiments section where MS-MARCO test-set performance is reported, rather than from any other section (e.g., introduction or related work).
Must preserve the table label and caption structure when generating the slide text, including the table index ('Table 1' or 'Tab 1') and the phrase 'Performance on MS-MARCO test set'.

decisions: How does the model quantitatively analyze and relate boundary, content, and verification scores for answer candidates in a multi-passage MRC example?

requirements.description: Must identify that the slide illustrates the relationship between three types of scores for answer candidates: boundary scores, content scores, and cross-passage verification scores, and that these scores are described in the paper as being usually positively correlated/relevant.

Must retrieve from the paper the definition or description of the cross-passage answer verification module, specifically that it computes verification scores for answer candidates based on their content representations across multiple passages.

Must cover the section (or subsection) in the paper where quantitative analysis of predicted scores is presented, including any example or case study that analyzes boundary, content, and verification scores for individual answer candidates.

Must describe the figure or example in the paper that shows a concrete question and multiple passages/answer candidates with associated numerical scores (e.g., boundary/content/verification), which the slide instantiates with the 'What is the difference between a mixed and pure culture' example.

Must retrieve the numeric pattern from the paper’s quantitative example that boundary, content, and verification scores for correct answer candidates are relatively high and mutually consistent, and that this pattern is used to support the statement that these scores are usually positively relevant.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and explain why a separate content model is necessary in addition to start/end boundary prediction for long answers in multi-passage MRC?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper distinguishes between boundary-based answer prediction (start and end probabilities) and a separate content-based probability that evaluates internal answer tokens.

Must describe that the baseline span prediction model uses only start probability and end probability over passage positions to select an answer span, without considering a separate content probability.

Must explain that the proposed content model assigns a content probability to each token within the candidate answer span, in addition to start and end probabilities, to better capture answer semantics.

Must mention the specific rationale given in the paper that when the answer span is long, boundary words (start/end tokens) carry little information about the true semantics of the answer, motivating the content model.

Must reference the figure or diagram in the paper that visually contrasts a model using only start/end probabilities with one that also includes content probability for each token in the answer span (i.e., a schematic showing 'start probability', 'end probability', and 'content probability').

decisions: Does the system correctly retrieve and summarize the paper’s visualization of the start and end answer probability distributions over content tokens in the multi-passage MRC model?

requirements.description: Must state that the visualization depicts probability distributions over answer span positions, specifically separate start and end probabilities assigned to tokens in the content.

Must identify and describe the specific figure (or subfigure) that visualizes the probability distribution over content tokens, including that it has axes or labels corresponding to 'content', 'start probability', and 'end probability'.

Must explain that the probabilities shown in the visualization are produced by the model’s answer prediction module (e.g., pointer or span predictor) applied over the concatenated or per-passage token sequence.

Must reference the section of the paper where the probability distribution visualization is introduced (e.g., the model description or analysis/visualization subsection) and use information from that section to describe what is being visualized.

Must mention any interpretive point the paper makes about the visualization (e.g., how the distribution highlights the most likely answer span or contrasts multiple candidate spans across passages) as described in the text accompanying the figure.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the paper’s main contributions and findings in the conclusion regarding multi-passage MRC and the proposed end-to-end model?

requirements.description: Must state that multi-passage machine reading comprehension (MRC) produces more misleading or confusing answers compared to single-passage MRC, as described in the problem motivation section of the paper.
Must describe that the proposed approach is an end-to-end neural model specifically designed for multi-passage MRC, as characterized in the model overview or introduction of the method section.

Must identify and mention three distinct functional modules of the model: (1) a module to find or predict the answer boundary (span extraction), (2) a module to model the answer content (content representation/scoring), and (3) a cross-passage answer verification module, as defined in the model architecture section.
Must state that these modules are trained jointly in a single framework (joint training) and used together for final answer prediction, as specified in the training or learning objective subsection.

Must report that the proposed model achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance on two datasets constructed from real-world web data, as indicated in the experimental results or conclusion section (including the fact that there are exactly two such datasets).

decisions: Does the summary correctly identify and present the main introductory aims and design choices of the Linear A/Minoan digital corpus as described in the paper?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper describes the Linear A/Minoan digital corpus and the approaches or methods applied to develop it, using terminology equivalent to the abstract's focus on 'Linear A/Minoan digital corpus' and 'approaches we applied to develop it'.
Must explicitly mention that the corpus is implemented or encoded using XML-TEI EpiDoc, and that the paper provides reasons or justification for choosing XML-TEI EpiDoc for the Linear A corpus.
Must cover the paper's motivation for developing a Linear A corpus, i.e., the stated aim to set up a suitable study resource for Linear A and Minoan, and present this as a 'why' or rationale section.

Must identify and summarize the description of available resources for Linear A/Minoan and the corpus developing process (e.g., data sources, digitization steps, encoding workflow) as presented in the paper.
Must state that the Linear A corpus is framed or presented as part of cultural heritage (e.g., treating Linear A inscriptions as cultural heritage objects or resources) as described in the paper.

decisions: Does the summary correctly describe the relationship between Linear A, Linear B, and the Minoan civilization as presented in the paper for the introductory slide?

requirements.description: Must state that the Linear A script was used by the Minoan civilization on Crete in the approximate period 2500–1450 BC and that it remains undeciphered, as described in the paper's introductory/background discussion of Linear A.

Must explain that many symbols are shared by both Linear A and Linear B and that these shared symbols are assumed to have phonetic values, while the remaining Linear A symbols are probably logograms, following the paper's description of symbol types and values.
Must mention that Linear B has been deciphered (in the 1950s) and identified as writing an Ancient Greek dialect, as reported in the paper's historical/linguistic background on Linear B.

Must state that, because Linear B is deciphered and shares symbols with Linear A, many scholars are attempting to decipher Linear A, reflecting the motivation for the Linear A/Minoan digital corpus described in the paper.

Must reference or reproduce the paper's tabular or illustrative presentation that contrasts Linear A/B shared symbols with Linear A-only symbols and labels their 'value', 'syllable', and 'logogram' roles (e.g., a table or figure aligning Linear A/B, Linear A symbols, and their functional category).

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the paper’s stated lack of existing digital resources for Linear A and the resulting motivation for creating a new digital corpus?

requirements.description: Must state that, according to the paper, no deciphering attempts for Linear A have been successful even after decades of research.
Must state that the paper explicitly notes that no heavy or large-scale computational approaches have yet been applied to Linear A.
Must identify John G. Younger as the only person or source mentioned in the paper as providing a complete digital collection of Linear A inscriptions.
Must describe the limitations of Younger’s resource as given in the paper: that it is stored in two simple HTML pages, lacks a strict structure, and is transcribed only as transliterations.
Must report that the paper motivates the creation of a new Linear A digital corpus by stating that a well-organized corpus in a suitable format would be a useful study resource.

decisions: Which existing external resources for Linear A/Minoan inscriptions and corpora does the paper identify as available and relevant for building the Linear A Digital Corpus?

requirements.description: Must identify that the paper explicitly lists existing external resources for Linear A/Minoan as part of the motivation or background for the Linear A Digital Corpus.
Must retrieve and name the 'GORILA' paper collection specifically as a resource of inscriptions and transcriptions (e.g., 'GORILA paper collection of inscriptions and transcriptions').
Must retrieve and name 'John G. Younger' (or 'John G. Youngers website') explicitly as a web-based resource for Linear A inscriptions.
Must retrieve and name the 'Petrolito, Winterstein, Perono Cacciafoco Linear A Corpus' explicitly as a corpus resource, including the date '30 July 2015' if present in the paper.

Must base the list of resources on the specific part of the paper where available/previous Linear A or Minoan resources are enumerated (e.g., a section or subsection describing existing corpora or tools), not infer or add resources not mentioned there.

decisions: What are the main components and indexing features of the Linear A/Minoan digital corpus described in the paper?

requirements.description: Must state that the corpus includes a catalog of symbols associated with numeric codes for the Linear A script.
Must specify that the documents in the corpus are indexed with information about their original place of discovery and the type of support (material/medium).
Must mention that the indexing scheme for documents (place and support) is based on or originally defined by Pope & Raison.
Must indicate that each indexed document entry includes descriptive information together with pictures and/or drawings of the inscriptions.
Must note that the corpus provides handmade transcriptions of the documents as part of the document descriptions.

decisions: What specific resources and quantitative details about John G. Younger’s Linear A website does the paper provide that are needed to describe its structure and coverage in the digital corpus slide?

requirements.description: Must state that John G. Younger's Linear A website is organized into two HTML pages, explicitly distinguishing one page for Haghia Triadas documents and another page for all other places of origin.
Must report the exact number of transcriptions available on John G. Younger's website as 1,077 and indicate that they include Linear B phonetics and GORILA code numbers.
Must specify that the 1,077 transcriptions correspond to 75.5% of the total amount of existing documents listed in GORILA, including the percentage value and its relation to GORILA.
Must mention the existence of a conversion table on or derived from John G. Younger's website that maps GORILA code numbers to syllables.
Must identify the bibliographic or attribution information linking this resource to the Linear A Corpus work by Petrolito, Winterstein, and Perono Cacciafoco, including the date 30 July 2015.

decisions: How does the paper describe the conversion of the Linear A corpus from Younger's syllable transcription and GORILA codes to Unicode, including scope and timeline?

requirements.description: Must state that a Unicode set of characters specifically for Linear A was released in June 2014, matching the month and year.
Must report that exactly 1,077 documents from Younger's website are involved in the conversion process.

Must describe that the documents were automatically converted from a syllable transcription (which coexists with GORILA code numbers for symbols not included in Linear B) to a full GORILA code numbers transcription.
Must state that there is a subsequent conversion step from GORILA code numbers to Unicode for Linear A characters.
Must identify the part of the paper that attributes the Linear A corpus work to Petrolito, Winterstein, and Perono Cacciafoco and associates it with the date 30 July 2015.

decisions: How does the paper describe the ways in which separation between sign groups is indicated in the Linear A digital corpus, and how is this illustrated with a concrete example line?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper identifies exactly two main ways in which separation between sign groups is indicated in Linear A inscriptions.
Must explain that one of the main separation methods is isolating sign groups with numbers or logograms, which implies a separation between adjacent sign groups.
Must mention that dots between sign groups are used as a separation device, and that they are always used when there are long strings of sign groups.
Must reference the example Linear A line presented in the paper/slide as an illustration of segmentation issues (i.e., an explicit example line is shown to demonstrate separation).

Must report that in the example, a specific sign is interpreted as a number (assumed to be the number 5), and that this numeric interpretation leads to treating the adjacent elements as separated sign groups.

decisions: How does the paper describe the chosen corpus data format and its relation to existing epigraphic standards and practices?

requirements.description: Must state that XML is used as the corpus data format and that it provides advantages for metadata on several levels of annotation, including elements and entities for unsupported glyphs or symbols, using wording consistent with the slide text.
Must identify EpiDoc specifically as a TEI DTD (Document Type Definition) customized for epigraphy, as described in the paper's discussion of the corpus encoding standard.
Must cover the part of the paper that discusses the TEI/EpiDoc-based encoding framework, including the role of the TEI-using community in providing support and online best-practice examples.

Must explain the comparison between the old Leiden system annotation task and the XML TEI EpiDoc annotation process, explicitly stating that they are quite similar and that the former is familiar to epigraphers.

Must retrieve the bibliographic or authorship information associated with the corpus description (naming Petrolito, Winterstein, and Perono Cacciafoco) in connection with the Linear A Corpus and its data format.

decisions: What is the exact bibliographic header text used in the paper to label the 'Corpus data format example' slide?

requirements.description: Must identify that the slide text corresponds to a bibliographic/header line associated with the Linear A digital corpus rather than descriptive corpus content.
Must retrieve and reproduce the three author surnames exactly as they appear in the paper for this corpus resource: 'Petrolito, Winterstein, Perono Cacciafoco'.
Must retrieve and reproduce the corpus/project name exactly as it appears in the paper in this context: 'Linear A Corpus'.
Must retrieve and reproduce the full date string exactly as it appears in the paper in this context: '30 July 2015'.
Must locate and use the specific line in the paper where the authors, corpus name, and date are presented together as a single header or caption, not assembling them from separate unrelated sections.

decisions: How does the Linear A Digital Corpus specify and use glyph elements to represent unsupported characters in its TEI encoding?

requirements.description: Must state that unsupported characters are represented using TEI 'g' elements that refer to predefined glyph elements.
Must explain that glyph elements are defined inside the TEI header within the EncodingDesc>CharDecl section.
Must reference the part of the paper that describes the TEI encoding scheme for characters and glyphs (i.e., the EncodingDesc/CharDecl configuration), not a general description of the corpus.
Must explicitly mention that the purpose of these glyph and g elements is to handle or represent unsupported characters/glyphs in the corpus.
Must identify that the mechanism involves a link or reference from each 'g' element in the text to a corresponding glyph element defined in CharDecl.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the corpus size, sources, format, and processing status of the Linear A Digital Corpus as described in the paper?

requirements.description: Must state that the GORILA resource contains 1,427 Linear A documents, matching the numeric value and association with GORILA.
Must state that John G. Younger's website provides 1,077 Linear A transcriptions and explicitly indicate that this represents 75.5% of the total.
Must state that the planned Linear A corpus will contain up to 1,077 documents encoded as XML TEI EpiDoc documents.
Must explain that Unicode conversions of John G. Younger's transcriptions were converted into XML automatically, and that tagging of these XML documents has been only partially completed.
Must describe that the main remaining work, still in progress, is the manual checking of the data against the GORILA volumes.

decisions: What does the paper state about the limitations of existing Linear A fonts before Unicode 7.0 and the development and naming of the new John_Younger.ttf font?

requirements.description: Must state that before the release of Unicode 7.0 there was no way to properly visualize Linear A characters using standard Unicode encoding, as explicitly described in the paper.
Must state that the traditional Linear A font referred to as LA.ttf is described in the paper as having wrong (incorrect) Unicode positions for characters.
Must identify that the authors developed a new Linear A font as part of the corpus resources, explicitly named John_Younger.ttf in the paper.
Must explain that the font name John_Younger.ttf is explicitly motivated in the paper as a way to show appreciation for John Younger's work.

Must attribute the font-related information to the part of the paper that describes technical resources or implementation details of the Linear A digital corpus (e.g., the section discussing fonts or encoding), not to unrelated sections such as abstract or conclusions.

decisions: Does the summary correctly explain how the Linear A digital corpus informs our understanding of Minoan culture, specifically in economics/commerce and religion, as described in the paper?

requirements.description: Must state that the Linear A corpus is described in the paper as an important cultural monument that stores information about the tradition, knowledge, and lifestyle of Minoan people (using all three aspects: tradition, knowledge, lifestyle).

decisions: How does the ACE generator in Adversarial Contrastive Estimation learn to select negative examples, and what training framework is used?

requirements.description: Must state that selecting or picking a negative example in ACE is modeled as a discrete choice that is not directly differentiable.
Must identify that the ACE generator is trained using Policy Gradient methods, specifically naming the REINFORCE gradient estimator as the simplest or primary approach used.
Must describe that the negative sampler (ACE generator) participates in an adversarial learning setup where it seeks harder negatives for the main model.
Must explicitly characterize the training of the ACE generator and the main model as a GAN-style min-max game (adversarial objective between generator/sampler and main model).
Must extract these details from the part of the paper that introduces or defines the ACE generator (the adversarial negative sampler), not from unrelated background or results sections.

decisions: What specific training techniques does the paper propose to stabilize and improve adversarial contrastive estimation, particularly addressing mode collapse, false negatives, and high-variance gradients in the generator?

requirements.description: Must identify and describe the problem of GAN-style mode collapse in the adversarial negative sampler, specifically the case where the generator collapses onto a small set of its favorite negative examples.

Must explain the entropy regularization added to the generator's loss, explicitly mentioning that H(g(y|x)) is the entropy of the categorical distribution over k choices and that c = log(k) is the entropy of the uniform distribution used as a reference.

Must describe the two-step false-negative handling technique: (1) maintaining an in-memory hash map (or equivalent index) of the training data to detect false negatives, and (2) using the discriminator to filter out these false negatives while penalizing the generator when it produces them.

Must state that REINFORCE is used for training the generator, note that it has extremely high variance, and describe the use of a self-critical baseline (and possibly other baselines/gradient estimators) to reduce this variance.

Must explain that the generator is not directly learning from NCE samples under the basic setup and that importance sampling is introduced so the generator can leverage NCE samples for exploration in an off-policy scheme, including that the reward is modified accordingly.

decisions: Which contemporary GAN-based NLP methods does the paper identify as most closely related to its adversarial contrastive estimation approach?

requirements.description: Must identify that the discussed works are GAN-based methods applied to NLP that are described as being 'close to our work' or closely related to adversarial contrastive estimation.

Must retrieve content from the part of the paper corresponding to related or contemporary work (e.g., a 'Related Work' or similarly titled section) where GANs for NLP are compared to or positioned relative to the proposed method.

Must extract the reference to MaskGAN including both the method name 'MaskGAN' and the authorship/year attribution 'Fedus et al. 2018' as it appears in the paper's related work discussion or references.

Must extract the reference to 'Incorporating GAN for Negative Sampling in Knowledge Representation Learning' including the full method/paper title and the authorship/year attribution 'Wang et al. 2018' as it appears in the paper.
Must extract the reference to 'KBGAN' including the method name 'KBGAN' and the authorship/year attribution 'Cai and Wang 2017' as it appears in the paper.

decisions: Does the summary correctly describe how knowledge graph embeddings represent triplet data and the learning objective for link prediction as presented in the paper?

requirements.description: Must state that the knowledge graph data are represented as triplets of the form (head entity, relation, tail entity).
Must provide a concrete example of a triplet involving a country, a spatial relation, and an ocean, matching the structure of {United States of America, partially contained by ocean, Pacific}.

Must describe the basic embedding idea that the vector representations of head, relation, and tail are constrained to approximately satisfy a compositional relationship of the form h + r ≈ t (or equivalent notation indicating that h, r, t embeddings should 'roughly satisfy' a relation).
Must state that the learning uses observed positive entity–relation triplets as training data.
Must state that the goal of the learned embeddings is to predict missing links (i.e., infer missing entities or relations in the knowledge graph).

decisions: How does Adversarial Contrastive Estimation (ACE) generate negative triplets for knowledge graph embeddings in terms of which entity is corrupted and how the generator is parameterized?

requirements.description: Must state that a negative triplet for knowledge graph embeddings is formed by corrupting exactly one entity in a positive triplet, specifically either the head or the tail entity, while keeping the relation fixed.

Must identify that the ACE generator defines conditional distributions g(t | r+, h+) and g(h | r+, t+), i.e., one distribution for sampling a negative tail given a positive relation and head, and another for sampling a negative head given a positive relation and tail.
Must specify that the ACE generator g(·) used for sampling negative heads or tails is parameterized by a feed-forward neural network (not, for example, by a lookup table or recurrent network).

Must retrieve this information from the part of the paper that describes applying ACE to knowledge graph embeddings (e.g., the knowledge graph or KG embedding application subsection), rather than from the general ACE framework or other application domains.

Must indicate that the relation r in the conditional distributions g(t | r+, h+) and g(h | r+, t+) is the positive relation from the original (positive) triplet, not an independently sampled or modified relation.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize how ACE is applied to order embeddings for hypernym prediction and hierarchical structure constraints?

requirements.description: Must define a hypernym pair as a pair of concepts where the first concept is a specialization or instance of the second, matching the paper's description used in the ACE-for-order-embeddings context.
Must state that the goal is to learn hierarchy-preserving embeddings when applying ACE to order embeddings (i.e., embeddings that respect the hypernym hierarchy).

Must specify that in the order-embedding space the root node is located at the origin and all other embeddings lie in the positive semi-space (all coordinates non-negative), as described in the paper's order-embedding formulation.

Must describe the constraint that for a parent–child hypernym pair, the magnitude (value) of the parent’s embedding is enforced to be smaller than the child’s in every dimension, reflecting the order-embedding inequality constraint in the paper.

Must explicitly note that sibling nodes (concepts sharing the same parent) are not subjected to the parent–child magnitude constraint in the embedding space, as stated in the paper’s description of the hierarchy constraints.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the paper’s problem setting, proposed model, and deployment/use-case as presented in the Summary slide?

requirements.description: Must state that the task is short title (very short headline) generation specifically for a news aggregation service where professional editors create short titles to introduce important articles, as opposed to generic headline generation.

decisions: How does the paper define and position the neural headline generation task for short title editing support in the news aggregator setting?

Must reference any figure or schematic (if present) that illustrates the pipeline from selected news article to (headline, lead) input and short title output in the editor support workflow.

decisions: What example does the paper provide to illustrate that generating short titles/headlines is a difficult task?

decisions: How does the paper describe the encoder–decoder with attention architecture used as the conditional language model for neural headline generation?

decisions: How does the proposed GateFusion method combine headline and lead contexts for neural headline generation in this case study?

decisions: What does the paper report about how well the proposed neural headline generation model performed on the usefulness measure, and what type of outputs it can generate?
