Must reflect the tabular or schematic layout (if present) that jointly lists 'Input Resource' as WordNet and 'Shifter Labels' as lemma and word sense, preserving these three specific label terms.

decisions: Does the system correctly retrieve and summarize the paper’s findings on verb polysemy, verbal polarity shifters by word sense, and the specific ‘mark down’ examples illustrating sense-dependent shifting behavior?

requirements.description: Must state the proportion of verbs that are polysemous as given in the paper ("50% of verbs are polysemous.").
Must state the proportion of verbs that are polarity shifters in at least one word sense as given in the paper ("12% of verbs are shifters in at least one word sense.").
Must state the proportion of polysemous verbal shifters that are shifters in all their word senses as given in the paper ("23%" with the wording "only 23% are shifters in all their word senses").

Must explain that verbal polarity shifting can be sense-dependent, using the verb "mark down" as the example, explicitly distinguishing the sense "reduce in price" (shifter) from the sense "write down" (non-shifter).

Must reproduce or describe the two example sentences for "mark down" from the paper, including their polarity annotations: (1) "The agency [marked down [their assets]+]-" where the inner phrase is positive and the outer phrase is shifted, and (2) "She [marked down [his confession of guilt]-]-" where both inner and outer scopes are negative but the verb sense is annotated as non-shifter.

decisions: What does the paper describe as the scope of a verbal polarity shifter within a sentence, and how is this scope exemplified and annotated?

requirements.description: Must state that when a phrase contains a polarity shifter, it is necessary to determine which part of the phrase (its scope) the shifter can affect.
Must mention that the scope of polarity shifters is annotated on the basis of syntactic dependency relations (i.e., scope annotated for dependency relations).
Must identify that verbs can function as polarity shifters in the examples, specifically using verbs like 'defeated' and 'surrendered' as shifters that influence sentiment toward their arguments.

Must describe an example sentence where sentiment-marked entities (e.g., 'the villain' with negative polarity and 'the hero' with positive polarity) are shown with bracket notation to illustrate the scope of the shifter.

Must retrieve content from the part of the paper that discusses shifter scope (often illustrated with example sentences) rather than from sections that only define the lexicon or list shifters without scope discussion.

decisions: What author and affiliation information from the paper must be retrieved to correctly generate the 'Annotation Workflow' slide title block?

requirements.description: Must identify the paper's first (or presenting) author name exactly as written in the author list (e.g., 'Marc Schulder').
Must identify the institutional affiliation corresponding to that author exactly as written in the paper (e.g., 'Saarland University').
Must extract the author name from the paper's front-matter metadata section (title/author block), not infer it from citations or references.
Must extract the affiliation from the same front-matter metadata section where author affiliations are listed, not from acknowledgments or body text.
Must preserve the linear ordering of 'Author Name' followed by 'Affiliation' as it appears in the paper's title/author block when generating the slide text.

decisions: What information about the annotators and their roles does the paper provide that should appear on the 'Annotators' slide?

requirements.description: Must state that both annotators are authors of the paper, as explicitly indicated in the annotator description section.
Must retrieve from the paper's annotation/annotators or data creation section that the annotators have prior experience in linguistics and annotation work.
Must specify that the second annotator labelled 400 word senses, as reported in the annotation procedure or inter-annotator agreement description.
Must identify and include the name 'Marc Schulder' as one of the annotators, as given in the author or annotator description part of the paper.
Must retrieve the institutional affiliation 'Saarland University' associated with Marc Schulder from the author or affiliation information in the paper.

decisions: How does the paper exemplify individual verbal polarity shifters in its lexicon, specifically for the verb 'blow out' and its different synsets and syntactic roles?

requirements.description: Must identify that the slide is illustrating entries from the lexicon of verbal polarity shifters using the verb 'blow out' as the example lemma.
Must retrieve the lexicon entry for 'blow out' with Synset ID 00436247 and include its role as a SUBJ shifter together with its gloss 'melt, break, or become otherwise unusable'.
Must retrieve the lexicon entry for 'blow out' with Synset ID 02767855 and include its role as a DOBJ shifter together with its gloss 'put out, as of fires, flames, or lights'.
Must indicate that these entries specify syntactic dependency roles (e.g., SUBJ, DOBJ) under which the verb acts as a polarity shifter.
Must attribute the slide/example to the author 'Marc Schulder' and 'Saarland University' as shown in the slide footer.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the paper’s main contribution and its key properties as stated in the conclusion slide?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper introduces a lexicon of English verbal polarity shifters (verbal shifters) as the main contribution.
Must specify that the lexicon covers all verbs contained in WordNet, using wording that clearly indicates complete coverage (e.g., 'covers all verbs in WordNet').
Must mention that the lexicon includes annotations at the word-sense level, i.e., 'annotations for each word sense' rather than only at the lemma or word-form level.
Must retrieve the authorship information identifying Marc Schulder as an author or contributor and include his name as presented in the paper.

Must base the summary on content from the paper’s conclusion or summary statements that explicitly describe the introduced lexicon and its coverage/annotation properties, not on unrelated sections such as experiments or related work.

decisions: What are the main aspects of text preprocessing and representation used in the proposed news clustering approach based on discourse text structure?

requirements.description: Must identify that the paper includes a dedicated discussion of text preprocessing and representation as a distinct aspect of the overall clustering approach (e.g., as a subsection or clearly delimited part of the methodology).
Must describe how snippets are transformed into augmented syntactic parse trees as the core text representation used for clustering.
Must explain how discourse information is incorporated into the text representation (e.g., by augmenting parse trees with discourse-related annotations or structure).
Must state that pattern structures are constructed over these text representations (augmented syntactic parse trees) and are the basis for the clustering process.
Must extract information specifically from the part of the paper that describes preprocessing and representation of web search snippets (not from sections focused solely on evaluation or results).

decisions: Which prior text representation models and their key references does the paper list in the context of news/text clustering?

requirements.description: Must identify that the slide enumerates different text representation models (e.g., suffix trees, n-grams, parse thickets) as alternative approaches for representing documents/snippets in clustering or related tasks.
Must retrieve and list the Becker and Kuropka, 2003 reference exactly as it appears in the paper as one of the text representation models.
Must retrieve and list the Polyvyanyy and Kuropka, 2007 and Hammouda and Kamel, 2004 references exactly as they appear in the paper as text representation models.
Must retrieve and list the Suffix Tree model with its citation Zamir and Etzioni, 1998 and the N-Grams model with its citation Schenker et al., 2007 exactly as they appear in the paper.
Must retrieve and list the Parse Thickets representation with its citation Galitsky, 2013 and indicate that it is presented in matrix form, matching the wording used in the paper.

decisions: What are the basic characteristics of parse thickets as defined in the paper's description of the discourse-based clustering representation?

requirements.description: Must state that parse thickets preserve the linguistic structure of a text paragraph, not just individual sentences.
Must describe that parse thickets are constructed by building a separate syntactic parse tree for each sentence within a paragraph.
Must specify that inter-sentence relations are added as links between nodes of different sentence parse trees to form the parse thicket.

Must draw these three characteristics (paragraph-level preservation, per-sentence parse trees, and inter-sentence relations) from the paper's section that introduces or defines 'parse thickets' or the underlying text representation used for clustering.

decisions: Which types of discourse relations are used in the paper’s parse thickets representation for news snippet clustering?

requirements.description: Must identify that one type of discourse relation used in parse thickets is based on Rhetoric Structure Theory (RST) as introduced by Mann et al. (1992).
Must identify that another type of discourse relation used in parse thickets is based on Communicative Actions as introduced by Searle (1969).

Must state that both Rhetoric Structure Theory (RST) and Communicative Actions are explicitly used as discourse relation types within the parse thickets representation, not merely mentioned as general background theories.

Must retrieve these discourse relation types from the part of the paper where parse thickets or discourse relations for clustering are defined or described, rather than from unrelated literature review sections.
Must correctly reproduce the cited forms of the two sources, including the author names (Mann, Searle) and publication years (1992, 1969) associated with RST and Communicative Actions respectively.

decisions: Does the system correctly retrieve and reproduce the specific 'Coreferences example' slide content from the paper, including its exact title and body text?

requirements.description: Must identify that the slide is an illustrative 'Coreferences example' related to discourse information or coreference phenomena in the context of news/snippet clustering.
Must preserve the slide title text exactly as 'Coreferences example' if present in the source, without substitution by other section or figure titles from the paper.

Must reproduce the two-line body text of the slide as a visual/textual example (even if noisy or non-lexical), rather than replacing it with a paraphrased or cleaned-up linguistic example from the paper.

Must associate this example with the part of the paper that discusses discourse information or coreference handling in the clustering approach, not with unrelated sections such as evaluation, reduction method, or pattern structure construction details.

Must explicitly link the example on the slide to the methodological use of discourse/coreference information in the post-retrieval snippet clustering approach, rather than treating it as a generic or unrelated text sample.

decisions: How does the paper describe the role of Rhetorical Structure Theory (RST) in characterizing discourse relations and discovering text patterns for news/snippet clustering?

requirements.description: Must state that, according to the paper, Rhetorical Structure Theory (RST) characterizes the structure of text in terms of relations that hold between parts of the text (e.g., text spans or discourse units), not merely in terms of isolated sentences or words.

Must state that the paper describes RST as defining relations between clauses or text spans that may not be syntactically linked, emphasizing that these discourse relations can cross or go beyond simple syntactic dependencies.
Must state that the paper uses RST to identify or discover text patterns based on a nucleus/satellite structure, where one part of the text is the nucleus and the other is the satellite.

Must list at least two specific RST relation types explicitly mentioned in the paper (e.g., evidence, justify, antithesis, concession) as examples of the relations used to characterize discourse structure.

Must attribute the above RST-related descriptions to the part of the paper where discourse or rhetorical structure is introduced as background or as a component of the proposed clustering approach (e.g., the section describing discourse information or RST-based representation), rather than to unrelated sections such as evaluation or implementation details.

decisions: Did the system correctly retrieve and present the example of a parse thicket built from multiple Iran–UN nuclear dispute news snippets as shown in the paper’s illustrative example slide?

requirements.description: Must identify that the slide illustrates the concept of a 'parse thicket' as an example of discourse-level representation constructed from multiple related news snippets about the same topic (Iran–UN nuclear dispute).

Must retrieve content from the paper’s example or case-study section where the Iran nuclear dispute news snippets are used to demonstrate parse thickets or discourse-based clustering (i.e., not from unrelated methodological or theoretical sections).

Must include all distinct news snippets shown in the example, specifically: (1) Iran refusing to accept a UN proposal to end the dispute over nuclear weapons work; (2) a UN nuclear watchdog resolution about a second uranium enrichment site in secret; (3) an IAEA report with diagrams suggesting secret nuclear weapons work; (4) an Iran envoy claiming peaceful nuclear development and fabricated US evidence; (5) a UN resolution condemning Iran’s work on nuclear weapons; (6) Iran’s claim that its nuclear research is for peaceful purposes; and (7) an envoy to the IAEA proceeding with the dispute, developing an enrichment site in secret, and confirming that evidence of a weapons program is fabricated while proceeding with a second enrichment site.

Must state that these Iran-related snippets are used as input texts for constructing an augmented syntactic parse representation (parse trees combined into a 'parse thicket') that underlies the proposed clustering approach.

Must recognize that the slide corresponds to an illustrative example (e.g., a figure or example block) in the paper where the raw textual snippets are listed together to visually demonstrate the set of sentences from which a parse thicket is built, rather than showing algorithmic pseudocode or numerical results.

decisions: Did the system correctly retrieve and use the paper’s discourse-based parse thicket clustering example about Iran’s nuclear program to generate the slide text?

requirements.description: Must identify that the slide illustrates the paper’s core concept of clustering news snippets using discourse information encoded in augmented syntactic parse trees (parse thickets), rather than simple keyword or bag-of-words similarity.

Must locate and use the specific example section in the paper where multiple news snippets about Iran’s nuclear program are presented as a case study for discourse-based clustering (e.g., an example or case-study subsection describing Iran/IAEA/UN snippets).

Must state that in this example, discourse relations (e.g., claims, evidence, condemnation, dispute) between entities such as Iran, the US, UN, and IAEA are extracted from augmented syntactic parse trees and used to form a pattern structure or parse thicket that drives clustering of these snippets.

Must reference any figure or illustrative example in the paper that shows or lists the Iran nuclear program snippets (or their parse thickets) as an example cluster, and indicate that the slide text corresponds to that same example set of snippets.

Must retrieve the full set of example snippets about Iran’s nuclear program used in the paper (including mentions of fabricated evidence by the US, peaceful purpose claims, UN/IAEA resolutions, secret uranium enrichment sites, and diagrams suggesting nuclear weapons work) and preserve their distinct sentence-level content when generating the slide.

decisions: How does the paper define and compute similarity between parse thickets for clustering news snippets?

requirements.description: Must state that similarity between parse thickets is defined in terms of matching sub-trees (i.e., sub-tree based similarity, not bag-of-words or full-tree matching).
Must specify that the sub-tree matching operates over nodes that are annotated with part-of-speech (POS) information.
Must specify that the sub-tree matching operates over nodes that are annotated with the stem (lemma/root form) of the word, not the raw surface form alone.
Must explicitly mention that the objects being compared are 'parse thickets' (augmented syntactic parse trees), not generic parse trees or other graph structures.

Must draw the similarity definition from the part of the paper that introduces or formalizes parse thickets and their similarity measure (e.g., the section describing the construction and comparison of augmented syntactic parse trees), rather than from unrelated background or results sections.

decisions: Does the system correctly retrieve and represent the example of discourse-based paragraph clustering using generalized syntactic parse trees with POS-tagged token patterns as shown in the slide?

requirements.description: Must state that the slide illustrates clustering/generalisation of paragraphs based on augmented syntactic parse trees where each token is represented as 'WORD-POS' (e.g., 'NN-work', 'IN-on', 'JJ-nuclear').

Must explain that the example shows a generalized pattern structure over multiple related sentences/snippets, where some tokens are replaced by wildcards '*' to indicate abstraction across clustered snippets (e.g., 'IN-*', 'DT-*', 'NNS-*', 'VBN-*').

Must reproduce the specific POS-tagged token sequences for at least three of the bracketed patterns exactly as in the paper's example, including both word and POS tags, such as '[NN-work IN-* IN-on JJ-nuclear NNS-weapons ]', '[DT-the NN-dispute IN-over JJ-nuclear NNS-* ]', and '[VBZ-passes DT-a - NN-resolution]'.

Must identify and draw from the section or subsection that presents the concrete example of pattern structures or generalized syntactic trees for news/snippet clustering (the part of the paper where these POS-tagged bracketed sequences are shown as an illustration).

Must mention that these bracketed sequences correspond to discourse units (e.g., clauses or sentences within news snippets) used as input objects for the clustering algorithm based on pattern structures on augmented syntactic parse trees.

decisions: Does the system correctly extract and represent the discourse-based generalized parse-tree structure used for clustering news snippets about Iran’s nuclear activities?

requirements.description: Must identify that the clustering approach is based on augmented syntactic parse trees enriched with discourse information (e.g., communicative actions, RST relations) rather than on plain bag-of-words or unannotated parse trees.

Must describe the use of generalization nodes in the parse trees (e.g., 'NN-generalization-<UN/nuclear watchdog>', 'NN-generalization-<Iran/envoy of Iran>') as a mechanism to abstract over specific named entities for clustering.

Must explain that communicative actions are explicitly encoded in the tree structure (e.g., labels like 'Communicative action' attached to subtrees representing actions such as work/develop, condemn, suggest) and are used as discourse features for clustering.

Must reconstruct or describe a tree-like representation where tokens are annotated with POS tags (e.g., 'NN-Iran', 'VBG-developing', 'JJ-nuclear', 'NNS-weapons') and nested bracketed structures, matching the hierarchical organization shown in the slide.

Must capture the inclusion of discourse relations such as RST-style evidence (e.g., 'RST-evidence VBN-fabricated IN-by DT-the NNP-US') linking propositions about 'evidence' and 'fabricated by the US' within the same structured representation used for clustering.

decisions: How does the paper define the goals and proposed solution for clustering groups of news snippets based on their discourse-aware parse structures?

requirements.description: Must state that the approach aims to adequately represent groups of texts (e.g., news snippets) that have overlapping or similar content, as described in the problem motivation in the abstract/introduction.
Must state that the clustering objective includes obtaining text clusters at different levels of refinement or granularity, corresponding to more and less detailed groupings of snippets.
Must explicitly mention that the overall structural goal of the clustering is a multi-level or hierarchical structure of text clusters (not just a flat partition).
Must identify that the proposed solution is based on the construction of pattern structures defined over parse thickets (augmented syntactic parse trees) extracted from the texts.

Must connect the use of pattern structures on parse thickets specifically to the clustering process, i.e., state that these pattern structures are the representation used to perform or derive the text clusters.

decisions: Does the system correctly extract and present the formal mathematical definition of the pattern structure used for clustering parse thickets, including the triple (G, (D, u), δ) and the Galois connection (A′, d′)?

requirements.description: Must state that the mathematical object underlying clustering is a triple (G, (D, u), δ) (or equivalent notation), where G is a set of objects, (D, u) is a complete meet-semilattice of descriptions, and δ is a mapping from objects G to descriptions D.
Must explicitly describe that (D, u) forms a complete meet-semilattice of descriptions, not just a generic set or lattice, matching the formal definition given in the paper.

Must define the pair (A, d) as a pattern (or concept) where A′ = d and d′ = A (or equivalent notation), indicating the mutual relationship between the extent A and the description d via Galois connections.

Must specify the Galois connection A′ as the meet (infimum) over descriptions of all objects in A, i.e., A′ = ⋂_{g∈A} δ(g) (or equivalent formulation such as A′ = u_{g∈A} δ(g)), directly reflecting the formula in the paper.

Must draw these definitions from the section that introduces the mathematical foundation of pattern structures or clustering of parse thickets (the formalism with G, (D, u), δ and Galois connections), not from unrelated narrative or experimental sections.

decisions: How does the paper define objects, pattern concepts, and clusters in its pattern-structure-based news clustering approach, and what key scalability drawback is identified?

requirements.description: Must state that an individual original paragraph of text is treated as a single object in the pattern structure (e.g., 'an original paragraph of text � an object a').

Must describe that parse thickets are constructed from paragraphs and that the description of an object is given by a set of its maximal generalized sub-trees (i.e., parse thickets � set of maximal generalized sub-trees).
Must explain that a pattern concept in the pattern structure corresponds to, or is interpreted as, a cluster of texts/snippets (i.e., 'a pattern concept � a cluster').
Must explicitly mention the identified drawback that the number of clusters grows exponentially with the number of texts (objects).

Must retrieve these definitions and the drawback from the part of the paper where the pattern structure on parse thickets is formally introduced (e.g., the section that defines objects, descriptions, pattern concepts, and discusses scalability).

decisions: How does the paper formally define the meaningfulness scores (maximum and average) of reduced pattern concepts over sub-trees in a cluster?

requirements.description: Must identify that the scores are defined over sub-trees ("chunks") within a cluster of augmented syntactic parse trees, and that these scores quantify the meaningfulness of a reduced pattern concept.

Must retrieve the formal definition of the maximum score over all sub-trees in a cluster, including the notation "Score_max^{A,d} := max Score(chunk)" (or an equivalent expression explicitly using a max operator over chunks in the cluster).

Must retrieve the formal definition of the average score of sub-trees in a cluster, including the notation "Score_avg^{A,d} = Σ_{chunk ∈ d} Score(chunk) / |{chunk ∈ d}|" (or an equivalent expression explicitly using a sum over chunks divided by their count).
Must retrieve the local scoring function for a chunk, specifically that "Score(chunk) = Σ_{node ∈ chunk} w_node" (or an equivalent expression that defines the chunk score as a sum over node weights).

Must locate and use the section (or subsection) where the paper introduces the reduced pattern structure and defines the pattern concept meaningfulness measures, rather than inferring formulas from unrelated parts of the paper.

decisions: How does the paper formally define and quantify the loss of meaning introduced by using reduced pattern structures for clustering, both in the minimal-loss and average-loss senses?

requirements.description: Must identify that the discussed scores quantify 'lost meaning' of cluster content when using reduced pattern structures, explicitly relating them to differences between reduced representations and the original texts in a cluster.

Must retrieve the formal definition of the minimal lost meaning score, including the maximization over A and d and the minimization over g in A, corresponding to the expression 'Score_max(A, d) = min_{g ∈ A} Score_max(g, d, g)'.

Must retrieve the formal definition of the average lost meaning score, including the average over A and d and the normalization by |d − g_A| (or equivalent notation), corresponding to the expression 'Score_Loss_avg(A, d) = Score_avg(A, d) / |d − g_A| Score_max(g, d, g)'.

Must locate and use the specific section or subsection where the loss estimates for reduced pattern structures are introduced and mathematically defined, rather than inferring or reconstructing the formulas from other parts of the paper.

Must preserve the two-part structure of the slide content by clearly separating (1) the minimal lost meaning estimate and its formula and (2) the average lost meaning estimate and its formula, as they are presented in the paper (e.g., as separate definitions, equations, or bullet points).

decisions: How does the paper define and represent the loss of meaning when constructing reduced pattern structures, and what are the key components involved in the ScoreLoss representation?

requirements.description: Must identify that the paper introduces a notion of 'loss of meaning' specifically in the context of constructing reduced pattern structures from original texts/snippets.
Must state that the paper defines or uses a metric or function named 'ScoreLoss' to quantify or control the loss of meaning between original and reduced pattern structures.
Must reference the representation (figure, schema, or table) in the paper where 'ScoreLoss' is shown together with the symbols 'A1', 'A2', 'd1', and 'd2' as its components or arguments.
Must correctly retrieve the exact labels 'ScoreLoss', 'A1', 'A2', 'd1', and 'd2' from the paper as they appear in the formalization or illustration of the reduced pattern structures generalization.

Must draw information from the section or subsection that discusses reduced pattern structures (or reduction method) and explicitly addresses how loss of meaning with respect to the original texts is controlled or evaluated.

decisions: How does the paper define and control the trade-off between loss of meaning and cluster distinguishability when constructing reduced pattern structure hierarchies for news snippet clustering?

requirements.description: Must state that reduced pattern structures are used to make the clustering approach scalable while preserving the semantic content ("meaning") of clusters.
Must explicitly mention that the method controls the loss of meaning with respect to the nearest, more meaningful neighbors in the cluster hierarchy (i.e., parent or higher-level clusters).
Must explicitly mention that the method controls the distinguishability of each cluster with respect to its nearest neighbors in the hierarchy of clusters (i.e., sibling or adjacent clusters).
Must describe that these controls (loss of meaning and distinguishability) are applied within a hierarchical clustering structure derived from pattern structures on augmented syntactic parse trees.

Must reference the part of the paper where reduced pattern structures are introduced as a reduction method to speed up clustering while discussing their impact on meaning preservation and cluster distinguishability (e.g., the section describing the reduction method or scalability analysis).

decisions: What specific elements from the paper describe the reduced pattern structure constraints and the associated ScoreLoss comparison between pattern structure and reduced pattern structure (with and without reduction using parameters A1, A2, d1, d2)?

requirements.description: Must identify and state the distinction between the original 'pattern structure' and the 'reduced pattern structure' as defined in the paper, using the exact terminology 'pattern structure' and 'reduced pattern structure'.
Must retrieve and reproduce the term 'ScoreLoss' exactly as it appears in the paper in the context of evaluating or constraining pattern structures.
Must retrieve the specific parameter labels 'A1', 'A2', 'd1', and 'd2' from the paper as they appear in the table or formula associated with ScoreLoss and reduced pattern structures.
Must describe or reconstruct the tabular layout that juxtaposes 'pattern structure' and 'reduced pattern structure' under the same header row containing 'ScoreLoss', 'A1', 'A2', 'd1', and 'd2'.

Must indicate that the paper compares cases 'without reduction' and 'with 1' (or equivalent phrasing used in the paper) as constraints or settings applied to the reduced pattern structure in the ScoreLoss context.

decisions: What concrete tools and algorithmic component does the paper report using in its implementation?

requirements.description: Must state that the implementation uses the Apache OpenNLP library specifically for performing common NLP tasks (e.g., tokenization, POS tagging, parsing) as described in the implementation section.
Must identify that the Bing search API is used explicitly as the source to obtain news snippets for clustering.
Must specify that the pattern structure builder in the system is based on a modified version of the AddIntent algorithm.
Must attribute the AddIntent algorithm to van der Merwe et al., 2004, matching the citation given in the implementation description.

Must extract all three implementation components (Apache OpenNLP, Bing search API, modified AddIntent-based pattern structure builder) from the paper's implementation/experimental setup description rather than inferring or introducing additional tools.

decisions: How does the paper motivate the need for clustering news search results returned by web search engines?

requirements.description: Must state that web search engines typically return a long list of documents/snippets as described in the abstract ("a web search engine usually returns a long list of documents").
Must explain that within this long list there exist many groups of pages/documents with similar or related content, motivating clustering of search results.

Must derive the motivation from the paper's problem statement or introductory discussion (e.g., the part of the abstract or introduction describing user difficulty navigating long result lists), not from the method or results sections.
Must connect the existence of many similar-content pages in the result list to the need for a clustering or grouping approach (post-retrieval snippet clustering) as mentioned in the abstract.

decisions: How does the paper’s user study demonstrate inconsistency in human-labeled, non-overlapping partitions of web news snippets?

requirements.description: Must identify that the user study is conducted on web search result snippets about several distinct 'world’s most pressing news' topics, including F1 winners, fighting Ebola with nanoparticles, 2015 ACM awards winners, reading facial expressions through a webcam, and turning brown eyes blue.

Must state that human annotators produced non-overlapping (partition-style) clusterings of the snippets, i.e., each snippet is assigned to exactly one cluster in the human-labeled partitions.
Must report that the inconsistency of human-labeled partitions is quantified using pairwise Adjusted Mutual Information (AMI or MI_adj) scores computed between different human partitions.
Must explicitly state that the pairwise Adjusted Mutual Information scores between human-labeled partitions are low (close to 0), indicating high inconsistency among human partitions.

decisions: What specific textual statistics are presented in the paper’s Ebola news example set that must appear in the slide titled 'Example The Ebola News Set'?

Must retrieve that the Ebola news example set explicitly reports counts for 'quoted speech' and 'reported speech' for each text (e.g., as distinct columns or fields).

decisions: How does the paper characterize the accuracy and dependency factors of conventional (non-overlapping) clustering methods when applied to overlapping text groups, and which specific method–linkage–distance combinations are considered?

requirements.description: Must state that the accuracy of conventional clustering methods for overlapping text groups is described as low in most cases.
Must state that the accuracy of these conventional clustering methods greatly depends on the human-labeled partition used as ground truth.
Must identify that a 'human-labeled partition' is explicitly used as the reference or ground truth partition in the evaluation of clustering accuracy.
Must list the clustering methods 'average' and 'complete' as the linkage methods associated with the human-labeled partition in the reported evaluation.
Must list the distance measures 'cityblock', 'euclidean', and 'cosine' as the distances associated with the human-labeled partition and linkage methods in the reported evaluation.

decisions: What does the paper report about the accuracy of conventional (non-overlapping) clustering methods across four human-labeled news snippet partitions?

requirements.description: Must identify that the evaluated methods are conventional, non-overlapping clustering methods (e.g., standard baseline clustering algorithms) as contrasted with the proposed discourse-based approach.

decisions: What specific example of a reduced pattern structure used in pattern structures clustering with maximal score is presented in the paper?

requirements.description: Must identify that the example is explicitly described as a 'reduced pattern structure' used in the context of pattern structures clustering.
Must state that the example illustrates clustering 'clusters with maximal score' or an equivalent phrase directly tied to the scoring of clusters in the pattern structure approach.
Must reproduce the literal token sequence 'INNP-* NNP-sierra NNP-leone J,' as it appears in the example of the reduced pattern structure.
Must include the phrase fragment 'reduced pattern structure with 1 and' exactly or with only trivial formatting differences, as part of the example description.

decisions: Does the summary correctly capture the paper’s main conclusions about discourse-based short text clustering and its efficiency improvements?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper addresses the short text (snippet) clustering problem and positions it as a limitation of traditional clustering methods for web search results.
Must identify 'Parse Thickets' (augmented syntactic parse trees incorporating discourse information) as the central text representation model proposed in the paper.
Must explain that text similarity is computed using pattern structures built over the Parse Thickets, explicitly referencing pattern structures as the basis for similarity.
Must describe the introduction of reduced pattern structures with constraints as a scalability mechanism to make the clustering algorithm efficient on typical collections of snippets.

Must mention the use of Score and ScoreLoss measures both to improve computational efficiency and to remove or avoid redundant clusters, and connect these to improved browsing and navigation for users through the set of texts.

decisions: Does the slide accurately summarize the paper’s problem setting and proposed method for inducing a Moroccan Darija–English translation lexicon via French loanwords in low-resource, historically unwritten language contexts?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper addresses historically unwritten languages that are only now being written due to informal electronic communications (e.g., social media, web comments, text messaging).
Must state that for these historically unwritten languages there are extremely limited linguistic resources available, specifically mentioning translation lexicons as an example.
Must describe that the paper presents a method for inducing portions of translation lexicons using expert knowledge (e.g., from a language informant) in these low-resource settings.
Must specify that the method relies on bridging via French loanwords to connect the historically unwritten language to English.
Must mention that the effectiveness of the proposed method is quantified through experiments on inducing a Moroccan Darija–English translation lexicon.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the paper’s motivation for inducing translation lexicons for historically unwritten languages?

requirements.description: Must state that translation lexicons are described as a core resource for multilingual processing of languages, matching the motivation text.
Must state that manual creation of translation lexicons by lexicographers is characterized as time-consuming and expensive.
Must retrieve and mention the quantitative claim that there are more than seven thousand languages in the world, as cited in the paper (Lewis et al.).
Must state that many of these languages are historically unwritten, explicitly linking this fact to the large number of world languages.
Must state that many historically unwritten languages are being written for the first time due to the explosive growth of informal electronic communications (e.g., social media).

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the paper’s description of prior work on automatic translation lexicon induction and its data requirements?

requirements.description: Must cover the paper's prior work / related work discussion specifically on 'automatic translation lexicon induction' rather than other topics (e.g., not general MT or lexicon construction in unrelated settings).
Must state that there has been extensive prior work on automating translation lexicon induction (i.e., convey that 'there has been a lot of work on automating translation lexicon induction').
Must describe that the best prior methods for automatic translation lexicon induction use multiple sources of information, explicitly including word-level information and temporal information.
Must specify that prior methods require particular types of data, explicitly including bilingual seed dictionaries and monolingual text from the same time period for each language.
Must attribute the use of temporal information in prior translation lexicon induction methods to work by Klementiev and Roth (or an equivalent explicit reference to that cited prior work).

decisions: What specific challenges does the paper identify for working with historically unwritten languages that are just beginning to be written in code-switched environments?

requirements.description: Must state that for historically unwritten languages that are just being written for the first time, there are extremely limited resources of any type available, including the absence of large amounts of monolingual text, using wording consistent with the paper's description.
Must describe that the written data that can be obtained for these languages often has non-standard spellings, explicitly mentioning 'non-standard spellings' as in the source text.
Must describe that the written data often involves code-switching, explicitly using the term 'code-switching' as in the paper.

Must explain that code-switching can occur within words, where the base is borrowed but the affixes are not borrowed, matching the paper's phrasing about 'base is borrowed' and 'affixes are not borrowed'.

Must reference the analogy to the multi-language categories V and N from (Mericli and ...), indicating that the within-word code-switching phenomenon is linked to these categories as cited in the paper.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the paper’s proposed high-level solution for acquiring translation lexicons for historically unwritten languages?

requirements.description: Must state that the target languages are historically unwritten and are now appearing in written form (e.g., in informal electronic communication or code-switched environments).
Must state that many of these historically unwritten languages borrow parts of their lexicons (e.g., loanwords) from more highly resourced written languages.
Must describe that the proposed method relies on a language informant who can provide guidance on how the language’s sounds would be rendered in a written script if words were to be written.

Must explain that the method uses loanwords from a higher-resourced written language as a bridge to induce or acquire portions of a translation lexicon into a target language (e.g., Moroccan Darija to English via French).
Must explicitly state that the outcome of applying this method is the rapid acquisition of parts of a translation lexicon, emphasizing speed or efficiency (e.g., 'quickly' or 'rapidly').

decisions: How does the paper define and describe the high-level method for generating candidate loanwords from a donor language to a borrowing language?

requirements.description: Must state that the method starts from word pronunciations (phonological forms) in the donor language, not from orthographic spellings or other representations.
Must describe that these donor-language pronunciations are systematically converted or mapped into their expected realizations in the borrowing language (i.e., how they would sound if borrowed).
Must explicitly identify the outputs of this conversion process as 'candidate loanwords' (or equivalent term clearly indicating hypothesized borrowed forms).

Must draw from the part of the paper that introduces the loanword candidate generation step (e.g., the method overview or loanword induction subsection), not from sections focused solely on evaluation or results.

Must preserve the directional roles of the two languages by clearly distinguishing which is the donor language (source of pronunciations) and which is the borrowing language (target of the converted forms).

decisions: How does the paper categorize the possible outcomes for a generated candidate loanword in the borrowing language?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper defines exactly three possible cases for any generated candidate loanword in the borrowing language.
Must describe the 'true match' case as when the candidate string occurs in the borrowing language and is in fact a loanword from the donor language.
Must describe the 'false match' case as when the candidate string occurs in the borrowing language by coincidence but is not a loanword from the donor language.
Must describe the 'no match' case as when the candidate string does not occur at all in the borrowing language.

Must identify and extract the specific passage where the three loanword candidate cases (true match, false match, no match) are enumerated and defined, rather than inferring or reinterpreting them from other parts of the paper.

decisions: How does the paper construct a Moroccan Darija–English translation lexicon using French as a bridging language?

requirements.description: Must state that the specific use case is inducing a Moroccan Darija–English translation lexicon using French as a bridging language.
Must identify that the process begins from an existing French–English bilingual dictionary, explicitly mentioning both French and English sides.
Must specify that French word forms are represented in IPA (International Phonetic Alphabet) and that these IPA pronunciations are the basis for further processing.
Must describe that the IPA pronunciations are converted into their expected rendering in Arabic script, not into another script or language.
Must mention that the conversion from IPA to Arabic script is performed via a multi-step (multiple step) transliteration process, not a single direct mapping.

decisions: How does the paper describe the multi-step transliteration process used to convert IPA pronunciations of candidate loanwords into Arabic script strings?

requirements.description: Must list all four transliteration steps in order, starting from IPA pronunciation and ending with merged Arabic script strings for each candidate loanword.
Must state that the process begins with breaking the pronunciation into syllables (Step 1) before any transliteration is applied.
Must specify that each IPA syllable is first converted to a string in modified Buckwalter transliteration (Step 2), and only then converted from modified Buckwalter to Arabic script (Step 3).
Must mention that modified Buckwalter transliteration is described as a commonly used transliteration scheme that supports a one-to-one mapping to Arabic script.
Must describe the final step (Step 4) as merging the resulting syllables to generate Arabic script strings for each candidate loanword string.

decisions: How does the paper describe the specific Buckwalter character sequences provided by the language expert in Step 2 of the method?

requirements.description: Must state that the Buckwalter characters or character sequences were supplied or defined by a language expert (or language informant), not automatically induced.
Must identify that these Buckwalter character sequences are part of a specific step in the procedure (e.g., Step 2 of the method for inducing the translation lexicon).
Must explicitly list at least the example Buckwalter sequences 'aa', 'kk', and 'y:iy' as they appear in the paper when describing the expert-supplied characters.

Must draw the information from the part of the paper that details the construction or specification of the Buckwalter transliteration scheme or character inventory used in the lexicon induction process.

decisions: What experimental data sources does the paper use to build the French-English dictionary and to test the method?

requirements.description: Must state that the French-English bilingual dictionary is extracted from the English Wiktionary dump specifically identified as the 20131101 version.
Must identify that the English Wiktionary resource used is a freely available dump (not a proprietary or paid resource).
Must report that the test data consists of approximately one million lines of user comments (not articles, tweets, or other text types).
Must specify that the user comments used for testing were crawled from a Moroccan news website (not a generic or non-Moroccan source).
Must draw all of the above details from the paper's experimental setup or data section that describes corpus construction and resources, rather than inferring them from the abstract or introduction.

decisions: What initial corpus and loanword statistics does the paper report for French loanword candidates in the Hespress Moroccan Darija corpus?

requirements.description: Must state that converting each of the French pronunciations from the dictionary into Arabic script yielded exactly 8,277 unique loanword candidates.
Must report that exactly 1,150 of the 8,277 loanword candidates appear in the Hespress corpus.
Must report that there are more than one million loanword candidate instances in the corpus, with the exact count given as 1,169,087.
Must indicate that the statistics concern French loanword candidates converted into Arabic script and their occurrences in the Hespress Moroccan Darija corpus.

Must identify and use the specific part of the paper where initial corpus statistics or data description for the Hespress corpus and loanword candidates are reported (e.g., data or corpus statistics subsection).

decisions: How does the paper handle false matches caused by very short words when selecting candidate loanwords, and what is the resulting size of the candidate set and its corpus instances after filtering?

requirements.description: Must state that false matches are particularly likely to occur for very short words, explicitly linking short word length to higher false match probability.
Must describe the filtering rule that candidates shorter than four characters (length less than four) are removed from consideration.
Must report the exact number of remaining candidate types after filtering as 838 candidates appearing in the corpus.
Must report the exact number of remaining candidate instances (tokens) after filtering as 217616 candidate instances in the corpus.

Must locate and use the part of the paper that discusses candidate filtering or pruning (e.g., the subsection on filtering short word candidates) rather than unrelated sections such as introduction or conclusions.

decisions: How does the paper describe the human annotation setup used to classify candidate instances as Arabic, French, or uncertain for computing the percentage of true versus false matches?

requirements.description: Must state that an annotation exercise was conducted specifically for classifying candidate instances by origin (Arabic vs. French vs. unsure).
Must specify that exactly two annotators participated and that they were native Moroccan Darija speakers.
Must indicate that both annotators also had at least intermediate knowledge of another language (e.g., French or English, as described in the paper).
Must report that a random sample of 1185 candidate instances was drawn from the corpus for this annotation exercise.

Must describe the three annotation labels and their meanings: 'A' for instances originally from Arabic, 'F' for instances originally from French, and 'U' for instances where the annotator was not sure.

decisions: What does the paper report about the annotation results, specifically the number of word instances annotated by category and in total?

requirements.description: Must identify and reference the specific table in the paper that reports annotation results as counts of word instances (i.e., the table whose caption or surrounding text indicates it shows the 'Number of word instances annotated').
Must state that the annotation results are broken down by language category labels corresponding to at least 'Arabic', 'Unknown', and 'French'.
Must retrieve from the annotation table the presence of a 'Total' column or row that aggregates the number of word instances across the listed categories.

Must locate and use the part of the paper where annotation statistics are reported (e.g., the section or subsection describing annotation or data collection) rather than unrelated sections such as introduction or related work.
Must indicate that the counts in the annotation table correspond to word instances produced by human annotators (i.e., are the result of an annotation process, not automatically extracted counts).

decisions: What specific example translations does the paper present in the section illustrating translations found by the proposed lexicon induction method?

requirements.description: Must identify that the slide is illustrating concrete example entries from the induced translation lexicon (i.e., example translations found by the method), not describing the algorithm or results summary in general.
Must retrieve the exact example string 'omelette I JE @; and' from the paper as it appears in the examples of translations found (e.g., in an examples table or example list).

Must locate and use content from the specific part of the paper that presents example translation pairs or example induced lexicon entries (e.g., an 'Examples of Translations Found' subsection, table, or figure caption), rather than from unrelated sections such as introduction or related work.

Must preserve the original formatting or tokenization of the example 'omelette I JE @; and' as it is visually presented in the paper (including spacing and special characters), rather than normalizing or paraphrasing it.

Must treat the retrieved example 'omelette I JE @; and' explicitly as an instance of a translation found by the proposed method, indicating it is part of the induced translation lexicon output rather than input data or unrelated text.

decisions: How does the induced Moroccan Darija-English translation lexicon affect machine translation performance in the Hespress corpus experiment?

requirements.description: Must cover the experimental setup section describing the machine translation experiment on the Hespress corpus, including how the test set sentences were selected and translated.

Must state that a random set of sentences was selected from the Hespress corpus, each containing at least one candidate instance, and that 273 sentences were manually translated into English by a Modern Standard Arabic/Moroccan Darija/English trilingual translator to form the test set.
Must describe the baseline MT system as being trained using all GALE MSA-English parallel corpora from the Linguistic Data Consortium (years 2007–2013) with Moses 3.0 using default parameters.
Must report the baseline system BLEU score of 7.48 on the code-switched Moroccan Darija test set as given in the machine translation experiment results.

Must report that a second MT system was trained with the induced translation lexicon appended to the end of the training data, achieving a BLEU score of 8.11, corresponding to a gain of 0.63 BLEU points over the baseline.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the paper’s main conclusions about inducing a Moroccan Darija–English translation lexicon via French loanwords in the context of historically unwritten languages emerging in informal electronic text?

requirements.description: Must state that the work addresses colloquial, historically unwritten languages that are now being written for the first time in informal electronic communications (e.g., social media, web comments).
Must explicitly mention that the primary technical challenge motivating the work is Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) issues for multilingual processing technology arising from these new written forms.
Must describe the proposed method as a translation lexicon induction approach that specifically exploits loanwords as the central mechanism.

Must indicate that historically unwritten languages in this setting borrow a significant amount of vocabulary from relatively well-resourced written languages, and that this borrowing is central to the approach.

Must identify the concrete case study as induction of a Moroccan Darija–English translation lexicon via bridging French loanwords, including all three languages (Moroccan Darija, English, and French) and the bridging role of French.

decisions: What future research directions do the authors propose for extending and improving their method for acquiring translation lexicons for historically unwritten languages?

requirements.description: Must identify and use content explicitly from the paper's 'Future Work' or equivalent concluding section that discusses prospective research directions, not from earlier methodological or results sections.

Must state that one proposed future direction is to apply or explore the presented method on additional languages beyond the specific case study (e.g., beyond Moroccan Darija-English via French loanwords).
Must describe that another proposed future direction involves adapting or modifying the existing method itself, rather than replacing it, to improve its performance or applicability.
Must specify that the intended outcome of the proposed adaptations is to increase the 'yield' of the method, i.e., to obtain a larger or more complete induced translation lexicon.

Must preserve the distinction between the two separate future work items: (1) extension to other languages, and (2) adaptations to increase yield, rather than merging them into a single undifferentiated goal.

decisions: What relative merits of neural reranking for machine translation quality does the paper identify and support?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper investigates neural reranking (using neural attentional MT models) as an additional component to a baseline syntax-based statistical machine translation system, and that this reranking improves subjective (manual) translation quality.
Must identify that the paper explicitly claims neural MT reranking leads to more fluent output compared to the baseline system, as evidenced in the analysis or discussion sections.

Must report that the paper finds neural MT reranking is particularly effective at improving the translation of low-frequency or rare words, as discussed in the detailed analysis of reasons for quality increase.

Must explain that the neural attentional MT model is used as a probabilistic model to assign scores to candidate translations produced by another (syntax-based SMT) system, i.e., it can score the output of other systems for reranking.

Must connect the reported improvements in objective metrics (e.g., BLEU) with corresponding improvements in manual/subjective evaluation, indicating that the gains from neural reranking are confirmed by human judgments as stated in the paper.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and present the core reranking setup using neural MT models, including the use of N-best lists with MT and neural features, as illustrated in the paper?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper uses neural attentional machine translation models specifically for reranking outputs of a baseline syntax-based statistical machine translation system.
Must describe that reranking is applied to an N-best list of candidate translations produced by the baseline MT system (i.e., an 'N-best' input list).
Must explain that the reranking model combines traditional MT features (from the baseline SMT system) with additional neural features derived from the neural MT model when scoring N-best candidates.
Must mention that the work evaluates the impact of neural reranking on subjective (manual) translation quality, not only on automatic metrics like BLEU.

Must reflect the slide’s schematic structure by explicitly including the three-part pipeline elements: (1) 'Input N-best', (2) 'w/MT Features', and (3) 'Neural Features' as distinct components of the reranking process.

decisions: Does the paper show that neural reranking substantially improves BLEU scores, even over strong baseline SMT systems, and that it improves subjective translation quality?

requirements.description: Must state that the system uses a neural attentional machine translation model specifically as a reranking component on top of a syntax-based statistical machine translation baseline.
Must explicitly mention that neural MT reranking yields a large gain in BLEU or similar automatic evaluation metrics compared to the baseline system, as reported in the experimental results section.

Must retrieve at least one concrete BLEU score comparison from a results table (e.g., baseline BLEU vs. baseline+neural reranking BLEU) demonstrating that reranking improves over a strong baseline system.
Must state that the paper confirms that improvements from neural reranking extend to manual or subjective evaluation of translation quality, not only to BLEU.

Must draw on the experiments or evaluation section where both automatic metrics (BLEU) and manual/subjective evaluation results are reported, rather than only describing the system architecture or related work.

decisions: What open questions about the effects of neural MT reranking on subjective translation quality and qualitative output differences does the paper raise and investigate?

requirements.description: Must identify that the central concept is 'neural reranking' applied on top of a syntax-based statistical machine translation system, as stated in the abstract.

Must state that the paper investigates whether neural MT reranking improves subjective or manual evaluation of translation quality, not only automatic metrics like BLEU, as explicitly mentioned in the abstract.

Must retrieve from the abstract that previous work showed large gains in objective evaluation measures such as BLEU, and that this paper confirms these gains also carry over to manual (subjective) evaluation.
Must mention that the reranking component uses neural attentional machine translation models, as specified in the abstract.

Must reference that the paper performs a detailed analysis of reasons for the increase in quality, implying examination of qualitative differences before and after reranking, as stated in the abstract's final sentence.

decisions: What experimental setup did the authors use to evaluate neural reranking for machine translation in this paper?

requirements.description: Must state that the baseline system is the NAIST WAT2014 tree-to-string syntax-based SMT system, described explicitly as a strong baseline achieving high scores.
Must specify that the baseline system is implemented using Travatar and include the Travatar URL exactly as given in the paper: 'http://phontron.com/travatar'.
Must describe the neural MT reranking model as an attentional model trained on approximately 500k sentences with 256 hidden nodes and using a 2-model ensemble.

Must identify the evaluation data as the ASPEC Scientific Abstracts and list both automatic evaluation metrics (BLEU and RIBES) and the manual evaluation metric (WAT 2015 HUMAN Score).

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the paper’s main empirical finding that neural reranking improves both automatic and manual evaluation metrics across multiple language directions?

requirements.description: Must state that the central contribution is showing that neural reranking improves the subjective (manual) quality of machine translation, in addition to previously known gains in objective (automatic) metrics such as BLEU.
Must draw from the paper’s results/evaluation section(s) where both automatic (e.g., BLEU) and manual evaluation outcomes are reported and discussed, not only from the system description or abstract.

Must retrieve the set of language directions evaluated at WAT2015 and list them as four distinct directions matching the slide layout (en-ja, ja-en, zh-ja, ja-zh), as reported in the paper’s results tables or task description.

Must explicitly distinguish between automatic evaluation results (e.g., BLEU improvements due to neural reranking) and manual/subjective evaluation results, indicating that improvements are observed in both types of evaluation.

Must identify that the reranking component is based on neural attentional machine translation models applied on top of a syntax-based statistical machine translation system, as described in the system overview/method section.

decisions: How does the paper define and categorize the types of translation quality changes analyzed when applying neural reranking to machine translation outputs?

requirements.description: Must state that the analysis concerns how neural reranking affects the subjective quality of machine translation outputs (i.e., whether translations become better or worse after reranking).

Must identify and use the specific analysis section (or subsection) where the authors perform a detailed categorization of changes introduced by neural reranking, rather than only the general system description or overall results sections.
Must describe that each translation pair (before vs. after reranking) is annotated with a binary judgment of whether the sentence is better or worse after ranking.
Must list the main error-type categories used in the paper’s analysis as insertion, deletion, substitution, reordering, and conjugation, explicitly as the primary error labels for corrected errors.
Must mention that, in addition to the main error categories, the paper defines more fine-grained or detailed subcategories of errors and uses them in the analysis of changes due to neural reranking.

decisions: According to the paper, what qualitative effect does neural reranking have on machine translation output, and which linguistic aspects primarily account for the observed improvements?

requirements.description: Must state that neural reranking using neural attentional machine translation models improves the subjective (manual/human-judged) quality of machine translation output, not only objective metrics like BLEU.

Must explicitly connect the improvement in subjective quality to the reranking component, distinguishing it from the baseline syntax-based statistical machine translation system without neural reranking.
Must state that the main gains from neural reranking are attributed to grammatical factors (e.g., word order, agreement, syntactic well-formedness) rather than lexical selection.

Must reference the paper's detailed analysis section (e.g., error analysis or qualitative analysis of outputs) as the source that identifies grammar versus lexical selection as the primary locus of improvement.

Must retrieve at least one explicit statement from the paper’s results or analysis (e.g., a sentence or summarized finding) that contrasts improvements in grammatical correctness with relatively smaller changes in lexical choice.

decisions: What open research questions about neural reranking and neural MT does the paper explicitly pose or imply as still unknown?

requirements.description: Must identify that the central topic is 'Neural Reranking Improves Subjective Quality of Machine Translation' as the main theme or contribution of the paper (e.g., from the title and abstract).

Must extract that the paper distinguishes between neural translation models (full neural MT systems) and neural language models used within SMT or reranking, and treats them as separate model types for comparison.
Must identify that neural models are used specifically for reranking syntax-based statistical MT outputs, as opposed to being used as a standalone 'pure' neural MT system.

Must recognize from the results and analysis sections that the paper compares reranking with neural MT baselines or discusses the need to compare reranking approaches against pure neural MT systems, forming the basis for the question 'How does reranking compare with pure neural MT?'.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the paper’s motivation that ML should support cost/accuracy prediction from limited pilot data, emphasizing data collection cost and the unclear relationship between data size/quality and accuracy, as presented on the slide?

decisions: Does the system correctly identify that the paper’s goal is to design ML/NLP systems to meet specified performance and resource desiderata by extrapolating performance from small pilot datasets to predict accuracy on much larger training sets, including estimating required labeled examples?

decisions: What are the main contributions and experimental setup of the paper on predicting accuracy on large datasets from smaller pilot data?

Must mention that the paper introduces a new accuracy (performance) extrapolation task whose goal is to predict system accuracy on larger training sets from smaller ones.

decisions: How does the paper define and set up the accuracy extrapolation task, including the corpora split and overall goal?

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize how the biased power-law model extrapolates performance on the AGNews corpus using pilot data binomial weights and the role of hyperparameter optimization across pilot subsets?

decisions: Which development (dev) corpora are used when reporting relative residuals in the paper’s performance extrapolation experiments?

decisions: How does the paper evaluate extrapolation accuracy using RMS relative residuals on test corpora, and what modeling and pilot-data conditions affect this error?

decisions: Does the summary correctly capture the paper’s main conclusions about data requirement prediction and the proposed future work on extrapolation methods?

decisions: How does the paper define and characterize multiword expressions, specifically verb–noun combinations, as idiomatic expressions of multiple words?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper focuses on verb–noun combinations (VNCs) such as 'blow the whistle', 'hit the roof', and 'see stars' as the target expressions.

Must indicate that these expressions consist of multiple words (i.e., are multiword expressions rather than single tokens).

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and present example verb–noun combinations (VNCs) illustrating idiomatic vs. literal usages as used in the paper?

Must retrieve and use the exact example sentence pair for "see stars" from the paper’s example section (or equivalent), preserving the idiomatic sentence "It caught him on the head and he went down seeing little sparkling stars" and the literal sentence "It’s still dark enough to see the brightest stars" (allowing only minor orthographic differences such as capitalization or apostrophe formatting).
Must explicitly label each example sentence as idiomatic (I) or literal (L), matching the idiomatic/literal status of each sentence as given in the paper.
Must indicate that these example sentences are used in the paper as illustrative instances for the classification task (idiomatic vs. literal VNC usage), not as model outputs or synthetic examples.

decisions: How does the paper define and exemplify the task of token-level idiomaticity classification for English verb-noun combinations (MWEs)?

requirements.description: Must state that the core task is token-level classification of individual instances of multiword expressions (specifically verb-noun combinations) as idiomatic or literal, not type-level idiom identification.

Must explicitly mention that the decision is framed as determining whether a given MWE/VNC instance in context is idiomatic or literal (i.e., a binary idiomatic vs. literal label for each occurrence).
Must indicate that the classification is performed at the token (instance-in-context) level using contextual information from the sentence containing the verb-noun combination.

Must draw from the paper's task/problem definition section (or equivalent introductory description of the classification task) rather than from sections describing representation learning details or evaluation metrics.

Must identify that the examples used to illustrate the task involve ambiguous expressions that can be interpreted either idiomatically or literally, consistent with the paper's description of VNC ambiguity.

decisions: How does the paper represent verb-noun combination (VNC) token instances within its overall modeling approach?

requirements.description: Must state that each VNC token instance is mapped to a distributed representation rather than using only symbolic or hand-crafted features.
Must explicitly mention that the distributed representation for VNC token instances is obtained using an embedding model (e.g., word embeddings, sentence embeddings, or similar).
Must describe that the representation is constructed at the token-instance level (i.e., for each occurrence of a VNC in context), not just at the VNC type level.

Must connect the use of embedding-based representations directly to the task of classifying VNC usages as idiomatic or literal.

decisions: What lexico-syntactic patterns does the paper identify as characteristic of idiomatic usages of English verb–noun combinations?

requirements.description: Must state that idiomatic meanings of verb–noun combinations are typically restricted to a small number of lexico-syntactic patterns, as explicitly described in the paper's discussion of lexico-syntactic fixedness.

Must identify that the lexico-syntactic patterns are defined in terms of grammatical voice (e.g., active vs. passive) and noun phrase properties (e.g., presence/absence of determiner, number of the noun).
Must list a pattern corresponding to 'active voice, no determiner, plural noun' as one of the idiom-associated lexico-syntactic patterns described in the paper.
Must list a pattern corresponding to 'active voice, determiner, singular noun' as one of the idiom-associated lexico-syntactic patterns described in the paper.
Must list a pattern corresponding to 'passive voice, plural noun' as one of the idiom-associated lexico-syntactic patterns described in the paper.

decisions: From which prior work does the paper draw its notion of lexico-syntactic fixedness patterns for verb–noun combinations, as cited on the 'Patterns' slide?

requirements.description: Must identify that the 'Patterns' slide refers to prior work on lexico-syntactic fixedness of verb–noun combinations, not to a new method or result introduced in the current paper.

Must state that the patterns attributed to 'Afsaneh Fazly et al. 2009' are used as a basis or reference for modeling or measuring lexico-syntactic fixedness of verb–noun combinations in the current paper.

decisions: What is meant by the 'canonical form' of verb–noun combinations in this paper, and to which prior work does the paper attribute this notion?

requirements.description: Must state that 'canonical form' refers to lexico-syntactic patterns (or lexico-syntactic fixedness) in which idiomatic usages of verb–noun combinations tend to occur.
