decisions: What shortcomings and data loss issues does the paper report when extracting parallel speech corpora from the dubbed movie "The Man Who Knew Too Much"?

requirements.description: Must state that copyright restrictions are identified as a shortcoming specifically limiting the distribution of the extracted speech corpus.
Must identify that the shortcomings are framed as 'main bottlenecks in capturing data' during the corpus extraction process from dubbed movies.
Must report the quantitative loss rate for the original-language sentences as approximately 15% sentences lost.
Must report the quantitative loss rate for the dubbed-language sentences as approximately 49% sentences lost.

Must mention that these loss percentages and bottlenecks are reported in the context of processing the specific movie example "The Man Who Knew Too Much," including the issue of translation differences between dubbed audio and subtitles.

decisions: Does the system correctly retrieve and present the example of subtitle–dubbed dialogue differences used to illustrate extracted parallel speech segments from dubbed movies?

requirements.description: Must identify that the slide illustrates an example of parallel speech segments across three aligned text streams: 'Extracted English (Sub + audio)', 'Spanish Sub', and 'Spanish Dub', and must preserve these three column labels in the same order.

Must reproduce the full English dialogue sequence in the first column exactly as in the paper example: 'Daddy , you're sure I've never been to Africa before ?', 'It looks familiar.', 'You saw the same scenery last summer driving to Las Vegas .', 'Where Daddy lost all that money at the crap', 'Hey, look!', 'A Camel.', 'Of course this isn't really Africa, honey.', 'It's the French Morocco .', 'Well , it's northern Africa .', in this order and with line breaks between utterances.

Must reproduce, for each English utterance row, both corresponding Spanish text variants exactly as in the ground truth: the 'Spanish Sub' version and the 'Spanish Dub' version, including differences such as 'Papa , estas seguro de que nunca estuve antes en Africa ?' vs 'Papa, estas seguro que no habiamos estado ya en Africa?', and 'Viste el mismo panorama el verano pasado cuando manejamos a Las Vegas .' vs 'Vimos un paisaje muy parecido cuando fuimos a Las Vegas', preserving accents, punctuation, and word order as shown.

Must include the alignment indicator in the fourth column for each row, using the tokens 'yes' or 'no' exactly as in the example, and must place them on the correct rows (e.g., 'yes' for the first Africa question row, 'no' for 'It looks familiar.', 'yes' for the Las Vegas line, etc.).

Must preserve the tabular row structure that aligns each English utterance with its 'Spanish Sub', 'Spanish Dub', and 'yes/no' alignment indicator on the same row, so that differences between subtitle and dub translations can be visually compared line by line.

decisions: Does the system correctly summarize the paper’s main conclusions about the automatic construction and applicability of multimodal bilingual corpora from dubbed media?

requirements.description: Must state that the proposed method automatically builds multimodal bilingual (parallel) corpora specifically from dubbed media or dubbed movies.
Must indicate that the resulting corpora contain conversational speech and are explicitly described as useful for speech-to-speech translation applications.
Must mention that the approach is applicable to any language pair, with the explicit condition that an acoustic model for the language pair is trained or available.
Must report that, once the required acoustic model exists, the system does not require any further training to build new corpora from dubbed media.

Must identify that the implementation code is publicly available and provide the specific URL http://www.github.com/TalnUPF/movie2parallelDB as stated in the conclusions or implementation-related part of the paper.

decisions: What future work directions do the authors propose for improving and extending their automatically extracted parallel speech corpora from dubbed movies?

requirements.description: Must state that the authors plan to replace the current proprietary audio-text aligner with an open-source aligner, explicitly mentioning p2fa based on the CMU Sphinx ASR system as an example.
Must describe the planned change in corpus organization from using only a directory-based structure to using an XML-based structure as corpus metadata.
Must mention the future work item of automatically identifying the speaker of each sentence in the corpus.
Must state that the authors intend to extend the corpus and make it publicly available (publish the corpus) as part of their future work.
Must indicate that extending and publishing the corpus is contingent on obtaining agreement or permission from the copyright holders.

decisions: What specific ProsodyPro-generated files related to prosodic parameter extraction from dubbed movie speech corpora are listed or illustrated in the appendix of the paper?

requirements.description: Must identify and reference the appendix section (e.g., 'Appendix B') where ProsodyPro output files are described or listed.
Must state that the listed files are generated by the ProsodyPro tool as part of extracting prosodic parameters from the parallel speech corpora.

Must enumerate the specific file types or filenames shown in the appendix for ProsodyPro outputs (e.g., text grids, pitch files, intensity files, formant files, or similarly named concrete file artifacts).
Must describe any figure or screenshot in the appendix that visually presents a directory listing, table, or example of ProsodyPro-generated files, if such a visual element exists.

Must connect the ProsodyPro-generated files to their methodological role, explicitly stating that these files store extracted prosodic parameters (e.g., F0, duration, intensity) used in the speech-to-speech translation or prosody transfer framework.

decisions: How does the paper define the concept of self-disclosure, including the specific formulations and citations it adopts?

requirements.description: Must state that self-disclosure is defined as 'the verbal expressions by which a person reveals aspects of self to others' exactly or near-exactly as in the paper.
Must state that self-disclosure is defined as the 'process of making the self known to others' exactly or near-exactly as in the paper.
Must attribute the first definition ('the verbal expressions by which a person reveals aspects of self to others') to Jourard 1971b, matching the [Jourard1971b] citation in the paper.
Must attribute the second definition ('process of making the self known to others') to Jourard & Lasakow 1958, matching the [Jourard&Lasakow1958] citation in the paper.

Must retrieve these definitions from the section where the paper introduces or defines 'self-disclosure' (e.g., conceptual background or introduction), not from unrelated methodological or results sections.

decisions: How does the paper define and categorize different levels of self-disclosure for use in its computational analysis?

requirements.description: Must identify that the paper explicitly defines multiple discrete levels of self-disclosure rather than treating disclosure as a continuous or binary variable.
Must state that one of the defined categories is a 'general' or 'no disclosure' level representing tweets or messages without self-disclosure content.
Must state that one of the defined categories is a 'medium' or 'moderate' self-disclosure level representing partial or limited self-revealing content.
Must state that one of the defined categories is a 'high' self-disclosure level representing strong or extensive self-revealing content.
Must indicate that these self-disclosure levels are used as labeled categories or classes in the semi-supervised machine learning or topic modeling framework described in the paper.

decisions: How does the paper define the G-level (general) category of self-disclosure in its self-disclosure topic model for Twitter conversations?

requirements.description: Must state that the G-level of self-disclosure is characterized as 'general information and ideas' rather than personal content.
Must state that G-level content includes no information about the self of the speaker (author of the tweet).
Must state that G-level content includes no information about someone personally close to the speaker (e.g., friends or family).
Must extract the G-level definition from the section where the paper defines or operationalizes self-disclosure levels in its topic model (e.g., the coding scheme or annotation guideline section).
Must identify that G-level is one of the discrete self-disclosure levels used as labels or categories in the semi-supervised machine learning or annotation framework described in the paper.

decisions: How does the paper define the medium level (M-level) of self-disclosure in terms of the types of personal information shared?

requirements.description: Must identify the specific self-disclosure level labeled as 'M level' (or equivalent medium-level category) in the paper's self-disclosure taxonomy or coding scheme.
Must state that this M-level self-disclosure involves 'general information about self or someone close to him' (or an equivalent phrase describing non-intimate but personal-identifying information).
Must state that this M-level self-disclosure includes 'personal events' as an example of the type of content disclosed at this level.
Must state that this M-level self-disclosure includes information about 'age' and 'occupation' as explicit examples of content at this level.
Must state that this M-level self-disclosure includes information about 'family members' as part of the definition or examples for this level.

decisions: What specific types of highly intimate (high-level) self-disclosure topics does the paper define and categorize for Twitter conversations?

requirements.description: Must identify that the paper defines a high-level (most intimate) self-disclosure category that includes 'sensitive information about self or someone close to him/her' as a distinct topic description.
Must state that 'problematic behaviors of self and family members' is explicitly listed as one of the high-level self-disclosure topic types in the paper's taxonomy or coding scheme.
Must state that 'physical appearance, health, death, sexual topics' are grouped together as a single high-level self-disclosure topic category in the paper's definition or annotation guidelines.

Must retrieve the exact or near-exact phrasing of all three bullet items (sensitive information; problematic behaviors; physical appearance/health/death/sexual topics) from the paper's table, figure, or text where self-disclosure levels or topic categories are enumerated.

Must draw from the section (e.g., annotation scheme, coding manual, or topic model description) where the paper operationalizes self-disclosure levels or topics, rather than from results or discussion sections.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the paper’s conceptual background on how self-disclosure relates to relationship strength, social support, and coping with stress, including the cited sources?

requirements.description: Must state that the degree or amount of self-disclosure in a relationship depends on, or varies with, the strength of the relationship, as described in the paper’s theoretical/background discussion.
Must state that strategic or deliberate self-disclosure can strengthen or improve interpersonal relationships, as presented in the paper’s conceptual or literature review section.
Must state that self-disclosure enables or leads to receiving social support from others, matching the claim attributed in the paper to Derlega et al. (1993).
Must state that self-disclosure helps individuals cope with stress, consistent with the discussion in the paper that cites Derlega et al. (1993) and Tamir and Mitchell (2012).

Must retrieve these four relationship-focused functions of self-disclosure (dependence on relationship strength, strengthening relationships, gaining social support, coping with stress) from the paper’s introductory or theoretical background section rather than from methods or results sections.

decisions: How does the paper characterize the key methodological limitations of prior self-disclosure research that its computational Twitter-based approach aims to address?

requirements.description: Must identify that prior self-disclosure research predominantly relies on asking questions directly to participants (e.g., questionnaires, self-reports) as a primary data collection method.
Must state that a core limitation of asking questions to participants is bias introduced by participants' memory or recall (e.g., memory bias, recall bias).
Must describe that previous studies analyze datasets via manual or human coding/annotation of self-disclosure content.
Must explicitly mention that human/manual analysis in prior work does not scale or cannot be applied to large datasets (i.e., a limitation in dataset size or scalability).
Must report that earlier experiments are typically conducted in laboratory or otherwise artificial/controlled environments rather than using naturally occurring conversational data.

decisions: What research questions about detecting and analyzing self-disclosure in large, naturally occurring Twitter conversations does the paper pose?

requirements.description: Must state the overarching research question about automatically finding self-disclosure in a large, naturally occurring corpus (e.g., Twitter conversations), using wording that clearly includes both 'self-disclosure' and 'large & naturally occurring corpus' or equivalent.

Must state the overarching research question about the relationship between self-disclosure and social dynamics in a large, naturally occurring corpus, including both 'relations between self-disclosure' and 'social dynamics' or equivalent terms.

Must explicitly include the sub-question labeled as Q1 that asks whether high self-disclosure leads to longer conversations, preserving the causal phrasing 'Does high self-disclosure lead to longer conversations?' or an unambiguous paraphrase.

Must explicitly include the sub-question labeled as Q2 that asks about differences in conversation length patterns over time depending on overall self-disclosure level, including both 'over time' and 'overall self-disclosure level' or clear equivalents.

Must mention the concept of different self-disclosure levels across dyads, including a reference to a 'low self-disclosure (SD) level dyad' or an equivalent phrase indicating a dyad with low self-disclosure.

decisions: What criteria does the paper use to define a Twitter conversation instance for analysis?

requirements.description: Must state that a Twitter conversation unit is defined as a multi-tweet exchange between two or more users, not a single tweet in isolation.
Must specify that each conversation in the dataset is required to contain at least 5 tweets (e.g., as described in the data preprocessing or conversation construction subsection).
Must specify that, for a conversation to be included, each participating user must post at least one reply within that conversation thread.

Must draw these conversation inclusion criteria (minimum tweet count and per-user reply requirement) from the paper's dataset description or conversation sampling section, not infer them from results or discussion sections.
Must correctly retrieve any explicit numeric thresholds related to conversation length (e.g., '5 or more tweets') used to filter or construct the Twitter conversation dataset.

decisions: What does the paper report about the range of conversation topics users discuss with others on Twitter in the context of self-disclosure analysis?

requirements.description: Must identify that the paper uses a topic model (or equivalent topic categorization method) to characterize the content of Twitter conversations.
Must retrieve and use information from the section that introduces or describes the discovered conversation topics (e.g., a section describing topic modeling results or topic categories).
Must reference any figure that summarizes or lists the main conversation topics (e.g., a figure showing topic distributions or example topics) if such a figure exists.

Must extract at least two concrete example topics or topic labels that the model finds in users' Twitter conversations (e.g., health, relationships, daily activities), if such labels are provided in tables or text.
Must note that the conversation topics are derived from a large-scale Twitter dataset (on the order of millions of tweets or conversations) rather than from small, manually coded samples.

decisions: What challenges and gaps in existing self-disclosure (SD) research does the paper identify as motivation for its computational study of Twitter conversations?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper explicitly notes a lack of ground-truth datasets that quantify or label the level/intensity of self-disclosure (SD level).
Must identify that the paper mentions there is no existing tagged or annotated dataset specifically for self-disclosure in Twitter conversations.
Must capture that the paper points out the absence of accessible self-disclosure datasets in general (beyond Twitter), as part of its discussion of prior resources or data limitations.
Must report that the paper highlights a lack of prior studies on self-disclosure within the field of computational linguistics or NLP, distinguishing this from social psychology work.

Must mention that the paper refers to definitions and examples of self-disclosure from social psychology and to related word categories in LIWC (citing Houghton 2012) as existing but insufficient resources for SD research.

decisions: How did the authors construct the ground truth dataset for self-disclosure classification in terms of annotators and annotation platform?

requirements.description: Must state that the ground truth labels for self-disclosure were obtained via human annotation rather than automatic labeling or distant supervision.
Must specify that each item (e.g., tweet or conversation segment) was evaluated by three separate human judges/annotators to create the ground truth.
Must indicate that annotation was conducted using a web-based platform or web interface, not paper forms, email, or standalone software.
Must reference the figure or screenshot in the paper that shows the annotation web-based platform interface used by the judges.
Must draw from the paper's dataset/annotation or experimental setup section where the construction of the ground truth dataset and annotation procedure are described.

decisions: How does the paper justify using first-person pronouns as features for detecting self-disclosure in Twitter conversations, and what examples from the annotated dataset support this assumption?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper assumes first-person pronouns are good indicators of self-disclosure, explicitly linking pronoun use to the self-disclosure construct.
Must identify that first-person pronouns are used as features in the classification/modeling of self-disclosure (e.g., as discriminative lexical features in the topic/modeling framework).

Must retrieve the part of the paper where prior work is cited to justify this assumption, specifically referencing previous research by Joinson et al. (2001) and Barak et al. (2007) in the context of first-person pronouns and self-disclosure.

Must report that first-person pronouns were empirically observed as highly discriminative features between the G and M/H categories in the annotated dataset, using the same category labels as in the paper.

Must extract or accurately paraphrase example n-grams or short phrases from the annotated dataset that contain first-person pronouns (e.g., phrases beginning with 'my', 'I', 'I'm', 'I've', including family-related mentions like 'my dad' or 'my mom') to illustrate their discriminative role.

decisions: How does the paper define and exemplify topic-level differences between general and sensitive self-disclosure in Twitter conversations using LDA topics from Bak (2012)?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper distinguishes between different self-disclosure levels (e.g., M and H levels) based on topic content, specifically contrasting general versus sensitive information about self or intimate matters.
Must identify that self-disclosure related topics are obtained using an LDA-based topic model and explicitly attribute this to Bak (2012) or an equivalent citation in the paper.
Must retrieve the specific LDA topic labels used for self-disclosure analysis, including at least the six topic names: Location, Time, Adult, Health, Family, and Profanity.

Must retrieve representative top words for each of the six LDA topics as shown in the paper (e.g., for Location: 'san', 'live', 'state', 'texas', 'south'; for Time: 'tonight', 'time', 'tomorrow', 'good', 'ill'; for Adult: 'pants', 'wear', 'boobs', 'naked', 'wearing'; for Health: 'teeth', 'doctor', 'dr', 'dentist', 'tooth'; for Family: 'family', 'brother', 'sister', 'uncle', 'cousin'; for Profanity: 'nigga', 'lmao', 'shit', 'ass', 'bitch').

Must report that the paper formalizes self-disclosure as topics describing general information about self and provide example categories such as name, location, email address, job, physical appearance, health, sexuality, and death.

decisions: Does the summary correctly identify and describe the Self-Disclosure Topic Model (SDTM) structure and its use for classifying self-disclosure levels and inferring self-disclosure in Twitter conversations?

requirements.description: Must describe the graphical model of the Self-Disclosure Topic Model (SDTM) as presented in the paper, explicitly noting it as a probabilistic/graphical model for self-disclosure.
Must explain that SDTM classifies self-disclosure at a coarse level by distinguishing between a general (G) level and merged medium/high (M/H) self-disclosure levels.
Must explain that SDTM further classifies within the merged M/H group to distinguish between separate medium (M) and high (H) self-disclosure levels.
Must state that SDTM uses predefined seed words for each self-disclosure level (G, M, H or G vs M/H) as part of its semi-supervised topic modeling approach.

Must describe, in procedural terms, how SDTM infers the self-disclosure level of tweets or conversations (e.g., using the learned topic/level distributions over words and documents), corresponding to the paper's figure or text that gives a rough inference process.

decisions: How does the paper describe the maximum entropy classifier used in relation to other classifiers and prior topic modeling work?

requirements.description: Must state that the maximum entropy classifier is trained/learned from an annotated (labeled) dataset, as explicitly described in the paper's methodology section on classification.
Must explicitly report that the maximum entropy classifier performs better than the alternative classifiers evaluated in the paper, not just that it is competitive or comparable.

Must list the specific baseline classifiers that the maximum entropy classifier is compared against in the paper: C4.5, Naive Bayes, and SVM with linear, polynomial, and radial basis function (RBF) kernels.
Must identify that the maximum entropy classifier is used to identify or classify aspects and opinions (self-disclosure related content) within the topic model framework described in the paper.

Must reference that the use of the maximum entropy classifier for identifying aspects and opinions is linked to or inspired by prior work by Zhao et al. (2010), including an explicit citation or mention of [Zhao2010] as given in the paper.

decisions: How does the paper obtain and define seed words as prior knowledge for different self-disclosure levels in its topic model?

requirements.description: Must state that seed words are used as prior knowledge for each self-disclosure level and that there is also a condition with no seed words corresponding to a symmetric prior.
Must describe the data-driven approach using the Twitter conversation dataset to derive seed words by extracting frequently occurring trigrams that begin with the first-person pronouns 'I' and 'my'.

Must list at least three example trigrams for each of the four Twitter-based categories: Name (e.g., 'My name is', 'My last name', 'My real name'), Birthday (e.g., 'My birthday is', 'My birthday party', 'My bday is'), Location (e.g., 'I live in', 'I lived in', 'I live on'), and Occupation/School (e.g., 'My job is', 'My new job', 'My high school').
Must explain that an external dataset, Six Billion Secrets, is used to obtain additional seed words by extracting high-ranked word features from user-written secret posts.

Must report at least two example seed words for each of the three Six Billion Secrets categories: Physical appearance (e.g., 'chubby', 'fat', 'acne'), Health condition (e.g., 'addicted', 'surgery', 'syndrome', 'disorder'), and Death (e.g., 'dead', 'died', 'suicide', 'funeral').

decisions: What feature sets does the paper report using for classifying self-disclosure in Twitter conversations?

requirements.description: Must identify that one feature set is explicitly described as 'Bag of Words + Bigrams + Trigrams features' in the classification approach.
Must identify that a second feature set is explicitly described as 'Seed words and trigrams features' in the classification approach.
Must identify that a third feature set is explicitly described as 'FirstP and SEED feature' (or equivalently named with both 'FirstP' and 'SEED') in the classification approach.

Must retrieve these three feature set names from the part of the paper that describes the classification model or experimental setup for self-disclosure detection (e.g., methods or experiments section), not from unrelated sections such as introduction or related work.

Must treat each of the three feature sets ('Bag of Words + Bigrams + Trigrams features', 'Seed words and trigrams features', and 'FirstP and SEED feature') as distinct configurations used for classifier training or evaluation, not as generic or interchangeable feature descriptions.

decisions: How does the paper’s analysis of self-disclosure topics and conversation length (CL) characterize high-, mid-, and low-level self-disclosure groups and their effects on conversation dynamics over time?

requirements.description: Must identify that the three self-disclosure levels are explicitly labeled as G, M, and H levels (e.g., low/medium/high self-disclosure groups) in the context of topic ranking.

Must describe the representation of high-ranked topics by listing example high-probability words from at least one topic line that includes political terms (e.g., a line containing 'obama', 'romney', 'vote', or 'president').
Must state that topic quality or topic characterization is shown using 'high probability words in each topic' as the basis for presenting high-ranked topics for each self-disclosure level.

Must report that there is a positive relationship between the initial self-disclosure (SD) level and changes in conversation length (CL), explicitly answering Q1 that higher initial SD leads to longer conversations.

Must report that for Q2, high and mid self-disclosure groups show increasing CL over time while the low group does not, and must additionally state that high groups talk more in a conversation than both mid and low groups.

decisions: What are the main contributions of the paper regarding self-disclosure level analysis in Twitter conversations?

requirements.description: Must identify that the paper introduces a novel semi-supervised/self-disclosure topic model method specifically named or described as SDTM for identifying self-disclosure (SD) levels in Twitter conversations.

Must state that the authors constructed a ground-truth Twitter conversation dataset labeled with self-disclosure (SD) levels, explicitly indicating that SD level annotations are present at the conversation or tweet level.

Must extract from the contributions or dataset/annotation description sections that this is the first annotated Twitter conversation dataset for SD level and that the dataset is intended to be shared or made available to other researchers.
Must report that SDTM is empirically shown (via experiments, metrics, or comparisons) to perform better than baseline or alternative methods for SD level identification.

Must retrieve that the paper analyzes and demonstrates relations between self-disclosure (SD) and social dynamics (e.g., relationship strength, subsequent conversation behavior), and concludes that strategic self-disclosure can strengthen relationships in Twitter conversations.

decisions: What future research directions does the paper propose regarding using self-disclosure on Twitter to predict user states and provide social support and feedback?

requirements.description: Must identify that the paper proposes extending self-disclosure analysis from individual tweets/conversations to a user's general messages or overall message history (e.g., phrasing like 'self-disclosure for a user's general messages' or equivalent).

Must state that the paper explicitly links self-disclosure to online social network usage, including citing or referencing Trepte (2013) or an equivalent prior work on self-disclosure and online social network usage.

Must extract the proposed application that self-disclosure signals could be used to predict users' loneliness or related psychosocial states, as described in the paper's discussion or future work section.

Must identify the proposed methodological direction of using self-disclosure patterns to infer or model users' usage patterns on online social networks (e.g., frequency, type, or style of use) as a future research step.
Must cover the paper's discussion or future work section where the authors propose using inferred self-disclosure to provide social support and feedback to users based on their usage patterns.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the paper’s motivation and high-level contributions in the introduction, specifically regarding multi-source attention and the proposed techniques and tasks?

requirements.description: Must state that modeling attention over multiple source sequences (multi-source sequence-to-sequence learning) is relatively unexplored, reflecting the motivation text in the abstract/introduction.

Must identify that the paper proposes two novel approaches/techniques for combining attention over multiple sources, corresponding to the 'flat' and 'hierarchical' strategies described in the abstract/introduction.
Must extract from the abstract/introduction that the proposed attention combination methods are applied to two tasks: WMT16 Multimodal Translation and Automatic Post-editing.

Must mention that there is no universal method that explicitly models the importance of each input source in multi-source settings, capturing the stated gap/problem motivation in the abstract/introduction.

decisions: Does the slide correctly present the core setting and example applications of multi-source sequence-to-sequence learning as described in the paper?

requirements.description: Must state that the model can take any number of input source sequences, not just two, reflecting the general multi-source setting described in the paper.
Must explicitly mention that the multiple input sequences can come from different modalities (e.g., text and images), aligning with the paper's multimodal focus.
Must reference Figure 1 by name ("Figure 1") and identify it specifically as a multimodal translation example illustrating the use of multiple modalities as inputs.

Must list multimodal translation and automatic post-editing as example tasks or applications of the proposed multi-source sequence-to-sequence framework, as described in the task/experiment sections (WMT16 Multimodal Translation and Automatic Post-editing).
Must identify multi-source machine translation as an additional application scenario of the multi-source sequence-to-sequence setting, distinct from multimodal translation and automatic post-editing.

decisions: How does the paper formally define the single-source attention computation at each decoder step, and how is this formulation used as a starting point to motivate handling multiple input sequences?

requirements.description: Must state that at each decoder step i, the model computes a probability distribution (attention weights) over encoder hidden states conditioned on the current decoder state.
Must present the attention scoring function in the form e_ij = v_a^T tanh(W_a s_i + U_a h_j) (or an equivalent notation clearly matching eij va tanh(Wasi Uahj) from the paper).
Must explain that the decoder receives a context vector at each step, computed as a weighted sum of encoder hidden states using the attention distribution.
Must draw from the section that introduces the baseline single-source attention mechanism (before multi-source extensions), not from sections describing flat or hierarchical multi-source attention.

Must explicitly mention that the described single-source attention formulation is the basis for asking how to extend attention to handle multiple inputs (e.g., multiple source sequences or modalities).

decisions: How does the paper describe the context vector concatenation strategy for combining attention over multiple source sequences in multi-source sequence-to-sequence learning?

requirements.description: Must state that, in the context vector concatenation strategy, attention over each input/source sequence is computed independently (i.e., separate attention mechanisms per source).

Must describe that the outputs/context vectors from the independent attention mechanisms are concatenated or otherwise combined only at a later stage in the decoder/network, rather than during the attention computation itself.

Must identify and draw from the specific part of the paper where the authors introduce and define the context vector concatenation (or equivalent baseline) as an attention combination strategy for multi-source inputs.

Must distinguish this late combination (concatenation of independently computed context vectors) from the paper's proposed flat or hierarchical attention combination methods, explicitly indicating it is a different, simpler strategy.

Must reference any figure or diagram (if present) that illustrates multiple attention modules over different sources feeding their context vectors into a later combination layer (e.g., concatenation before the decoder state update).

decisions: How does the paper define and parameterize the flat attention combination mechanism for multiple sources, and what design question does it raise about sharing projection parameters?

requirements.description: Must state that in flat attention combination the importance of different inputs (multiple sources) is reflected in a single, joint attention distribution over all source positions.
Must specify the attention energy computation for the single-source case in the form e_ij = v_a^T tanh(W_a s_i + U_a h_j) (or equivalent notation clearly showing v_a, W_a, U_a, s_i, and h_j).

Must specify the attention energy computation for the multi-source flat combination case in the form e_ij^(k) = v_a^T tanh(W_a s_i + U_a^(k) h_j^(k)) (or equivalent notation clearly indicating a source index k and source-specific projection matrix U_a^(k)).

Must describe that source hidden states h_j^(k) are projected into a common representation space using source-specific projection matrices U_a^(k) and U_c^(k) (or equivalent notation), and that these projections are applied before forming the context vector c_i.

Must explicitly mention that the paper raises the design question of whether the projection parameters for attention and context, U_a^(k) and U_c^(k), should be shared (i.e., U_a^(k) = U_c^(k)) across their respective roles.

decisions: How does the paper define and compute hierarchical attention combination for multi-source sequence-to-sequence learning?

requirements.description: Must state that in the hierarchical attention combination strategy, the attention distribution is first computed separately (factored) for each input/source sequence rather than jointly over all sources.

Must describe the first attention step where, for each source k, a context vector is computed as a weighted sum over encoder hidden states h_j^(k) using a vanilla attention distribution α_ij^(k) (i.e., c_i^(k) = Σ_j α_ij^(k) h_j^(k)).

Must describe the second attention step where another attention distribution is computed over the intermediate context vectors c_i^(k) to obtain the final context vector c_i, including the use of an energy term e_i^(k) defined with parameters v_b, W_b, and U_b^(k) in a tanh nonlinearity (e_i^(k) = v_b^T tanh(W_b s_i + U_b^(k) c_i^(k)) or equivalent).
Must state that, as in the flat attention combination scenario, the per-source context vectors (or their projections) must be mapped into a shared space before being combined.

Must mention that the paper explicitly raises the design question of whether to share or not share the projection matrices U_b^(k) and U_c^(k) (or similarly named per-source projection parameters) across different sources in the hierarchical attention combination.

decisions: What experimental setups and evaluation configurations were used to assess flat and hierarchical attention strategies in multimodal translation and automatic post-editing?

requirements.description: Must identify and use the paper's experiments/results section that reports evaluations on both the multimodal translation (MMT) task and the automatic post-editing (APE) task.
Must state that experiments are conducted for both flat and hierarchical attention scenarios and that, for each, configurations with sharing and without sharing the projection matrices are compared.
Must describe the use of the sentinel gate mechanism (citing Lu et al., 2016) as an experimental condition that allows the decoder to decide whether or not to attend to any encoder.
Must mention that the experiments are implemented using the Neural Monkey toolkit and that the code availability (e.g., a repository link) is explicitly referenced in the experiments section.

Must retrieve from the relevant results table(s) that: (a) evaluation metrics include BLEU and METEOR for MMT and BLEU and HTER for APE, (b) experiments are run on the Multi30k dataset and the APE dataset, and (c) the table contains columns 'share' (indicating whether the projection matrix is shared for energies and context vector computation) and 'sent.' (indicating whether the sentinel vector is used).

decisions: Does the system correctly retrieve and reproduce the example illustrating an attention-based translation output and its reference from the paper?

requirements.description: Must state that the example illustrates an output generated with an attention-based model (e.g., explicitly include the phrase 'Output with attention').

Must identify and extract the specific example segment that contains both the German source sentence and its English gloss/translation as presented in the paper's example section (the 'Source: Output with attention:' block).
Must reproduce the German source output with attention exactly as in the paper example, including word order and spacing errors: 'ein Mannschlaft auf einemgrunenSofain einemgrunenRaum.'
Must reproduce the English gloss/translation line exactly as in the paper example: 'A man sleeping in a green room on a couch.'
Must reproduce the German reference sentence exactly as in the paper example: 'ein Mann schlaft in einem grunen Raum auf einem Sofa .' including the final space before the period.

decisions: Does the summary correctly capture the paper’s main empirical conclusions about the two proposed multi-source attention combination methods compared to the concatenation baseline?

requirements.description: Must state that both proposed attention combination methods (flat and hierarchical) achieve results that are comparable to the existing baseline approach, explicitly identified as concatenation of the context vectors.

Must report that hierarchical attention combination achieves the best results specifically on the WMT16 Multimodal Translation (MMT) task, as shown in the corresponding results section or tables for that task.

Must indicate that hierarchical attention combination is faster to train than the baseline or alternative methods, as supported by the training-time or efficiency discussion in the experiments or analysis sections.

Must explain that both proposed attention combination methods make it straightforward ("trivial") to inspect or analyze the attention distribution with respect to each individual input source, as described in the discussion or analysis of interpretability/inspection in the paper.

Must base all of the above points on the paper’s concluding or results discussion sections (e.g., final results/analysis or conclusion), rather than inferring them solely from the abstract or introduction.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and state how neural machine translation (NMT) is characterized in the paper’s introductory/contextual discussion, specifically its state-of-the-art status and industrial adoption?

requirements.description: Must state that neural machine translation (NMT) is described in the paper as driving or underpinning the current state-of-the-art in machine translation performance.
Must extract this characterization of NMT (state-of-the-art and industry adoption) from the paper’s introductory or background/context discussion rather than from experimental or conclusion sections.
Must correctly retrieve and attribute the citation to Sennrich et al. (2016) as the reference supporting the claim that NMT is driving the current state-of-the-art.
Must explicitly state that NMT is widely adopted or widely used by industry, reflecting the paper’s description of its industrial uptake.

Must treat the statements about NMT’s state-of-the-art status and industry adoption as general contextual claims about NMT, not as specific claims about the proposed string-to-tree method in this paper.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize how prior syntax-based SMT approaches relate to newer neural MT systems in the context of this paper?

requirements.description: Must state that prior state-of-the-art machine translation before this work was syntax-based SMT systems that explicitly used syntactic information.
Must describe that the central motivation of the paper is to bring the benefits of syntax (e.g., parse-tree-based linguistic information) into neural machine translation systems.
Must explicitly mention that the syntactic information in earlier systems was typically represented as parse trees or constituency trees.
Must identify and reference the discussion in the paper that contrasts syntax-based SMT with syntax-agnostic NMT, including the claim that NMT had surpassed syntax-based SMT performance by 2016.
Must mention that the paper's approach is positioned as a response to syntax-based SMT being beaten by NMT, motivating a syntax-aware neural approach (string-to-tree NMT).

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize how the paper defines and characterizes constituency (phrase-structure) grammar and constituency structure?

requirements.description: Must state that a constituency (phrase-structure) grammar is defined in terms of a set of rewrite rules that describe the structure of the language.
Must explicitly mention that constituency structure groups words into larger units called constituents.
Must explicitly mention that constituency structure defines a hierarchy between constituents.
Must explicitly mention that constituency structure draws relations between different constituents, including words, phrases, and clauses.

Must extract these four properties (rewrite rules, grouping into constituents, hierarchy, and relations between words/phrases/clauses) from the part of the paper that introduces or defines constituency or phrase-structure grammar, rather than from unrelated sections such as experiments or results.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the paper’s stated reasons why incorporating target-side syntax can help neural machine translation?

requirements.description: Must state that syntax provides explicit hints about which word sequences or constituents belong together in the target sentence (i.e., grouping of words into phrases/constituents).
Must state that using syntactic structure helps produce well-formed or well-structured target sentences (e.g., grammatical or structurally coherent outputs).
Must state that syntactic information enables or improves informed reordering decisions during translation, specifically by using the target-side syntactic structure.
Must state that syntax encourages or supports modeling long-distance dependencies when selecting target-language translations (e.g., dependencies between distant words or phrases).
Must connect these benefits explicitly to the paper’s approach of translating into linearized, lexicalized constituency trees as the mechanism by which syntax is incorporated.

decisions: How does the proposed string-to-tree NMT approach incorporate target-side syntax while remaining compatible with standard seq2seq architectures?

requirements.description: Must state that the main idea is to translate a source sentence into a linearized, lexicalized constituency tree (i.e., a linearized tree) of the target sentence, not directly into a plain target sentence string.
Must explicitly mention that the syntactic information used is on the target side (target language syntax), not the source side.
Must explain that the approach uses a standard sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) neural machine translation framework without architectural changes, enabled by representing trees in linearized form.
Must identify that the linearized tree representation is inspired by prior work on RNN-based syntactic parsing, specifically citing Vinyals et al. (2015) and/or Choe & Charniak (2016).
Must draw from the paper's description of the proposed model/approach (the section where the string-to-tree NMT method is introduced), not from the abstract-only discussion of results or evaluation.

decisions: What experimental setup details does the paper specify regarding the NMT toolkit, subword segmentation, target-side parsing, and their integration for training?

requirements.description: Must state that the experiments use the Nematus toolkit and explicitly attribute it to Sennrich et al. 2017.
Must state that joint BPE (Byte Pair Encoding) segmentation is used and explicitly attribute it to Sennrich et al. 2016.
Must state that, for training, the target side of the parallel data is parsed using the BLLIP parser and explicitly attribute it to McClosky, Charniak and Johnson, 2006.

Must indicate that the described setup requires careful coordination or compatibility between BPE segmentation, tokenization, and the parser (i.e., making BPE, tokenization, and parser work together).

decisions: How do the large-scale WMT16 German-to-English experiments compare the syntax-aware NMT model against the baseline, and what is the outcome in terms of BLEU?

requirements.description: Must state that the large-scale experiments are conducted on German-to-English translation, explicitly identifying German as the source language and English as the target language.
Must report the training data size for the large-scale experiment as approximately 4.5 million parallel sentence pairs from the WMT16 dataset.
Must specify that two NMT models are trained for comparison: a syntax-aware model (string-to-tree) and a syntax-agnostic baseline model.
Must indicate that both NMT models are trained using the same experimental setup, matching the settings of the state-of-the-art (SOTA) neural system used in WMT16.
Must state that the syntax-aware NMT model outperforms the baseline in terms of BLEU score on the large-scale WMT16 German-to-English task.

decisions: Does the paper’s experimental evidence show that the syntax-aware (string-to-tree) NMT model consistently outperforms the syntax-agnostic baseline in low-resource settings, including the number of comparisons and BLEU score gains?

requirements.description: Must identify that the comparison is between a syntax-aware neural machine translation model (translating into linearized, lexicalized constituency trees) and a syntax-agnostic NMT baseline.
Must state that BLEU is the evaluation metric used to compare the syntax-aware model and the baseline in the low-resource experiments.
Must report that the syntax-aware model achieves better BLEU scores than the baseline in all reported low-resource comparisons, and that there are 12 such comparisons.
Must report the magnitude of improvement as being up to slightly more than 2 BLEU points (e.g., 'up to 2+ BLEU improvement') in the low-resource experiments.
Must attribute these findings specifically to the experimental section dealing with low-resource or reduced-data conditions, not to the full-data WMT16 German-English setting alone.

decisions: Does the system correctly report the paper’s empirical findings about the syntactic well-formedness of predicted target-side trees on the development set?

requirements.description: Must state that the evaluation concerns the syntactic quality of predicted target-side constituency trees produced by the syntax-aware NMT system, not source-side trees or generic parses.
Must report the specific quantitative result that approximately 99% of the predicted trees in the development set had valid bracketing (or an equivalent explicit percentage if given in the paper).

Must draw from the part of the paper where the authors analyze the well-formedness or validity of predicted trees on the development set (e.g., an analysis or evaluation subsection), not from sections discussing BLEU scores or human evaluation of translation quality.

Must indicate that the authors performed a manual, qualitative inspection ("eye-balling" or equivalent phrasing) of a sample of predicted trees to assess their form, in addition to the automatic bracketing validity check.

Must convey the qualitative conclusion from the manual inspection that the predicted trees were generally well-formed and followed expected syntactic patterns (or equivalent wording provided in the paper).

decisions: Does the summary correctly explain how the attention-based, syntax-aware NMT model affects source–target alignments compared to the baseline?

requirements.description: Must state that the NMT system uses an attention-based model that induces soft (probabilistic) alignments between source and target tokens or phrases.
Must explicitly distinguish between a syntax-agnostic baseline model and a syntax-aware model that incorporates target-side syntactic information (e.g., via linearized constituency trees).
Must state that the syntax-aware model produces more sensible or improved alignments compared to the baseline, specifically in terms of the attention-induced source–target alignment patterns.
Must reference or implicitly draw from the paper's analysis or discussion section where alignments or attention patterns of the syntax-aware model are compared to those of the baseline.

Must describe or allude to any figure or example in the paper that visualizes attention weights or alignment patterns (e.g., alignment heatmaps or attention matrices) used to argue that the syntax-aware model yields more sensible alignments.

decisions: Does the summary correctly describe how the syntax-aware NMT model’s attention behaves when producing opening brackets of target constituency trees, and what this implies about learning source syntax?

requirements.description: Must state that the analysis concerns attention weights specifically during the production of opening brackets in the linearized target constituency trees.
Must describe that the authors inspect or analyze the model’s attention distribution over the source sentence tokens while generating these opening brackets.
Must report that the model consistently attends to the main verb in the source sentence when producing tree opening brackets (e.g., a verb like "hatte").
Must report that the model also attends to structural or punctuation markers in the source sentence (e.g., question marks, hyphens) during this process.
Must explicitly state the authors’ interpretation that this attention behavior indicates the system implicitly learns aspects of source syntax and may use this to plan or organize decoding.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize how the paper analyzes and interprets reordering behavior in German-to-English translation using syntax-aware NMT?

requirements.description: Must state that German-to-English translation involves a significant amount of word/phrase reordering during translation, as a motivation for the analysis.
Must report that quantitative analysis of reordering shows the syntax-aware system performs more reordering than the baseline during training or translation.
Must describe that GHKM rules (Galley et al., 2004) are extracted from the development set using predicted target-side trees and attention-induced word alignments.
Must explain that the purpose of extracting GHKM rules is to interpret the increased reordering from a syntactic perspective.

Must specify that the most common extracted GHKM rules correspond to linguistically sensible transformations, including moving the verb from the end of a German constituent to the beginning of the corresponding English constituent.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize how the syntax-aware NMT model handles relative constructions and relative pronouns, including the specific German–English example translations provided in the paper?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper analyzes a specific linguistic structure: relative constructions (e.g., patterns like 'The XXX which YYY' or 'A XXX whose YYY') as part of evaluating the syntax-aware NMT system.

Must explain that the connecting words in these constructions are relative pronouns (e.g., who, which, whom) and that the syntax-aware system produces more relative pronouns due to access to syntactic context.

Must retrieve the German example sentence 'Guangzhou, das in Deutschland auch Kanton genannt wird' and at least one corresponding English translation variant discussed in the paper (e.g., 'Guangzhou, which is also known as Canton in Germany').

Must retrieve the German example sentence beginning with 'Zugleich droht der stark von internationalen Firmen abhangigen' and at least one corresponding English translation variant that includes a relative clause (e.g., 'At the same time, the image of the region, which is heavily reliant on international companies').

Must explicitly connect these relative-construction examples to a comparative outcome, namely that the syntax-aware system generates more appropriate relative pronouns/relative clauses than the syntax-agnostic baseline.

decisions: How did the authors conduct the small-scale human evaluation and what advantage did the syntax-aware system show over the baseline?

requirements.description: Must identify and summarize the specific subsection describing the small-scale human evaluation (including its purpose and setup) rather than general automatic evaluation or BLEU score sections.
Must state that the human evaluation was conducted on the first 500 sentences of the WMT/newstest 2015 test set (or equivalent wording explicitly indicating 'first 500 sentences in newstest 2015').
Must state that the human judgments were collected via Amazon Mechanical Turk (or explicitly 'mechanical turk') and that there were two human annotators/turkers per sentence.
Must state that the syntax-aware (string-to-tree) translation system had an overall advantage over the baseline system in the human evaluation (i.e., was preferred more often).

Must report the three-way outcome breakdown of the human evaluation in terms of preferences between systems, including that some sentences were 'neutral' and that there were counts or proportions where the baseline (e.g., 'bpe') was better and where the syntax-aware system (e.g., 'tree') was better (capturing the '2bpe better neutral 2tree better' style result).

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the paper’s main conclusions about the benefits and generality of target-side syntax in neural machine translation and related generation tasks?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper concludes neural machine translation benefits from incorporating target-side syntactic information (specifically, target-side syntax in the form of syntactic structure).
Must convey the high-level recommendation that symbolic linguistic information (linguistics) should not be discarded because neural systems can leverage it.
Must identify that the syntactic information used is target-side constituency structure, implemented as translation into linearized, lexicalized constituency trees.

Must cover the paper’s concluding discussion that the proposed syntax-aware approach is general and not limited to machine translation, i.e., it can be incorporated into other neural language generation tasks.

Must explicitly mention at least one example of other neural language generation tasks (such as summarization or image caption generation) as target applications for the general approach, as stated in the conclusions.

decisions: Did the system correctly identify that the slide is illustrating an example of a full-length, user-written product review used as target output for personalized review generation in recommender systems?

requirements.description: Must state that the slide content represents an example of a complete, natural-language product review (user-generated review text) rather than a model architecture, algorithm description, or quantitative result.

Must attribute the slide content to the part of the paper that provides qualitative examples or case studies of generated (or target) reviews, typically in an experiments, analysis, or examples subsection, and not to background, related work, or model description sections.

Must connect the example review on the slide to the paper's encoder-decoder framework for personalized review generation from short phrases (e.g., explain that such long-form reviews are the type of outputs produced from short input phrases like product titles or summaries).

Must mention that the review text on the slide is associated with a specific item (e.g., a tablet such as the Samsung Galaxy Tab E) and reflects user-level personalization, aligning with the paper's focus on user- and item-specific review generation.

Must explicitly describe the slide content as a qualitative result (an illustrative review example) used to demonstrate the coherence and usefulness of the generated or target reviews, rather than as training data statistics or evaluation metrics.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify that the paper’s assistive review-writing system expands short input phrases into full reviews and estimates user reactions to provide suggestions?

requirements.description: Must state that the system generates or writes personalized reviews by expanding short phrases such as review summaries or product titles, as described in the abstract.
Must explicitly connect the model’s purpose to helping users write reviews or building an assistive review-writing system, as framed in the abstract problem statement.
Must describe that an encoder-decoder framework is used to take short phrases as input and produce expanded review text as output, reflecting the phrase expansion process.

Must mention that aspect-aware user and item representations are learned via an aspect encoder and used to control or influence generation, implying the system estimates or conditions on user/item reactions or preferences.

Must extract information from the problem formulation or introduction-style description (e.g., the part of the abstract that defines the task and input-output behavior) to support both slide points: phrase expansion and suggestion/reaction estimation.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize how the paper incorporates aspect information and user/item attributes, including the representative aspect words shown in Table 1 and the related work context, to generate personalized reviews from short phrases?

requirements.description: Must state that the model generates personalized product reviews by expanding short user-provided phrases (e.g., review summaries or product titles) rather than generating from scratch.
Must describe that the system incorporates user and item attributes via an aspect encoder that learns aspect-aware user and item representations.

Must reference Table 1 explicitly as presenting 'representative words of aspects' and identify that it lists example words grouped by aspects such as Service, Price, Screen, Interaction, and a drive/storage-related aspect (e.g., Drive/disk).

Must retrieve at least three concrete representative words for each of the following aspects from Table 1: (a) Service (e.g., vendor, seller, supplier, reply, refund), (b) Price (e.g., price, value, overall, dependable, reliable), and (c) Screen (e.g., screen, touchscreen, browse, display, scrolling).

Must cover the part of the paper that discusses related work on incorporating user and item attributes for review generation, explicitly mentioning Dong et al. (EACL 2017) and Tang et al. (Arxiv 2016) as prior work on learning to generate product reviews and context-aware natural language generation with RNNs.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the architecture of the proposed personalized review generation method, including its encoders, attention mechanisms, and aspect-aware components, as depicted in the 'Proposed method' slide?

requirements.description: Must state that the proposed method uses three distinct encoders named 'Sequence Encoder', 'Attribute Encoder', and 'Aspect Encoder' to generate personalized reviews from short input phrases.

Must describe the presence of three corresponding attention mechanisms explicitly labeled 'Sequence attention', 'Attribute attention', and 'Aspect attention' that attend over the outputs of the respective encoders.

Must explain that the model incorporates 'Attribute latent factor' and 'Aspect-aware factor' representations, and uses an 'Aspect preference score' in combination with these factors to model user/item aspect preferences.

Must reference a projection or output layer explicitly labeled 'Projection layer' and 'Aspect bias' that combines aspect-related signals (including terms like Pv(display), Pdisplay in Ak(Ak), and Pw(display)) to produce the final generation-relevant representation.

Must mention that aspect inputs are represented as A1, A2, ..., Ak and that the model processes example text such as '<str> the display is beautiful and easy to' through embedding layers (referred to as 'Embedding layers easy to use') before applying the encoders and attention mechanisms.

decisions: How are the experiments configured in terms of vocabulary size and training objective for the personalized review generation model?

requirements.description: Must state that the model uses a fixed vocabulary of 30,000 tokens as part of the experimental configuration.
Must explicitly mention that this 30,000-token vocabulary is described as being much sparser than the vocabularies used in previous work or baselines in the paper's experimental setup section.
Must identify that the training procedure for the encoder-decoder model uses teacher-forcing during sequence generation.
Must specify that the loss function used for training is masked cross-entropy loss (i.e., cross-entropy computed only over non-masked / non-padding tokens).

Must attribute all three elements (30,000-token vocabulary, sparsity relative to prior work, teacher-forcing with masked cross-entropy loss) to the paper's experiment or training setup description rather than to the abstract or introduction.

decisions: What information from the paper is needed to correctly describe and label the automatic evaluation metrics comparison in Table 2?

requirements.description: Must identify that Table 2 is explicitly titled as a comparison of different algorithms (e.g., a caption containing the phrase 'Table 2 Comparison of different algorithms' or equivalent).
Must retrieve that Table 2 reports automatic evaluation metrics used to compare algorithms (e.g., BLEU, ROUGE, or other named metrics as listed in the table).
Must retrieve from Table 2 the list of algorithms or models being compared (e.g., baselines and the proposed personalized review generation model) as they appear in the table rows or columns.
Must link Table 2 to the section of the paper that discusses automatic evaluation metrics or experimental results, using the table number (Table 2) as the reference anchor.
Must recognize that Table 2 presents comparative performance results (numerical scores) for the different algorithms under the automatic evaluation metrics, not qualitative or human evaluation data.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and present the qualitative example comparing real and generated reviews across different models (Attr2Seq, ExpansionNet, +title, +attribute & aspect) for the same input summary?

requirements.description: Must state that the example illustrates personalized review generation by expanding a short input phrase/summary ("easy to use and nice standard apps") into a full review.

Must identify and use the qualitative examples section (often under an 'Examples of generated review' or similar qualitative analysis subsection) where concrete review texts for different models are shown.

Must reproduce or accurately paraphrase the layout of the example block that includes: the input 'Summary', the 'Real review', and separate lines for 'Attr2Seq', 'ExpansionNet', '+title', and '+attribute & aspect' outputs for the same item.

Must retrieve the exact or near-exact text of the real review: "the display is beautiful and the tablet is very easy to use. it comes with some really nice standard apps ." from the example in the paper.

Must distinguish between the different model variants shown in the example (baseline Attr2Seq, ExpansionNet, ExpansionNet +title, and ExpansionNet +attribute & aspect) and correctly associate each variant with its corresponding generated review text in the example.

decisions: Does the paper provide evidence that the proposed model achieves broader aspect coverage in generated reviews compared to baselines or real reviews, and how is this measured?

requirements.description: Must identify and describe the paper's definition of an 'aspect' and the notion of 'representative words' for an aspect as used in evaluating review coverage.
Must explain the evaluation procedure that counts an aspect as 'covered' (i.e., 'aspect plus one') when a generated review contains the representative words from that aspect.

Must retrieve the quantitative comparison (from the relevant table or figure) showing the number or proportion of aspects in generated reviews that are also covered in real reviews, for the proposed model versus at least one baseline.

Must describe the specific figure or table that visualizes or tabulates 'broader aspect coverage' (e.g., counts or percentages of aspects covered), including what each axis or column represents (generated review aspects vs. real review aspects).

Must state the direction of the main finding that the proposed model covers more real-review aspects than comparison methods, using the exact metric reported for aspect coverage (e.g., average # aspects per review, coverage ratio).

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the paper’s main conclusions and proposed future work about ExpansionNet, aspect-aware personalization, and extensions to other text generation tasks?

requirements.description: Must state that the proposed model (named ExpansionNet in the paper) is designed to generate personalized reviews by expanding short input phrases, explicitly mentioning the use of short phrases and/or product titles as inputs.

Must describe that the model incorporates aspect-level information via aspect embeddings or an aspect encoder, and that these aspect-aware representations capture user aspect preferences for personalized text generation.
Must indicate that the paper demonstrates the usefulness of aspect embedding and aspect extraction specifically for personalized text generation, not just for generic representation learning.

Must identify at least one explicit future work direction from the paper’s conclusion or discussion section that involves combining the current phrase-expansion review generation task with text rewriting or editing techniques.

Must mention that the authors propose or envision extending the system to generate longer-form texts beyond reviews, such as product recommendation articles or similarly longer recommendation-style content, as part of future work.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the paper’s problem framing about temporal distribution shift in document classification performance?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper investigates changes in the underlying data or language distribution over time (i.e., that the data distribution changes across time periods).

Must describe that the paper examines whether these temporal changes are systematic, explicitly referencing seasonal intervals (e.g., winter vs. summer) and non-seasonal intervals (e.g., specific years).

Must mention that the study evaluates document classifiers trained on documents from certain time intervals and tested on documents from other time intervals, highlighting cross-interval performance as the core experimental setup.

Must indicate that the temporal changes can involve subtle shifts in topic or how content is described (e.g., differences in how hotels are described in reviews across seasons), not only obvious or drastic changes.

Must convey that the paper’s motivation includes understanding whether and how models can be adapted or selected to handle these temporal distribution changes (e.g., that the best model may depend on the specific time period).

decisions: What experimental setup does the paper use to examine temporality in document classification, specifically regarding time periods, model type, features, and dataset grouping?

requirements.description: Must state that the experiments distinguish between two types of time periods (e.g., seasonal vs. non-seasonal) as part of the temporal analysis.
Must specify that logistic regression is the classification model used in the experiments.
Must specify that n-gram features are used as the input representation for the logistic regression classifier.
Must report that the experiments use six distinct datasets.
Must report that each of the six datasets is partitioned into approximately 4–6 time periods for the experiments.

decisions: How does document classification performance vary when training and testing across different temporal periods in the corpus?

requirements.description: Must state that classifiers are trained and evaluated separately on documents from each distinct time period (i.e., a model is trained on one time interval and tested on that same interval as a baseline).
Must describe that performance is explicitly measured when the test time period differs from the training time period, capturing cross-period generalization or performance drop.
Must indicate that the dataset is temporally balanced so that each time period contains the same number of documents used for training and testing.
Must mention that one observed or hypothesized temporal trend in the Yelp corpus is that reviews become more informative over time, as inferred from the temporal performance analysis.

Must note that the temporal performance analysis is used to reveal characteristics of the corpus (e.g., changes in language or content over time), while explicitly acknowledging that the underlying reasons for performance variation remain unexplained or are left as an open question.

decisions: How does the paper adapt document classifiers to temporal variations using domain adaptation, and how is this evaluated for future-time performance?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper frames temporal variation as a domain adaptation problem by treating explicitly defined time periods (both seasonal intervals and/or specific years) as separate domains.
Must identify the use of Daume III (2007)'s feature augmentation method and explain that it creates domain-specific copies of each feature, including a general copy and time-period-specific copies.

Must describe that for seasonal settings the feature space is split into at least four seasonal domains (e.g., General plus Jan–Mar, Apr–Jun, Jul–Sep, Oct–Dec) and that in non-seasonal settings the method is extended to include year-specific and season-specific feature copies, resulting in three copies per feature (general, year-specific, season-specific).

Must state that domain-specific features are weighted differently during training, i.e., the learning procedure separately weighs domain-specific feature copies rather than treating all copies identically.

Must describe the temporal evaluation protocol used to simulate performance on future data: train on initial time periods, tune hyperparameters on the second-to-last time period (held-out data from the chronological end of the corpus), and test on the final time period, and must note that this simple adaptation and tuning strategy leads to better performance on future data compared to not using it.

decisions: How does the paper illustrate parsing a simple sentence into a partial constituency tree using local transition decisions?

requirements.description: Must identify that the paper uses a transition-based constituency parser that builds trees incrementally via local decisions (e.g., shift/reduce or similar local transitions).
Must retrieve the section or subsection where the authors introduce an illustrative example sentence to demonstrate how the transition-based parser incrementally constructs a constituency tree.
Must describe the specific example of a short sentence (e.g., 'The cat took a nap' or an equivalent simple sentence) that is used in the paper to illustrate the parsing process.
Must extract the corresponding partial constituency tree representation from the paper that shows the top-level S node and at least an NP and VP constituent (e.g., '(S (NP ... (VP ...')).

Must explain that the example is used to demonstrate how local parsing decisions (transitions) map the input token sequence to the emerging bracketed tree structure, rather than to present experimental results.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and describe the example of non-local consequences in constituency parsing, including the specific token sequence and gold vs. predicted parse fragments used to illustrate error propagation?

requirements.description: Must state that the example illustrates a 'non-local consequence' in transition-based constituency parsing, where an early parsing decision affects later structure.
Must describe the concrete token sequence used in the example as exactly: 'The cat took a nap .' (including the final period as a separate token).
Must reproduce the sequence of predicted local labels above the sentence as 'NP NP VP NP' in that exact order.

Must distinguish between the gold/target parse and the model prediction by explicitly labeling them as 'Target' (or equivalent) and 'Prediction' (or equivalent) and showing that both begin with '(S (NP ...', with the prediction continuing '(S (NP (VP'.

Must identify and draw from the specific explanatory example section (or figure) in the paper that discusses non-local consequences or error propagation in the parser, rather than from experimental results or methodology sections.

decisions: What does dynamic oracle training do in constituency parsing, and how is it illustrated with true parse, prediction, and oracle examples in the paper?

requirements.description: Must state that dynamic oracle training involves exploring at training time and supervising each parser state with an expert policy (dynamic oracle).
Must explain that the dynamic oracle is used to choose actions that maximize achievable tree-level F1 (or log probability toward maximizing F1), as opposed to only following a static gold sequence.

Must describe the illustrative example that contrasts a 'True Parse', a 'Prediction', and an 'Oracle' parse, including that the true parse is of the form '(S (NP The cat', the prediction is of the form '(S (NP (VP The', and the oracle output is '(NP The The cat'.
Must identify that the dynamic oracle provides state-wise supervision by indicating the best next action (or structure) at each intermediate parser state, rather than only supervising the final tree.
Must draw from the part of the paper that defines or explains 'dynamic oracles' for transition-based constituency parsing, including how they relate to exploration during training.

decisions: Does the paper provide evidence that expert policies / dynamic oracles improve PTB constituency parsing F1, as reported in Coavoux and Crabbe (2016)?

requirements.description: Must identify and name the concept of 'expert policies' or 'dynamic oracles' as a supervision signal used for training constituency parsers.

Must locate and reference the part of the paper that discusses dynamic oracles or expert policies in the context of training constituency parsers (e.g., in the introduction, background, or related work section).
Must retrieve the reported PTB (Penn Treebank) constituency parsing F1 scores associated with dynamic-oracle or expert-policy training from the relevant table or results section.

decisions: Does the system correctly explain why training data from assisting languages must be judiciously selected for multilingual NER, including the potential negative influence on the primary language and illustrative cross-lingual examples?

requirements.description: Must state that multilingual NER often uses one or more assisting languages to improve performance on a primary language, explicitly identifying the roles of 'primary language' and 'assisting languages'.
Must state that annotated data from assisting languages can negatively influence or reduce the effectiveness of NER performance on the primary language when used naively.
Must mention that many languages have limited or scarce named entity annotated data, motivating the use of assisting languages in multilingual NER.

Must describe an example illustrating cross-lingual differences in capitalization of named entities, specifically that religions, languages, nationalities, etc. are uppercase in English but not in Spanish.

Must describe an example sentence pair contrasting English and another language (e.g., Hindi) that includes the named entity 'Washington' in both languages to illustrate cross-lingual variation in surface form or context (e.g., 'I am going to Washington' vs. its non-English counterpart).
