decisions: What specific cross-lingual tagging inconsistency between English and Spanish can undermine multilingual NER training in this paper?

requirements.description: Must identify that the paper discusses cross-lingual differences in how certain named entity categories (e.g., religions, languages, nationalities) are realized or tagged between English and Spanish.
Must state that the problematic difference highlighted is that these categories are written in uppercase in English but not in Spanish, leading to divergent tag distributions.

Must retrieve this English–Spanish capitalization example from the part of the paper where the authors explain what can go wrong or why multilingual learning for NER may fail (e.g., motivation/problem analysis section), not from unrelated background or experimental sections.
Must connect this capitalization/tagging inconsistency example to the paper's broader methodological point that divergence in tag distributions across languages can harm multilingual NER training.
Must explicitly mention both languages involved in the example (English and Spanish) when describing the uppercase vs. non-uppercase behavior for these entity types.

decisions: Did the system correctly retrieve and summarize the key prior work on data selection and cross-lingual variation as presented in the paper’s Related Work (Table 1) section?

requirements.description: Must cover the content associated with the 'Related Work' section that summarizes prior literature on data selection and cross-lingual variation, explicitly corresponding to what is listed in Table 1.

Must state that one line of related work focuses on selecting sentences from general-domain data that are most similar to in-domain data, and that a language model is used to measure similarity between general-domain and in-domain training data.

Must describe Ruder and Plank [2017] as learning to weigh various data selection measures, and Zhao et al. [2018] as selecting assisting data for multi-task domain adaptation where assisting language sentences with the highest log-likelihood values are selected.

Must explain that Ponti et al. [2018] measure cross-lingual syntactic variation by considering both morphological and structural properties, and that selecting an assisting language with a lower degree of anisomorphism is identified as crucial for knowledge transfer.
Must mention Table 1 explicitly as listing or summarizing the literature most relevant to the authors' work.

decisions: How does the paper’s proposed approach select assisting-language (English) sentences to improve Spanish NER performance?

requirements.description: Must state that the primary goal is to improve Spanish NER performance by adding English NER-annotated data as an assisting language.
Must describe that English sentences are selected based on the agreement in tag distributions of common named entities between English (assisting) and Spanish (primary).

Must explain that symmetric KL divergence (computed as KL(Eng‖Esp) and KL(Esp‖Eng) combined into SKL) is used to quantify tag distribution disagreement for common entities between English and Spanish.

Must specify that for each assisting-language sentence X, a sentence-level score Score(X) is computed by aggregating over words xi in X that also appear in the primary language, using their tag distributions Pa(xi) in both languages.
Must state that only assisting-language sentences whose sentence score Score(X) is below a predefined threshold are added to the primary-language (Spanish) training data.

decisions: What dataset statistics for English (Tjong Kim Sang and De Meulder NER dataset) are reported in the paper’s dataset statistics section/table for train and test token counts?

requirements.description: Must identify and use the paper's dedicated dataset statistics section or table (e.g., a table summarizing datasets per language) as the source for the slide content.
Must recognize that the English dataset used is the Tjong Kim Sang and De Meulder CoNLL NER dataset (or equivalent full citation) and associate it with the 'English' row in the dataset statistics.
Must retrieve the exact number of tokens in the training split for the English (Tjong Kim Sang and De Meulder) dataset as reported in the dataset statistics table.
Must retrieve the exact number of tokens in the test split for the English (Tjong Kim Sang and De Meulder) dataset as reported in the dataset statistics table.

Must preserve the tabular structure showing two separate columns labeled for training and test token counts (e.g., '(#Tokens) Train' and '(#Tokens) Test') when summarizing or recreating the slide content.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the paper’s description of the neural network architecture and its parameter sharing configuration across languages for multilingual NER?

requirements.description: Must state that the model uses parameter sharing configurations across multiple languages in the neural network for multilingual NER.
Must specify that sub-word feature extractors (e.g., character- or subword-level components) are shared across languages as part of the architecture design.
Must describe that the neural network is trained in a language-independent way, i.e., a single model is trained jointly for multiple languages rather than separate language-specific models.
Must reference Figure 1 in the paper as depicting the architecture of the neural network used in the multilingual NER setup.
Must attribute the neural network architecture in Figure 1 to Murthy and Bhattacharyya, matching the citation style used in the paper (e.g., 'Murthy and Bhattacharyya').

decisions: How do the F-scores from monolingual and multilingual NER training compare when using all assisting language data versus SKL-based data selection for German, Italian, and multiple Indian languages, and how is statistical significance reported?

requirements.description: Must retrieve from Table 3 that it reports F-scores on German and Italian test data comparing monolingual training ("Monolingual None") against multilingual strategies using assisting languages (e.g., Spanish, Dutch) with data selection settings "All" and "SKL".

Must retrieve from Table 4 that it reports test set F-scores for Indian languages (explicitly including Hindi, Marathi, Bengali, Malayalam, and Tamil) under two data selection conditions labeled "ALL" and "SKL".

Must identify that "SKL" in the tables refers to a symmetric KL-divergence-based data selection method applied to assisting language training instances, contrasted with using "All" assisting language data.

Must state that in both Table 3 and Table 4, SKL results that are statistically significant are explicitly indicated as being significant compared to using all assisting language data, with a p-value threshold of 0.05 using a two-sided Welch t-test.
Must note that in Table 4 the F-score result from monolingual training on the primary language is visually distinguished by being underlined, indicating the monolingual baseline within the table.

decisions: What visual analyses and experimental plots does the paper present to show how sentence-level symmetric KL (SKL) scores and SKL thresholds over assisting-language sentences affect multilingual NER performance for Italian?

requirements.description: Must identify and describe the figure that shows a histogram of English assisting-language sentences ranked or binned by their sentence-level SKL scores with respect to Italian (Figure 2: English-Italian histogram of English sentences).

Must identify and describe the figure that shows a histogram of Spanish assisting-language sentences ranked or binned by their sentence-level SKL scores with respect to Italian (Figure 3: Spanish-Italian histogram of Spanish sentences).

Must state that the sentence scores used in the histograms and subsequent analysis are based on symmetric KL (SKL) divergence between tag distributions of common named entities in the primary and assisting languages.

Must identify and describe the figure that plots the influence of varying the SKL-based sentence score threshold on Italian NER performance in the Spanish-Italian multilingual learning setting (Figure 4: Influence of sentence score (SKL) on Italian NER).

Must explain that Figure 4 reports Italian NER performance as a function of the SKL threshold applied to Spanish assisting-language sentences, i.e., performance values corresponding to different SKL cutoff points used to filter training instances.

decisions: How does the paper analyze the effect of adding Spanish and Dutch training sentences on Italian NER performance, and what role does SKL-based label drift analysis play in explaining these effects for European languages?

requirements.description: Must state that adding all Spanish sentences to Italian training data leads to a drop (degradation) in Italian NER performance, as reported in the experimental results section for European languages.

Must state that adding all Dutch sentences to Italian training data also leads to a drop (degradation) in Italian NER performance, paralleling the Spanish–Italian case in the European language experiments.

Must explain that 'label drift' arising from overlapping named entities between the primary language (Italian) and assisting languages (Spanish/Dutch) is explicitly identified in the paper as a reason for the poor multilingual NER results.

Must describe that the paper ranks sentences using a symmetric KL (SKL) divergence–based metric and compares histograms of English and Spanish sentences ordered by these SKL scores in the context of Italian multilingual learning.
Must note that the paper reports a similar SKL-based pattern for Dutch sentences as for Spanish sentences when analyzing their impact on Italian multilingual NER performance.

decisions: How does the proposed data selection strategy affect NER performance across Indian languages, specifically Bengali, Malayalam, Tamil, Hindi, and Marathi, when used as primary and assisting languages in multilingual training?

requirements.description: Must identify that Bengali, Malayalam, and Tamil are treated as low-resource Indian languages in the paper and are explicitly analyzed as a group in the multilingual NER experiments.

Must state that Bengali, Malayalam, and Tamil show improved NER performance when the proposed data selection strategy (based on symmetric KL divergence filtering of assisting-language instances) is applied, compared to using all assisting-language data without selection.

Must report that Hindi and Marathi NER performance improves when they are used as a primary–assisting pair for each other (i.e., Hindi as primary with Marathi assisting, and Marathi as primary with Hindi assisting), as shown in the corresponding experimental results table or subsection on Indian languages.

Must explicitly state that Hindi and Marathi do not gain NER performance benefits from multilingual learning when Bengali, Malayalam, and Tamil are used as assisting languages, as evidenced by the Indian-languages results table or analysis text (e.g., performance remains flat or degrades relative to monolingual baselines).

Must draw from the specific experimental analysis section that focuses on Indian languages (e.g., a subsection titled or described as analysis of Indian languages or low-resource Indian NER), rather than from general or non-Indian language experiments.

decisions: How does varying the symmetric KL (SKL) divergence threshold when selecting Spanish training sentences affect Italian NER performance in the multilingual setup?

requirements.description: Must state that Italian is the primary language and Spanish is the assisting language in the specific experiment being described (training Italian NER using Spanish training sentences).
Must describe that the multilingual NER model shares all layers across languages except for the output layer (i.e., a shared encoder with language-specific output layers).
Must specify that the SKL-based threshold for filtering Spanish training instances is varied from 0.0 to 9.0 in increments (steps) of 1.0.
Must report that the Italian test F-score initially increases as more Spanish sentences (with less divergent SKL scores) are added according to the threshold.

Must report that after a certain point, as the SKL threshold continues to increase and more divergent Spanish sentences are included, the Italian test F-score drops due to the influence of distributional drift becoming significant.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the paper’s stated conclusions and future work regarding tag-distribution divergence and data selection for multilingual Neural NER?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper addresses the problem of divergence in tag distributions between primary and assisting languages in the context of multilingual Neural NER (NNER).
Must describe the proposed use of a symmetric KL-divergence-based metric (or equivalent divergence metric) to filter out assisting-language training sentences with highly divergent tag distributions.
Must explicitly state that filtering out assisting-language sentences exhibiting significant divergence in tag distribution leads to improved NER accuracy for the primary language.

Must capture the future work plan to study the influence of data selection for multilingual learning on other NLP tasks, specifically including sentiment analysis, question answering, and neural machine translation.
Must mention the intention to explore additional or more principled data selection metrics for multilingual learning, with explicit reference to their relevance for morphologically rich languages.

decisions: Does the summary correctly capture the paper’s stated uncertainty about differences between RNN variants, the empirical observation that gated RNNs train better, and the theoretical claim that RNNs are Turing complete?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper highlights that we currently do not know much about the differences in computational power or behavior between different RNN variants (e.g., LSTM, GRU, Elman-RNN) beyond limited known facts.

Must mention that gated RNN architectures (such as LSTMs and GRUs) are known or reported to train better in practice than some non-gated RNNs, as described in the paper’s motivation or background discussion.

Must explicitly reference the well-known theoretical result that RNNs are Turing complete, as cited or discussed in the paper’s introduction or background, and indicate that this result assumes infinite precision and unbounded computation time.

Must draw all three slide elements (limited knowledge of differences, better training of gated RNNs, and Turing completeness of RNNs) from the paper’s high-level motivation or background discussion (e.g., introduction or related work), not from the technical results sections about finite-precision power.

Must clarify that the paper contrasts the classical Turing completeness result for idealized RNNs with its own focus on finite-precision, linear-time RNNs, thereby motivating why the current state of understanding about practical differences between RNN variants is limited.

decisions: How does the paper’s Turing-completeness construction use finite-precision stack-like behavior in specific state dimensions, and what are the practical limits of this mechanism under 32-bit precision?

requirements.description: Must identify that the Turing-completeness construction relies on implementing one or more stack-like data structures encoded in specific dimensions of the RNN state vector (i.e., "stack(s), maintained in certain dimension(s)").

Must describe the push operation for encoding zeros on the stack as a specific update of a state variable g using the formula g = g/4 + 1/4 (or an equivalent expression explicitly involving division by 4 and addition of 1/4).

Must retrieve the discussion that, under 32-bit finite precision, repeated applications of the push operation eventually reach a representational limit (e.g., due to rounding or saturation), thereby bounding the number of pushes possible.
Must state that this stack-based construction enables the RNN to perform additional computation steps after the input has been fully read (i.e., processing beyond the input sequence itself).

Must locate and use the part of the paper where the authors explicitly discuss the Turing-completeness construction as a non-standard or theoretical use case (e.g., noting that this is not the typical or intended practical use of such RNNs).

decisions: According to the paper, how do gated RNN architectures (specifically LSTM and GRU) compare in terms of practical performance and usage, and how clear is the choice between them?

requirements.description: Must state that, in the paper's discussion of practical or empirical aspects, gated RNN architectures are described as having the best performance compared to non-gated architectures (e.g., simple Elman RNNs).

Must explicitly identify LSTM and GRU as the two most popular gated architectures in practical use, as characterized in the paper's narrative (e.g., in introduction, motivation, or discussion sections).

Must draw from the part of the paper that discusses practical usage or empirical performance of different RNN variants (e.g., a motivation, background, or discussion section), rather than from the formal computational power results alone.
Must convey that, according to the paper, the choice between LSTM and GRU is described as unclear or unresolved in terms of which is definitively better in practice.

Must not introduce any specific numerical performance metrics, datasets, or benchmark names that are not mentioned in the paper's discussion of gated architectures' practical performance (i.e., the summary must reflect the qualitative nature of the 'best performance' and 'unclear choice' statements).

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the paper’s main comparative result about the computational power of different finite-precision RNN variants for language recognition?

requirements.description: Must state that, under the paper’s finite-precision and linear-time assumptions, all considered RNN variants are capable of simulating deterministic finite automata (DFAs).
Must identify that the paper’s notion of increased computational power is specifically tied to the ability of an RNN to implement counting behavior beyond DFA-like recognition.
Must specify that LSTM networks and ReLU-based Elman RNNs (often referred to as IRNNs in the paper) are proven to be able to implement counting behavior under finite precision.
Must specify that GRU and squashing-activation Elman RNNs (SRNNs) are proven not to be able to implement counting behavior under the same finite-precision and linear-time constraints.
Must explicitly state the comparative conclusion that LSTMs and IRNNs are strictly more powerful than GRUs and SRNNs in this setting because only the former can count while all can simulate DFAs.

decisions: How does the paper use counting behavior to explain why LSTMs have greater computational power than some other finite-precision RNNs for language recognition?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper identifies counting behavior (i.e., the ability to implement a counter over input length or symbol occurrences) as a key reason why LSTMs and ReLU-RNNs are computationally stronger than RNNs with squashing activations and GRUs.

Must explicitly connect LSTMs' ability to count to their superior capability to capture or recognize properties that depend on the target length of the input (e.g., languages defined by specific length constraints).

Must explain that the paper contrasts models equivalent to finite state machines (with no unbounded counting capability) against models that can simulate counter machines (with at least one unbounded or effectively unbounded counter).

Must describe that the paper formally analyzes finite-precision RNNs under the constraint that computation time is linear in input length, and uses this setting to distinguish between finite-state-like behavior and counter-like behavior.

Must cover the part of the paper where the authors classify the computational power of different RNN variants (LSTM, Elman RNN with ReLU, squashing-activation RNN, GRU) in terms of their equivalence to finite state machines versus counter machines.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and describe the definition and operational characteristics of k-counter machines (SKCMs) as presented in the paper?

requirements.description: Must state that k-counter machines (SKCMs) are similar to finite automata but additionally maintain k counters, matching the paper's definition of the model.
Must identify that the model considered is specifically a k-counter machine (SKCM), not a generic counter machine or other automaton, using the same terminology as in the paper.
Must list all four allowed counter operations exactly as defined in the paper: increment by one, decrement by one, do nothing, and reset.
Must state that counters are observed only via comparison to zero (e.g., tests of whether a counter equals zero or not), as specified in the formal definition of the k-counter machine.
Must attribute the k-counter machine model to Fischer, Meyer, and Rosenberg (1968), as given in the paper's section where SKCMs are introduced.

decisions: Which formal language classes are relevant to characterizing the computational power of finite-precision RNNs discussed in the paper?

requirements.description: Must list the term 'Context Free Languages' exactly as a formal language class referenced in the paper.
Must list the term 'Context Sensitive Languages' exactly as a formal language class referenced in the paper.
Must list the term 'Recursively Enumerable Languages' exactly as a formal language class referenced in the paper.

Must identify and extract these three language classes (CFL, CSL, RE) from the same conceptual discussion or section where the paper situates RNN computational power within the Chomsky hierarchy or formal language hierarchy.
Must preserve the standard abbreviations 'CFL', 'CSL', and 'RE' alongside the full names of the three language classes, as they appear in the paper.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and state the language classes and claim about SKCMs in relation to the Chomsky hierarchy as presented in the paper?

requirements.description: Must explicitly mention the three language classes by their full names: Context Free Languages, Context Sensitive Languages, and Recursively Enumerable Languages, as they are used in the paper when discussing the Chomsky hierarchy.

Must correctly associate the standard abbreviations CFL, CSL, and RE with Context Free Languages, Context Sensitive Languages, and Recursively Enumerable Languages respectively, matching the notation used in the paper.
Must state that SKCMs are related to or positioned with respect to the Chomsky hierarchy, using wording equivalent in meaning to 'SKCMs cross the Chomsky Hierarchy' as presented in the paper.

Must draw on the part of the paper where the Chomsky hierarchy is introduced or discussed (e.g., the theoretical background or language classes section) rather than from experimental or implementation sections.

Must treat SKCMs as a formal model or class of computational devices in the context of language recognition, consistent with how SKCMs are defined or referenced in the paper when relating them to language classes.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and state the paper’s claim that counter-like behavior gives additional formal power and that LSTMs can implement counting while GRUs cannot?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper attributes additional formal (computational) power specifically to the ability to implement counters or counting behavior.
Must explicitly identify that LSTM networks are claimed in the paper to be able to implement counting behavior (i.e., act as counters).

Must explicitly identify that GRU networks are claimed in the paper to not be able to implement counting behavior (i.e., cannot act as counters) under the finite-precision, linear-time setting considered.
Must connect the counting ability of LSTMs (and lack thereof for GRUs) to their differing formal language recognition power under the finite-precision, linear-time constraints described in the paper.

Must retrieve the portion of the paper where the authors make an explicit comparative claim about LSTM vs GRU computational power based on counting (e.g., in a theorem, proposition, or summary statement), not infer it solely from general background or related work.

decisions: Does the system correctly retrieve and present the formal update equations and gating structure of the popular RNN architectures (Elman/ReLU-RNN, GRU, and LSTM) as used in the paper’s analysis of their computational power?

requirements.description: Must identify that the slide is specifying the internal update rules of popular RNN architectures (including GRU and LSTM) rather than presenting results or theoretical proofs, and must treat the expressions as architecture-defining equations for hidden and cell states.

Must retrieve and state the GRU update equations from the paper, including the definitions of the update gate z_t, reset gate r_t, and hidden state h_t in terms of x_t, h_{t-1}, and parameters (W_z, U_z, b_z, W_r, U_r, b_r, and the candidate hidden state using W_h, U_h, b_h).

Must retrieve and state the LSTM update equations from the paper, including the forget gate f_t, input gate i_t, output gate o_t, candidate cell state \tilde{c}_t (or equivalent notation), cell state update c_t = f_t ⊙ c_{t-1} + i_t ⊙ \tilde{c}_t, and hidden state h_t = o_t ⊙ g(c_t), each expressed with their corresponding weight matrices W_f, U_f, W_i, U_i, W_o, U_o, W_c, U_c and biases.

Must retrieve and include the explicit use of the nonlinearity tanh in the candidate cell/hidden state equations (e.g., \tilde{c}_t = tanh(W_c x_t + U_c h_{t-1} + b_c) or equivalent) as it appears in the paper’s formal definitions of the architectures.

Must connect these architecture equations to the paper’s methodological point that certain architectures (LSTM and ReLU-RNN) can implement counting behavior, for example by referencing a section or passage where the paper explains how the gating or cell-state structure enables increment-by-one or interpolation-like operations.

decisions: How does the paper characterize the computational behavior of ReLU-based Elman RNN architectures, particularly regarding their update rule, boundedness, and ability to implement counting?

requirements.description: Must state that the Elman-RNN with ReLU activation is capable of implementing counting behavior (i.e., can act as a counter over input symbols).
Must correctly specify the ReLU-RNN hidden state update equation in the form h_t = max(0, W_h x_t + U_h h_{t-1} + b_h) or an equivalent notation matching the slide's ht = max(0, Whxt + Uhht-1 + bh).

Must identify that the counting behavior in the ReLU-RNN is implemented via parallel subtraction or increment operations on hidden state components (i.e., coordinate-wise updates that increase or decrease counts).
Must explicitly mention that, under the finite-precision and linear-time constraints considered in the paper, the ReLU-RNN's hidden state values are bounded (i.e., cannot grow without limit).

Must draw these properties (ReLU update rule, boundedness, and counting ability) from the part of the paper that analyzes and compares the computational power of different RNN variants (e.g., the section discussing Elman-RNN with ReLU versus squashing RNNs and GRUs).

decisions: Does the paper show that the ability to implement counting behavior gives certain finite-precision RNNs greater computational power for language recognition than other RNN variants?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper compares the computational power of different finite-precision RNN variants (at least LSTM, Elman-RNN with ReLU, squashing-activation RNN, and GRU) for language recognition.
Must explicitly state that the key differentiating capability identified in the paper is the ability of some RNN variants to implement counting behavior.

Must state that, under finite precision and linear-time computation constraints, LSTMs and ReLU-RNNs are shown to be strictly more powerful (in terms of language recognition) than RNNs with squashing activations and GRUs.
Must describe that the analysis is conducted under explicit constraints of finite precision in the hidden states and computation time linear in the input length.

Must connect the counting capability directly to the increase in computational power, i.e., must state that the greater computational power of LSTMs and ReLU-RNNs arises because they can easily implement counting behavior.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and describe the empirical activation behavior of LSTM vs GRU on the formal languages anbn and anbncn as presented in Figure 1 of the paper?

requirements.description: Must reference Figure 1 specifically as showing activations for LSTM and GRU networks on the formal languages anbn and anbncn.
Must state that the LSTM has clearly learned or uses an explicit counting mechanism, in contrast with the GRU.
Must report that the GRU begins failing at approximately n = 9 on the target language tasks, while the LSTM generalises up to around n = 101.
Must indicate that the activations are evaluated on positive examples up to length 100 (e.g., strings like a100b100c100).
Must state that the GRU did not learn any discernible counting mechanism and did not generalise well even within the training domain, as contrasted with the LSTM.

decisions: What is the main practical takeaway about the expressive power of different finite-precision RNN architectures that the authors want readers to remember?

requirements.description: Must state that different finite-precision RNN variants (e.g., LSTM, ReLU-RNN vs. squashing-activation RNN, GRU) have different computational or expressive power for language recognition.

Must explicitly connect the architectural differences (such as ability to implement counting behavior) to resulting differences in expressive or computational power, not just training performance or optimization behavior.

Must identify and use the paper's concluding or discussion content that summarizes the main practical message or 'take-home' point about model expressivity, rather than intermediate technical lemmas or proofs.

Must capture the authors' warning against relying solely on abstract Turing-completeness arguments (the 'Turing Tarpit') when reasoning about RNN capabilities in practical, finite-precision, linear-time settings.

Must reference that the analysis is conducted under explicit practical constraints (finite precision and computation time linear in input length), which are essential to the claimed differences in expressive power.

decisions: How does the system in the paper use news website context to categorize words for second language learning?

requirements.description: Must state that news articles are assigned a news category based on the URL pattern of the news website (e.g., path or section in the URL).
Must list that the system uses exactly seven news categories and must include at least the categories Entertainment, World, Finance, Sports, and Fashion as part of that set.
Must explain that words are classified into news categories using category-specific document frequency (i.e., frequency of the word across documents within each category).
Must provide the concrete example that the word 'superstar' is categorized as belonging to the Entertainment category based on the category document frequency approach.
Must specify that this news-category-based word classification is applied to both English and Chinese news articles and their corresponding words.

decisions: How does the paper perform word sense disambiguation for English–Chinese vocabulary in the WordNews system, including the dictionary used, the baseline, and the two proposed approaches?

requirements.description: Must identify that word sense disambiguation is performed using an expanded College English Test 4 (CET-4) dictionary containing English words, their Chinese translations with relative frequencies, and part-of-speech tags.
Must state the dictionary scale as 33,664 English–Chinese pairs and approximately 4,000 (~4k) unique English words, matching the counts given in the paper.

Must describe the baseline method as always choosing the most frequent Chinese translation (based on relative frequency) for a given English word, and note that this baseline has low accuracy because it does not model context.

Must explain Approach 1 (News Category) as selecting the Chinese translation whose category matches the news article's category, including the example that 'interest' in Finance news is disambiguated using a finance-related Chinese translation.
Must explain Approach 2 (Part-of-Speech) as selecting the Chinese translation whose part-of-speech (POS) matches the POS of the target English word in context.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the three Bing Translator-based matching approaches (Substring Match, Relaxed Match, Bing Alignment) and their behaviors/limitations as described in the paper for use in the slide?

requirements.description: Must identify and name all three approaches as distinct methods: 'Approach 3: Substring Match', 'Approach 4: Relaxed Match', and 'Approach 5: Bing Alignment'.
Must describe the behavior of Approach 3 (Substring Match) as relying on dictionary-based substring matching and explicitly note its limitation as 'Limited by dictionary coverage!'.
Must state that Approach 4 (Relaxed Match) uses a relaxed matching strategy related to Chinese segmentation and that it can produce 'two relaxed matches, both wrong'.
Must explain that Approach 5 (Bing Alignment) uses alignment information from Bing Translator and that it produces 'No output if the alignment is phrase to phrase'.
Must retrieve the example phrases used to illustrate the substring/relaxed matching behavior, including the contrast between 'into the worlds top 40 clubs' and 'into the worlds top clubs'.

decisions: What word sense disambiguation (WSD) baselines and Bing-based variants does the paper define and compare in its WSD evaluation?

requirements.description: Must identify that the WSD evaluation is organized around multiple baseline methods, explicitly including a baseline labeled 'News'.
Must extract from the WSD evaluation section that one baseline is based on part-of-speech information and is explicitly labeled 'POS'.
Must identify a WSD baseline that uses Bing without additional qualifiers and is explicitly labeled 'Bing -'.
Must identify a relaxed variant of the Bing-based WSD method explicitly labeled 'Bing - Relaxed' in the WSD evaluation description (e.g., in text, table, or figure captions).
Must identify a Bing-based WSD variant that uses category substring alignment and is explicitly labeled 'Bing - Align Category Substring' in the WSD evaluation materials.

decisions: According to the paper, what properties define a suitable set of distractor words for interactive vocabulary tests in the WordNews system?

requirements.description: Must state that suitable distractors must have the same form as the target word (e.g., same part of speech or morphological form) as explicitly described in the paper's criteria for distractor selection.
Must state that suitable distractors must fit the sentence context in which the target word appears, as defined in the paper's description of distractor properties.

Must state that suitable distractors must have a difficulty level appropriate to the user's level of mastery, as specified in the paper's discussion of adaptive or user-level-based distractor selection.
Must state that more difficult distractors are characterized as being more semantically similar to the target word, following the paper's explicit definition of distractor difficulty.

Must attribute all four properties (same form, sentence-fit, user-level difficulty, and semantic similarity for difficult distractors) to the specific part of the paper that defines criteria for constructing or selecting distractor options in the interactive tests (e.g., the section describing quiz or test item generation).

decisions: How does the paper define and operationalize the difficulty level of distractors for vocabulary learning in WordNews?

requirements.description: Must state that distractor difficulty is measured using Lin distance (a semantic similarity measure) between the target word and the candidate distractor in WordNet.
Must explain that the Lin distance computation relies on the lowest common subsumer (LCS) synset of the target word and the candidate distractor in WordNet.
Must describe that a distractor is classified as 'hard' when its similarity to the target word, as computed by the Lin measure, is above a specified threshold.
Must report the example numerical threshold value used for hard distractors (similarity above 0.1).

Must extract this information from the part of the paper that describes distractor generation or difficulty modeling for vocabulary tests (e.g., the methodology or system design section), not from unrelated sections such as introduction or conclusions.

decisions: How does the WordNews system generate and configure distractor options for vocabulary tests based on user knowledge level?

requirements.description: Must identify that the paper defines a distractor generation strategy specifically for vocabulary tests within the WordNews system.
Must extract from the paper that there are at least two distinct distractor sources or types, one labeled or described as 'WordNews Hard' and another as 'Random News'.
Must state that both 'WordNews Hard' and 'Random News' distractors are constructed using items that share the same word form as the target word (e.g., same lemma or inflected form).
Must retrieve that the number and type of distractors are varied based on the user's knowledge level (proficiency or estimated vocabulary knowledge).
Must report the specific configuration for beginners given in the paper: beginner-level users receive two random distractors and one hard distractor in each test item.

decisions: Did the system correctly retrieve and summarize the paper’s description of the human evaluation comparing WordGap with Random News and WordNews Hard, including the distractor generation strategy and evaluation metrics?

requirements.description: Must state that the human evaluation involves the WordGap system (attributed to Knoop and Wilske, 2013) as a baseline or comparison system.
Must describe WordGap’s distractor generation method as targeting 'synonyms of synonyms' using WordNet, matching the phrasing that distractors are based on synonyms of synonyms in WordNet.

Must identify and distinguish two separate human evaluation setups explicitly labeled or described as 'Evaluation 1: WordGap vs. Random News' and 'Evaluation 2: WordGap vs. WordNews Hard' (or equivalent clear comparisons).

Must explain the multiple-choice test item structure where one option is the target word, three options come from WordGap, and three options come from either WordNews Hard or Random News, corresponding to the example sentence about 'Most sex workers that Hail-Jares encounters...'.
Must report that the human evaluation results are summarized using at least two metrics labeled or described as '# of wins' and 'Avg. Score', and must note that lower scores are better.

decisions: Does the summary correctly capture the main conclusion points about the WordNews system’s features and planned evaluations as presented in the paper’s conclusion?

requirements.description: Must state that WordNews is implemented as a Chrome (web browser) extension that enables interactive second language vocabulary learning while reading online news.
Must describe that Word Sense Disambiguation in WordNews is performed using or based on Machine Translation, not a different disambiguation technique.
Must explain that distractor generation for vocabulary tests is derived from news context and semantic similarity, explicitly mentioning both context and semantic similarity as the basis.
Must mention the existence of a mobile client for WordNews as part of the system’s described components or future directions in the conclusion section.
Must note that a longitudinal user study is planned or conducted for evaluating WordNews, explicitly using the term 'longitudinal' or clearly indicating a long-term user study.

decisions: What introductory challenges and assumptions about searching digital libraries does the paper present that motivate the use of recommendation services for scholarly users?

requirements.description: Must identify and state the typical difficulty of 'vagueness between search and indexing terms' as described in the paper's introductory discussion of searching digital libraries.
Must identify and state the typical difficulty of 'weak rankings based on term frequency (tf*idf), also others ...' as a limitation of standard digital library search.
Must retrieve and state Assumption I that a user's search experience should improve by using recommendation services, explicitly attributing it to Mutschke et al. (2011).
Must retrieve and state Assumption II that scholarly users search with keywords, author names, and journal names and use search tactics, explicitly attributing it to Carevic & Mayr (2016, to appear).
Must indicate that these difficulties and assumptions are presented in the introductory or motivation part of the paper that discusses searching digital libraries (DL) and recommendation services.

decisions: What recommender services (STR, JNR, ANR) were developed in the IRM project at GESIS and how are they characterized in terms of input, underlying analysis method, and example outputs for the topic 'Soziale Systeme'?

requirements.description: Must identify and name all three recommender services as defined in the paper: Search Term Recommender (STR), Journal Name Recommender (JNR), and Author Name Recommender (ANR), including their full expanded names and abbreviations.

Must state the specific analysis method associated with each recommender as described in the paper: STR uses co-word analysis with the Jaccard index, JNR uses core journal identification via bradfordizing, and ANR uses co-authorship analysis with betweenness centrality.
Must indicate that the recommenders are part of the IRM project at GESIS (Liike et al., 2013) and are used to provide topic-specific recommendations when a user types a query.
Must retrieve from the paper the example of a core journal recommendation for the topic 'Soziale Systeme', including the journal name 'Soziale Systeme' and its associated count '(105)'.

Must retrieve from the paper the example author recommendations produced by the ANR for the same topic, including at least the following central authors: 'Luhmann, Niklas', 'Luhmann, Hans-Jochen', 'Schimank, Uwe', 'Tyrell, Hartmann', 'Hartmann, Jutta', and 'Fischedick, Manfred'.

decisions: Does the summary correctly describe the design and sample of the case study evaluating STR, JNR, and ANR recommendations at the Leibniz Institute for the Social Sciences?

requirements.description: Must state that the study involves assessing topical relevance of recommendations produced by three recommender services: Search Term Recommender (STR), Journal Name Recommender (JNR), and Author Name Recommender (ANR), for researchers' own research topics or familiar fields.

Must report that 19 social sciences researchers participated in the study and identify them as a mix of seniors, research staff, and PhD candidates (or equivalent phrasing such as practitioners, PhD students, and postdocs).
Must specify that 23 distinct research topics were assessed in the case study.
Must indicate that participants assessed 4–5 recommendations for each recommender service (STR, JNR, ANR).
Must state that all recommendations evaluated in the study were derived from the social sciences database SOLIS.

decisions: According to the study’s reported results, how relevant are the recommender outputs overall, and how do ANR, STR, and JNR compare in precision and in the relevance of JNR’s top-1 recommendation?

requirements.description: Must state that more than 70% of the recommendations produced by the recommender services are assessed as relevant by the social science researchers, using the explicit threshold '>70%'.
Must correctly identify and name the three recommender types as Search Term Recommender (STR), Journal Name Recommender (JNR), and Author Name Recommender (ANR) as defined in the paper.

Must report that the precision of the Author Name Recommender (ANR) is slightly higher than the precision of both the Search Term Recommender (STR) and the Journal Name Recommender (JNR), reflecting the comparative result given in the results section or corresponding table.

Must state that the top-1 recommendation of the Journal Name Recommender (JNR) is more often not relevant than relevant, as explicitly indicated in the results text or associated performance table for top-1 recommendations.
Must base all reported precision and relevance findings on the paper’s main Results section (or equivalent empirical findings section), not on the abstract or introduction alone.

decisions: According to the study’s reported results, how do practitioners and postdocs differ in their assessment of the relevance of author names versus journal names in topic-specific recommendations?

requirements.description: Must identify that the paper explicitly compares perceived topical relevance of different recommender types: Search Term Recommender (STR), Journal Name Recommender (JNR), and Author Name Recommender (ANR) for different researcher groups.

Must state that practitioners in the study tend to assess author name recommendations (ANR) as more relevant than the other recommendation types, as reported in the results section where group-wise relevance assessments are analyzed.

Must state that postdocs in the study tend to assess journal name recommendations (JNR) as more relevant than the other recommendation types, as reported in the results section where group-wise relevance assessments are analyzed.

Must retrieve the specific subgroup breakdown (practitioners, PhD students, postdocs) from the results or participant description and correctly associate the relevance assessment patterns with practitioners and postdocs only (not attributing them to PhD students).

Must draw the practitioner vs. postdoc relevance differences from the empirical results portion of the paper (e.g., results or findings section that reports group-specific relevance ratings), not infer them solely from the abstract or study design description.

decisions: What conclusions does the paper draw about the comparative precision of STR, JNR, and ANR recommendations and the differing preferences of practitioners versus postdocs, and what follow-up questions do the authors raise?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper evaluates three distinct recommender services explicitly named as Search Term Recommender (STR), Journal Name Recommender (JNR), and Author Name Recommender (ANR).
Must report the conclusion that the precision values of recommendations from STR, JNR, and ANR are all on a high level and are close together (i.e., no large precision differences between the three).
Must describe the user group preference result that practitioners favor author name recommendations (ANR), while postdocs favor journal name recommendations (JNR).
Must include the explicit follow-up question raised by the authors about external validity: whether the observed high and similar precision values would be similar in a real retrieval scenario.
Must include the explicit follow-up question raised by the authors about feature distinctiveness: whether author names are typically more distinctive features than journal names.

decisions: What future work and outlook do the authors propose regarding the integration and evaluation of recommender systems in real information retrieval tasks?

requirements.description: Must state that the outlook explicitly involves integrating different recommender systems into real retrieval tasks, described as search sessions.
Must mention that a proposed future evaluation approach is to measure task completion rates or goal satisfaction when using the recommenders.
Must describe that the recommenders are to be used and evaluated for query expansion and as dynamic features in information retrieval (IR) systems.
Must indicate that the authors propose developing new measures of utility specifically for the recommender systems as part of future work.
Must identify that these points appear in the paper's Outlook or Future Work section associated with the Leibniz Institute for the Social Sciences.

decisions: Does the system correctly summarize the OPT system’s overall approach and key performance characteristics as presented in the 'In Short' slide?

requirements.description: Must state that the system uses a classical or 'classic' pipeline architecture for shallow discourse parsing, as described in the paper’s system overview.

Must describe that explicit connectives and their arguments are handled using an approach adapted from prior work on detection of speculation and negation, explicitly referencing Velldal et al. (2012) and Read et al. (2012) as in the paper.
Must mention that model selection or tuning is performed via cross-validation on the training set, as specified in the experimental setup or training procedure sections.
Must specify that discourse sense disambiguation is performed using an ensemble of classifiers, matching the description of the sense assignment component in the paper.
Must report the end-to-end F1 score of 27.77 on the English blind test set, as given in the results section for the CoNLL 2016 shared task evaluation.

decisions: Does the summary correctly describe the non-explicit components of the OPT system architecture as shown in the system overview figure?

requirements.description: Must state that the OPT system includes a dedicated component for 'Non-Explicit Relation Detection' as part of its architecture.
Must state that the OPT system includes a dedicated component for 'Non-Explicit Argument Ranking' as part of its architecture.
Must state that the OPT system includes a dedicated component for 'Non-Explicit Sense Classification' as part of its architecture.
Must identify and reference the system overview diagram (the 'OPT system overview' figure) as the source that groups the three non-explicit components together.

Must extract these three non-explicit components from the part of the paper that describes the overall system architecture (e.g., the architecture or system overview section associated with the OPT system overview figure).

decisions: How does the OPT system perform explicit connective detection within its shallow discourse parsing pipeline?

requirements.description: Must state that the explicit connective detection component extends or builds on the method of Velldal et al. (2012) specifically for identifying expressions of discourse connectives.
Must specify that the system operates on a closed-class list of discourse connectives rather than an open vocabulary.
Must describe that only the heads of multiword connectives (i.e., connective heads only) are used or disambiguated in the explicit connective detection step.
Must identify that explicit connective detection is formulated as a binary classification task (connective vs. non-connective) rather than multi-class labeling.
Must explicitly name SVMlight as the classifier implementation used for the binary explicit connective detection.

decisions: What specific feature types and model selection procedures does the paper use for its classifiers in the shallow discourse parsing pipeline?

requirements.description: Must state that token and POS n-grams around the candidate connective are used as features, explicitly mentioning that these are taken from the local context around the candidate.
Must describe that features include parent, sibling, and path-related properties derived from PTB-style parse trees for the candidate.

Must specify that feature tuning is performed using ten-fold cross-validation on the training set, and that final model selection is made from among a large number (on the order of thousands) of runs.
Must report that twelve candidate models are tested against a development set and that smaller models with less variation across folds are preferred during final model selection.

Must indicate the detailed feature design choices: surface features are taken up to 3 tokens before and after the candidate, full feature conjunctions are used for self and parent categories, conjunctions for siblings are limited, and connected context features are explicitly not used.

decisions: How does the OPT system identify and model discourse arguments in its shallow discourse parsing pipeline?

requirements.description: Must state that the argument identification approach is explicitly based on prior work on the scope of speculation and negation by Read et al. (i.e., must mention the Read et al. work as the conceptual basis).
Must state the core assumption that discourse arguments basically correspond to phrases (i.e., arguments are modeled as phrasal units).
Must specify that the system extracts clausal syntactic constituents of types S, SBAR, and SQ as candidate arguments (all three labels must be present).
Must identify SVMlight as the specific classifier implementation used for argument-related classification.
Must report that ten-fold cross-validation on the training set is used for evaluating/training the argument classifiers.

decisions: How does the OPT system model and determine the position of discourse arguments, specifically the position of Arg2 relative to Arg1, for explicit and non-explicit relations?

requirements.description: Must state that the slide is about the position of Arg2 relative to Arg1, explicitly mentioning that this information comes from a table titled or described as 'Position of Arg2 relative to Arg1'.
Must describe that for non-explicit discourse relations, the system assumes Arg1 is located in the previous sentence (PS) relative to Arg2, as specified in the paper's argument position component.

Must describe that for explicit discourse relations, the system uses a classifier to decide whether Arg1 is in the previous sentence (PS) or in the same sentence (SS) as Arg2, matching the explicit-vs-non-explicit distinction in the paper.

Must identify and list the syntactic and lexical features used for argument position classification, including: (a) the path from the connective to the root in the parse tree, (b) the connective's position in the sentence divided into tertiles, and (c) the POS bigram of the connective and the following token.

Must reference that these argument position features and PS/SS distinctions are organized or summarized in a table in the paper (the table on Arg2 position relative to Arg1), not only in running text.

decisions: How does the OPT system represent and rank candidate argument constituents for explicit and non-explicit discourse relations in its argument identification component?

requirements.description: Must state that the system performs an ordinal ranking of clausal constituents as candidate arguments (i.e., not just binary classification but an ordered ranking of candidates).
Must describe that the feature set for argument ranking is constructed by iteratively building a pool of feature types, rather than using a fixed, one-shot feature set.

Must retrieve from the relevant table the three discourse relation categories explicitly labeled as 'Exp. PS', 'Exp. SS', and 'Non-Exp.' and indicate that these are separate columns or groupings in the table.

Must retrieve from the same table that for each of the three categories (Exp. PS, Exp. SS, Non-Exp.) there are separate feature columns for both Arg1 and Arg2 (i.e., Arg1 and Arg2 appear under each of the three categories).

Must identify that the table is titled or captioned as describing 'Feature types used to describe candidate constituents for argument ranking' and must mention the specific feature type 'Path to Initial Token' as one of the listed feature types.

decisions: What post-editing heuristics does the OPT system apply to improve the alignment of constituent yields with discourse arguments (Arg1/Arg2) in SS/PS configurations?

requirements.description: Must state that the post-editing heuristics are applied to improve the low initial alignment of full constituent yields with discourse arguments (Arg1 and Arg2) in sentence-internal (SS) or previous-sentence (PS) configurations.
Must reference the table titled or described as showing the 'Alignment of constituent yield with arguments (in SS or PS)' and indicate that it concerns Arg1 and Arg2 alignment.
Must describe the heuristic that adds a conjunction (CC) preceding the constituent to Arg1 when performing post-editing.

Must list at least three cutting heuristics applied to Arg1, including: (a) cutting a clause headed by the connective for explicit SS cases, (b) cutting constituent-final CC, and (c) cutting constituent-final wh-determiner.

Must list at least three additional cutting heuristics, including: (a) cutting constituent-initial CC for Arg2 in explicit cases, (b) cutting relative clauses realized as SBAR initiated by WHNP/WHADVP, and (c) cutting the connective itself and initial/final punctuation.

decisions: What argument extraction performance does the OPT system achieve on Arg1, Arg2, and Both for the WSJ test set and the blind set without error propagation?

requirements.description: Must retrieve the specific table that reports argument extraction results explicitly labeled as having 'no error propagation'.
Must extract the column headers from that table showing the two evaluation datasets, exactly identifying 'WSJ Test Set' and 'Blind Set'.
Must extract the argument role columns from that table, exactly identifying 'Arg1', 'Arg2', and 'Both' for each of the WSJ Test Set and Blind Set.
Must preserve the tabular layout that aligns Arg1, Arg2, and Both under each of the two dataset headings ('WSJ Test Set' and 'Blind Set') as in the original table.
Must indicate that the table concerns 'Argument extraction results' rather than other components of the pipeline (e.g., connective classification or sense classification).

decisions: How does the OPT system perform sense classification using ensemble classifiers for explicit and non-explicit discourse relations, and which base classifiers are combined?

requirements.description: Must state that the system uses separate ensemble classifiers for explicit discourse relations and for non-explicit discourse relations, rather than a single unified classifier.
Must identify that one of the ensemble components is an LSVC LIBLINEAR SVM classifier, explicitly attributed to or based on Wang & Lan (2015).

Must identify that another ensemble component is an XGBoost classifier implemented as decision trees with gradient boosting, using the same feature set as the LSVC LIBLINEAR SVM, and explicitly attributed to or based on Wang & Lan (2015).
Must describe the ensemble decision rule that the final prediction label is selected based on the sum (e.g., summed scores or votes) of the individual classifiers' outputs.

Must extract these details specifically from the part of the paper that describes the sense classification component of the pipeline (the discourse sense assignment stage), not from sections on connective identification, argument identification, or heuristic rules for non-explicit relations.

decisions: What isolated sense classification results does the OPT system (and its variants) achieve on the WSJ test set and the blind set for explicit, non-explicit, and all relations, as reported in the sense classification results table?

requirements.description: Must retrieve the table that reports isolated sense classification results with separate columns for the WSJ test set and the blind set, each further split into 'Exp', 'Non-Exp', and 'All'.
Must extract the system names listed in the sense classification results table under the 'System' column, including the specific bottom model that is explicitly noted as not part of the submission.
Must identify that the table reports isolated results specifically for the sense classification subtask, not end-to-end discourse parsing or other subtasks.

Must preserve the table's structural layout distinguishing rows for different systems and columns for 'WSJ Test Set' vs 'Blind Set' and 'Exp', 'Non-Exp', 'All', so that this structure can be rendered on the slide.
Must include the table caption or its key phrase indicating that it is 'Table : Isolated results for sense classification (the bottom model was not part of the submission)'.

decisions: How does the OPT system perform overall on the WSJ test and blind test sets, in comparison to the 2015 and 2016 CoNLL shared tasks, and what role do error propagation and automatic parses play in these results?

requirements.description: Must identify and report that overall end-to-end performance is evaluated on both the WSJ test set and the English 'blind' test set, as specified in the results section or corresponding results table.
Must retrieve the numeric end-to-end F1 score of 27.77 on the English blind test data from the paper's results (e.g., main results table or text summary).

Must state that the OPT system improves over the previous state of the art by close to four F1 points, explicitly referencing the comparison baseline Wang & Lan (2015) or the 2015 shared task results section where this is quantified.

Must cover the part of the paper that compares OPT results to both the 2015 and 2016 CoNLL shared task challenge systems, explicitly noting that performance is compared across challenge years (2015 and 2016).

Must identify and describe the discussion section or error analysis subsection where error propagation through the pipeline and the use of automatic parses (as opposed to gold parses) are explicitly mentioned as factors affecting overall performance.

decisions: What per-component performance results does the OPT system achieve on the WSJ test set and the blind test set, as reported in the paper’s per-component breakdown table?

requirements.description: Must identify and use the specific table explicitly titled or captioned as providing a 'Per-component breakdown of system performance' (the table from which the slide text is taken).

Must locate the section of the paper that reports evaluation results for individual pipeline components (e.g., connective classification, argument identification, sense classification) and use that section as the source for the table content.

Must extract the performance metrics (e.g., F1 scores or equivalent) for each pipeline component as reported in the per-component breakdown table, without substituting values from any other table or text.
Must distinguish and correctly associate performance values for the WSJ test set versus the blind test set when both are reported in the per-component breakdown table.

Must preserve the notion that the reported numbers are per-component (i.e., not only end-to-end scores) and explicitly reflect that the table decomposes performance by the main stages of the OPT shallow discourse parsing pipeline.

decisions: What are the main take-home messages and practical conclusions the OPT system paper draws about its end-to-end performance, argument identification method, overfitting control, and sense prediction approach?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper explicitly concludes that the overall end-to-end shallow discourse parsing problem remains unsolved or 'anything but solved', reflecting a limitation of the current system despite performance gains.

Must identify and describe the adaptation of a constituent ranking approach (originally for a different task) as the method used for argument identification, and state that the paper evaluates it as a good fit for this subtask.

Must retrieve from the experimental setup or training procedure that cross-validation over the available data (including WSJ) was used explicitly to reduce or control over-fitting to WSJ data, and present this as a key practical lesson.

Must identify that an ensemble of classifiers is used for discourse sense prediction (sense classification component of the pipeline) and that the paper reports this ensemble as improving sense prediction performance.

Must attribute the improvement in sense prediction to post-submission experiments or analysis (i.e., results obtained after the official shared-task submission), as explicitly noted in the paper when discussing the classifier ensemble.

decisions: How does the OPT system define and operationalize non-explicit discourse relation detection between sentence pairs in the PDTB framework?

requirements.description: Must state the four PDTB-based conditions that define a non-explicit relation between sentences A and B: (i) A and B are adjacent, (ii) A and B are in the same paragraph, (iii) A and B are not linked by an explicit connective, and (iv) a coherence relation or an entity-based relation holds between them.
Must describe that the system operationalizes conditions (i) and (ii) by traversing sentence bigrams (i.e., consecutive sentence pairs) within a paragraph.
Must explain that condition (iii) is enforced by checking for explicit connectives whose Arg1 lies in the previous sentence (PS), and excluding such pairs from non-explicit relation detection.
Must indicate that the categories NoRel and AltLex are treated as exceptions to condition (iv) and are currently ignored in the system's non-explicit relation detection.
Must report the specific PDTB corpus frequencies for the ignored relation types: NoRel (0.6% in PDTB) and AltLex (1.5% in PDTB).

decisions: What does the paper report about the module-level evaluation performed on gold standard explicit connectives for non-explicit relation detection?

requirements.description: Must identify and reference the specific subsection where the authors describe module-level evaluation (as opposed to end-to-end evaluation) for discourse parsing components.
Must state that the evaluation in question is performed on gold standard explicit connectives, i.e., using gold annotations for explicit connectives rather than system-predicted ones.
Must explain that the evaluation is at the module level (component-wise evaluation of the non-explicit relation detection module) rather than a full pipeline or end-to-end system evaluation.

Must retrieve the specific performance metrics (e.g., precision, recall, F1 or accuracy) reported for the non-explicit relation detection module when evaluated on gold standard explicit connectives from the relevant table or results paragraph.

Must distinguish the reported non-explicit relation detection module results on gold standard explicit connectives from other reported results (such as end-to-end F1 of 27.77 or results on predicted connectives) and not conflate them.

decisions: How does the paper’s framework characterize specific example relations between ideas (friends vs. rivals) and connect them to correlation/anti-correlation patterns for exploring relations between ideas?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper proposes a framework to quantitatively describe relations between ideas based on their occurrence patterns in a corpus (e.g., using co-occurrence and prevalence correlation over time).
Must identify that the framework distinguishes at least two types of relations between ideas labeled as 'friends' (cooperative) and 'rivals' (competitive or opposing).
Must retrieve the specific example pair 'undocumented immigrants' and 'illegal alien' and correctly label their relation as 'rivals' according to the paper’s examples of idea relations.

Must retrieve the specific example pairs 'small government'–'free market' and 'word alignment'–'machine translation' and correctly label their relations as 'friends' according to the paper’s examples of idea relations.

Must connect the notion of 'friends' and 'rivals' to correlation structure by stating that some idea pairs are correlated and others are anti-correlated over time or documents, and that these correlation patterns are used to explore relations between ideas.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the paper’s main contributions and illustrative examples of idea relations as presented in the 'Main contributions' slide?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper introduces the first quantitative framework to systematically describe or characterize relations between ideas in texts, using corpus-based statistics.
Must mention that the framework is based on combining two statistics derived from texts: co-occurrence of ideas within documents and correlation of their prevalence over time.

Must cover the paper’s stated main contributions section (or equivalent introductory summary) where the authors explicitly describe the framework as the first systematic quantitative approach to relations between ideas and its applicability across datasets.
Must report that the authors demonstrate effective explorations or applications of the framework on a wide range of datasets or corpora, not just a single dataset.

Must identify and reproduce at least two concrete example pairs of ideas used in the paper to illustrate different relation types, specifically that 'undocumented immigrants' is characterized as a rival of 'illegal alien' and that 'small government' is characterized as a friend of 'free market'.

decisions: How does the paper propose to use standard text-based approaches to trace and represent relations between ideas?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper's focus is on characterizing relations between ideas (or relations between ideas in texts), using textual data.
Must identify 'topics from latent Dirichlet allocation' as one of the standard approaches used to represent ideas in the corpus, explicitly referencing LDA.
Must identify 'keywords' as another standard approach used to represent ideas, distinct from topics/LDA.
Must retrieve and mention the citation to Michel et al. 2011 (Culturomics) as an example or source related to using large text corpora to trace ideas over time.

Must cover the part of the paper where the authors enumerate or motivate the different text-based representations of ideas (e.g., topics, keywords, culturomics-style frequency analysis), rather than sections focused solely on relational statistics (cooccurrence or prevalence correlation).

decisions: How does the paper formally set up a corpus of documents as sets of ideas and illustrate that simple cooccurrence cannot tell which competing idea (e.g., 'undocumented immigrants' vs. 'illegal alien') is winning or losing over time?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper models each document in the corpus as a set (or collection) of ideas, explicitly linking documents, ideas, and time (e.g., a corpus of documents over time where each document consists of a set of ideas).
Must identify that the paper uses cooccurrence of ideas within documents as one of the two core statistics for characterizing relations between ideas.

Must explain that cooccurrence alone is insufficient to determine which of two competing ideas is 'winning' or 'losing' over time, motivating the need for an additional temporal or prevalence-based statistic.

Must retrieve the specific example of two rival ideas referring to immigration terminology (e.g., 'undocumented immigrants' and 'illegal alien') used by the paper to illustrate competition or rivalry between ideas.

Must mention that the framework combines cooccurrence within documents with prevalence correlation over time (or an equivalent temporal prevalence measure) to characterize relations such as rivalry between ideas.

decisions: Which specific idea pair or cluster is used in the paper to illustrate a head-to-head relationship between concepts related to immigration status terminology?

requirements.description: Must identify that the slide refers to a specific set of competing or contrasted ideas/terms related to immigration status, namely variants of 'immigrant' vs. 'undocumented illegal alien' (or equivalent phrasing) as presented in the paper.

Must retrieve the exact lexical items (or the explicitly listed n-grams) from the paper that correspond to the slide text: 'immigrant', 'undocumented', 'illegal', and 'alien', as they appear together in the same example, table, or list.

Must locate and use the specific part of the paper (e.g., example, case study, or illustrative pair/cluster) where immigration-related terms are given as a concrete instance of the framework's idea relations, rather than inferring these terms from general discussion.

Must connect the retrieved immigration-related terms to the paper's methodological notion of a 'head-to-head' or competitive relation between ideas, as defined via cooccurrence and/or prevalence correlation, rather than treating them as a generic topical list.

Must, if the paper includes a figure, table, or diagram where these immigration-related terms are grouped or contrasted, explicitly use that visual element (e.g., a plotted pair/cluster or labeled example) as the source for the slide content.

decisions: How does the paper exemplify an instance of a 'friendship' relation between ideas using the terms 'immigrant, undocumented' and 'obama, president'?

requirements.description: Must identify that 'friendship' is a specific relation type between ideas as defined in the paper's conceptual framework (i.e., a cooperative or positively associated relation between ideas).
Must extract that the slide titled 'Friendship' corresponds to an example of this relation type instantiated by two idea pairs: one about immigration status and one about political leadership.
Must retrieve the exact idea terms 'immigrant' and 'undocumented' from the paper as a grouped idea or topic used in the 'friendship' example.
Must retrieve the exact idea terms 'obama' and 'president' from the paper as a grouped idea or topic used in the 'friendship' example.

Must identify the specific figure, table, or example visualization in the paper where the 'friendship' relation is illustrated using the idea sets {immigrant, undocumented} and {obama, president}, and use that as the source for the slide content.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and extract the specific pair of competing political ideas labeled as an 'arms race' relation in the paper?

requirements.description: Must identify that 'arms race' is one of the named relation types between ideas defined in the paper's conceptual framework for idea relations.
Must retrieve the exact idea pair 'immigration, deportation' from the paper as an example associated with the 'arms race' relation type.
Must retrieve the exact idea pair 'republican, party' from the paper as an example associated with the 'arms race' relation type.

Must locate and use the section or subsection where example idea pairs are categorized under specific relation types (including 'arms race') rather than unrelated parts of the paper (e.g., introduction or related work).
Must, if present, use the figure or table that explicitly lists example idea pairs under the 'arms race' category to obtain both 'immigration, deportation' and 'republican, party' exactly as written.

decisions: Which pair of ideas in the paper is characterized as a 'Tryst' relationship between 'immigration, deportation' and 'detainee, detention'?

requirements.description: Must identify that the slide labeled 'Tryst' corresponds to a specific type of relationship between ideas as defined in the paper's framework (i.e., a named relation type, not a generic co-occurrence).

Must retrieve the exact idea pair text strings 'immigration, deportation' and 'detainee, detention' from the paper's examples of idea relations (e.g., from a table, figure caption, or in-text example list).

Must associate the idea pair 'immigration, deportation' / 'detainee, detention' with the visual or tabular element in the paper where 'Tryst' relations are exemplified (e.g., a figure or table that lists named relation types and example idea pairs).

Must draw from the section where the paper presents concrete examples of relation types between ideas (e.g., the results or case-study section that lists example pairs for each relation type, including 'Tryst').

Must recognize that the example pair 'immigration, deportation' and 'detainee, detention' is derived using the paper's two-statistic framework (cooccurrence within documents and prevalence correlation over time), and not from an external or unrelated source.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify that the paper uses both newspapers and research articles as datasets for analyzing relations between ideas?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper analyzes relations between ideas using textual corpora drawn from multiple real-world sources, not synthetic or toy data.
Must explicitly identify newspapers as one of the main datasets or corpus types used in the study (e.g., a news archive, newspaper corpus, or similar term in the data description section).
Must explicitly identify research articles (e.g., scientific papers, journal articles, scholarly publications) as another main dataset or corpus type used in the study.

Must draw the mention of newspapers and research articles from the paper's data or corpus description section (e.g., 'Data', 'Corpora', 'Datasets', or equivalent), not infer them from unrelated sections such as 'Related Work' or 'Introduction'.
Must indicate that these datasets (newspapers and research articles) are used as examples of the wide range of textual sources to which the proposed framework is applied.

decisions: How does the paper describe the joint distribution of idea-pair statistics when they are correlated but still occupy all four quadrants?

requirements.description: Must identify that the paper analyzes a joint distribution over two statistics for idea pairs (specifically co-occurrence within documents and prevalence correlation over time).

Must reference the specific figure or plot in the paper that shows idea pairs positioned in a 2D space divided into four quadrants based on the two statistics (e.g., co-occurrence on one axis and temporal correlation on the other).
Must state that even when the two statistics are globally correlated, the visualization shows many idea pairs appearing in all four quadrants of the joint distribution.
Must explain that each point in the joint distribution corresponds to a pair of ideas, positioned according to their measured co-occurrence and prevalence correlation values.

Must report the qualitative result that the distribution of idea pairs across all four quadrants indicates diverse relational types (e.g., cooperation and competition) despite overall correlation between the two statistics.

decisions: How does the paper define and operationalize the strength of relations between ideas, and which pairs are considered most interesting under this definition?
