Must locate the bibliographic or related-work reference in the current paper that cites Wu et al. (2016) GNMT, sufficient to extract the authorship 'Wu et al. 2016' and the paper title.
Must associate the referenced GNMT figure with slide page 7 (P 7) in the 'The Best of Both Worlds' slide sequence, indicating correct slide placement of the Wu et al. (2016) figure.

decisions: What key properties of the convolutional sequence-to-sequence (ConvS2S) model, as contrasted with RNN-based models, are highlighted and visually illustrated in the paper for use on slide P8?

requirements.description: Must state that the convolutional sequence-to-sequence (ConvS2S) architecture is described in the paper as being more interpretable than RNN-based sequence-to-sequence models.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the paper’s characterization of the Transformer architecture (Vaswani et al. 2017), including its optimization properties, parallelism advantages, and noted drawbacks, as presented on page 9 with the referenced figure?

requirements.description: Must state that the Transformer architecture enables 'gradients everywhere' or an equivalent description of dense gradient flow that leads to faster optimization, as characterized in the paper when contrasting it with earlier seq2seq models.
Must state that the Transformer allows parallel encoding during both training and inference, explicitly contrasting this with more sequential architectures like RNN-based models.

Must describe the Transformer as combining many recent advances or techniques at once and identify this combination as a potential drawback or source of fragility, using language equivalent to 'Combines many advances at once' and 'Fragile'.

Must identify and reference the figure taken from 'Attention is All You Need' (Vaswani et al., 2017) that depicts the Transformer architecture, corresponding to the figure cited on page 9 of the paper.

Must retrieve content from the section or subsection where the authors discuss the Transformer model specifically (including its advantages in optimization and parallelism and its fragility), rather than from sections focused solely on RNN or convolutional seq2seq models.

decisions: What are the key architectural characteristics of the RNMT baseline model described in the paper that are needed to construct this slide?

requirements.description: Must identify that the described model is the RNMT (RNN-based Neural Machine Translation) architecture as defined in the paper, and not the convolutional or Transformer variants.
Must state that the RNMT encoder is bi-directional and implemented using LSTM layers, explicitly matching the 'Bi-directional encoder' description in the slide.
Must retrieve the exact encoder depth for RNMT from the paper (6 layers) and express it as '6 x LSTM' or an equivalent explicit indication of six stacked LSTM layers.
Must state that the RNMT decoder is uni-directional and implemented using LSTM layers, explicitly matching the 'Uni-directional decoder' description in the slide.

Must retrieve the exact decoder depth for RNMT from the paper (8 layers) and express it as '8 x LSTM' or an equivalent explicit indication of eight stacked LSTM layers, and must specify that the LSTM cell uses layer normalization (i.e., a 'layer normalized LSTM cell').

decisions: What BLEU score comparisons between different NMT architectures does the paper present on page 11 for the 'Model Comparison I' results?

requirements.description: Must retrieve the specific table or figure on page 11 that reports BLEU scores for multiple neural machine translation architectures (e.g., RNN-based, convolutional seq2seq, Transformer, and combined/best-of-both-worlds variants).

Must extract the numerical BLEU scores from the page 11 comparison (for all models listed in that table/figure) and preserve their relative ranking (which model scores higher or lower).
Must associate the BLEU score comparison on page 11 with the experimental results section or subsection that first introduces 'Model Comparison I' or its equivalent heading in the paper.

decisions: What specific page or slide reference from the paper is used to label the 'Model Comparison II Speed and Size' slide as 'The Best of Both Worlds P 12'?

requirements.description: Must identify that 'The Best of Both Worlds' is the exact title phrase taken from the paper's title and used verbatim on the slide.
Must locate the part of the paper (e.g., section, subsection, or page) that corresponds to 'Model Comparison II Speed and Size' and determine that it is associated with page 12.
Must extract the correct page number '12' from the paper's pagination or internal references and map it to the 'P 12' label on the slide.
Must reproduce the slide label text exactly as 'The Best of Both Worlds P 12' without additional words, symbols, or formatting changes.
Must confirm that no other content (figures, tables, equations, or explanatory text) from the paper is added to this slide beyond the title phrase and page indicator.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the paper’s stability ablation analysis on four key techniques for stabilizing training (especially with multi-head attention) and the specific findings about synchronous training and RNMT+?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper conducts a stability ablation study explicitly evaluating the importance of four key techniques for stabilizing training in the proposed NMT models.
Must explicitly mention that these techniques are critical to stabilize training when using multi-head attention, using wording that clearly links stability to multi-head attention.
Must retrieve and explain the paper’s notation or marker (e.g., an asterisk '*') that is used in the stability ablation results to indicate an unstable training run.
Must identify that one of the ablated conditions is synchronous training and that this condition is part of the stability ablation setup described in the paper.

Must report that under synchronous training there is a significant quality drop for RNMT+ and that RNMT+ is only successful with a tailored learning-rate schedule, reflecting the specific stability finding from the ablation.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the paper’s discussion of hybrid NMT architectures that combine strengths of different seq2seq models?

requirements.description: Must state that each individual architecture (e.g., RNN, convolutional, Transformer) is described in the paper as having a highly expressive, continuous state space representation as a key strength.
Must state that one of the highlighted strengths of at least one architecture is having a full receptive field that acts as a powerful feature extractor.

Must explicitly mention that the paper proposes or analyzes hybrid models that combine different seq2seq architectures to capture complementary information, described as achieving the 'best of both worlds'.
Must describe that the paper discusses trainability as an important concern when designing hybrid architectures, specifically in the context of combining different layer types.

Must state that the paper emphasizes that connections between different types of layers in hybrid models need to be carefully designed (e.g., how RNN, convolutional, and Transformer layers are linked).

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize how the paper contrasts the roles of encoder and decoder in encoder–decoder hybrid architectures for neural machine translation?

requirements.description: Must state that in the paper's encoder–decoder hybrid discussion, the decoder is treated explicitly as a conditional language model (conditional LM) that generates target tokens conditioned on source-derived context.

Must state that in the same discussion, the encoder is described as a component that builds or produces feature representations (i.e., representations of the source sequence) rather than directly generating output tokens.

Must attribute these role definitions to the part of the paper that analyzes or proposes encoder–decoder hybrids (e.g., the section where the authors compare or combine RNN, convolutional, and Transformer architectures), not to unrelated background or experiments sections.

Must explicitly mention that the paper's formulation is designed to contrast or separate the roles of encoder and decoder (i.e., that the architecture or analysis is intentionally structured to highlight this role distinction).

Must link the description of encoder–decoder roles to the specific slide or figure-equivalent content labeled or corresponding to 'Encoder Decoder Hybrids' (e.g., the conceptual diagram or text where encoder and decoder are contrasted), rather than inferring these roles solely from general seq2seq knowledge.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the paper’s description of encoder layer hybrid architectures and their key design components?

requirements.description: Must state that encoder layer hybrids are used to enrich stateful (e.g., recurrent or convolutional) representations with global self-attention, explicitly mentioning both 'stateful representations' and 'global self-attention' as described in the encoder section of the paper.

Must identify that the encoder hybrid design includes the use of pre-trained components to improve trainability, explicitly linking pre-training to encoder layers or encoder submodules as discussed in the model architecture or training methodology section.

Must mention that layer normalization is applied at layer boundaries in the encoder hybrid architecture, clearly indicating that normalization occurs at the boundaries between layers (not just generically within layers) as specified in the implementation or architecture description.

Must describe a 'Cascaded Hybrid' encoder configuration as a vertical combination of different encoder layer types (e.g., stacking RNN/convolutional layers with self-attention layers), using the term 'cascaded' or 'vertical' and tying it to encoder layers as defined in the paper.

Must describe a 'Multi-Column Hybrid' encoder configuration as a horizontal combination of different encoder layer types (e.g., parallel columns or branches whose outputs are combined), using the term 'multi-column' or 'horizontal' and tying it to encoder layers as defined in the paper.

decisions: What key lessons and high-level conclusions does the paper draw about combining recent NMT advances and training techniques, as summarized on the 'Lessons Learnt' slide?

requirements.description: Must state the lesson that improvements due to modeling and training techniques need to be separated from improvements due to the core architecture itself, using wording equivalent to 'Need to separate other improvements from the architecture itself'.

Must convey the idea that existing or older NMT architectures can perform very well when enhanced with modern modeling and training techniques, using wording equivalent to 'Your good ol architecture may shine with new modelling and training techniques'.
Must reference the use or importance of stronger baselines in NMT evaluation, explicitly mentioning the work of Denkowski and Neubig (2017) as an example of stronger baselines.

Must describe the knowledge distillation or teacher–student training insight summarized as 'Dull Teachers - Smart Students', i.e., that a comparatively simple or weaker teacher model can be used to train a stronger student model.

Must mention the critical role of the learning rate schedule in training NMT models, using wording equivalent to 'A model with a sufficiently advanced lr-schedule is indistinguishable from magic', and must identify it as a training technique rather than an architectural change.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the paper’s introduction of the active learning setting and the motivation for learning an active learning strategy instead of using fixed heuristics?

requirements.description: Must state that the setting involves raw unlabeled data points (explicitly referring to them as x1, x2 or equivalent notation for individual unlabeled instances).
Must identify the presence of a classifier oracle or expert that provides labels for queried data points in the active learning loop.
Must describe that at any time during the active learning process there is a current guess or current version of the classifier that is being iteratively improved.
Must mention an active learning strategy based on querying the point closest to the classifier’s decision boundary (i.e., a margin/uncertainty-based heuristic).

Must explicitly convey the motivation that hard-coded heuristics for active learning may not be optimal or universally good, and pose or imply the question of whether one can learn the best active learning strategy instead.

decisions: What information from the paper is needed to describe the setup of the agent-based active learning scenario, including the AL agent’s decision, its inputs, and the role of the classifier oracle/expert?

requirements.description: Must state that the method learns an active learning (AL) policy/agent that selects which unlabeled data points to query next, rather than using a fixed heuristic-based AL strategy.

Must describe that the AL agent’s decision is conditioned on (i) the previously selected and labeled data, (ii) the current pool of unlabeled data, and (iii) the state or outputs of the underlying classifier.

Must explain that the AL policy is implemented as a feedforward network that maps the current AL situation (including labeled and unlabeled data plus classifier state) to the choice of the most informative query datapoint.
Must identify the presence of an oracle or expert (classifier/expert) that provides labels for queried datapoints, as used in the imitation learning setup.

Must mention that the expert used in imitation learning is an algorithmic expert that supplies good actions (i.e., which datapoints to query) in encountered AL situations, which the AL agent then imitates.

decisions: How does the paper conceptualize the components and data flow in its active learning setup, specifically the agent, the student classifier, the oracle/expert, and the raw unlabeled data points used for querying?

requirements.description: Must identify that the active learning process operates on a pool of raw unlabeled data points, explicitly denoted as individual instances (e.g., x1, x2, ...), from which queries are selected.
Must state that there is an active learning agent (policy) whose role is to choose which unlabeled data points to query, corresponding to the 'Tutoring AL Agent' in the slide.
Must describe the presence of a learning model that is being trained using the queried labels, explicitly identifying it as a student classifier or equivalent supervised learner.
Must specify that an oracle or expert component exists in the system whose function is to provide labels for the queried unlabeled data points.

Must reference or reconstruct the conceptual diagram or description in the paper that depicts the interaction between (1) raw unlabeled data points, (2) the AL agent, (3) the learning student/classifier, and (4) the oracle/expert providing labels, matching the three textual elements shown on the slide.

decisions: How does the paper propose to train an active learning agent’s policy so that it can be transferred to new active learning problems?

requirements.description: Must state that the central idea is to train an active learning policy (agent) on a rich-data or simulated active learning task and then transfer that learned policy to the target active learning problem of interest.

Must explicitly characterize the approach as a form of meta-learning, described in the paper as "learning to actively learn" or equivalent wording indicating that the system learns an active learning strategy across tasks.
Must mention that the method involves synthesizing or generating many active learning problems (AL tasks) to create diverse training situations for the policy learner.
Must indicate that the training of the active learning policy uses imitation learning and/or reinforcement learning algorithms, as described in the paper’s method section.

Must draw from the part of the paper that describes the overall training framework for the AL policy (e.g., the method/approach section that explains simulation of AL tasks, policy learning, and transfer), not from unrelated sections such as experiments or related work alone.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize how imitation learning with an algorithmic oracle and DAGGER is used to learn the active learning policy in this paper?

requirements.description: Must state that an algorithmic oracle (expert) provides the correct action for each encountered world state in the active learning setting.

Must describe that the policy network is trained as a classifier to prefer the oracle's correct action over incorrect actions for each state (i.e., framed as a supervised classification problem on state-action pairs).
Must explicitly mention that the collected state-action pairs from the oracle are not i.i.d., and that this non-i.i.d. nature is problematic for standard classifier learning.

Must identify the use of the DAGGER (Data Aggregation) algorithm and explain that during training, the system occasionally uses the policy network's own predicted actions to generate states, rather than always querying the oracle first.

Must explain that the purpose of DAGGER in this context is to expose the policy to 'bad' states induced by its own predictions and to pair these with the oracle's corrective actions so the policy learns how to recover from such states.

decisions: How does the paper define and implement the algorithmic oracle used to provide expert actions for learning the active learning policy, and how is its computational cost mitigated?

requirements.description: Must state that the algorithmic oracle is defined as computing the 'correct' action in each active learning world state by selecting the most informative query datapoint from the pool.

Must describe that for each candidate query (x_i, y_i) in the pool, the underlying model is re-trained (or updated) using that query/action and then evaluated on a held-out evaluation set to measure prediction accuracy.

Must explicitly mention that the oracle selects the action by taking an argmax over all pool elements (x_i, y_i), i.e., choosing the query that yields the highest evaluation accuracy after retraining.
Must note that this exhaustive oracle procedure is described as computationally too slow or infeasible for typical large pools of data.

Must explain the efficiency improvement idea that instead of maximizing over the entire pool, the method randomly samples a subset of candidate queries and performs the argmax only over this subset, and that this is claimed to lead to efficient training and effective learned policies.

decisions: How does the paper define and set up the text classification experiments, including tasks and transfer/initialization conditions, for evaluating the learned active learning policy?

requirements.description: Must identify that one experimental task is Sentiment Classification, defined specifically as predicting Positive/Negative sentiment of a review.
Must identify that a second experimental task is Authorship Profiling, defined specifically as predicting the gender of the author of a tweet.
Must state that for the Sentiment Classification task, the AL policy is trained on reviews from one product and then applied to reviews of another product (cross-product transfer setup).
Must state that for the Authorship Profiling task, the AL policy is trained on tweets in one language and then applied to tweets in another language (cross-language transfer setup).

Must distinguish and define the three classifier initialization/transfer conditions: Direct transfer (initialize the classifier on the source data), Cold-start (start training the classifier from random initialization and continue training with the AL agent), and Warm-start (start training the classifier from the pre-trained model on the source data and continue training with the AL agent).

decisions: How does the paper describe the PAL baseline method used in the experiments, including its learning paradigm, model type, and active learning setting?

requirements.description: Must state that PAL is used as a baseline method in the experiments section of the paper.
Must identify PAL (Fang et al., 2017) as a deep reinforcement learning based approach for active learning.
Must specify that PAL uses a Q-network as the core model for decision making.
Must indicate that PAL is designed for stream-based active learning, not pool-based or other AL settings.
Must retrieve the description of PAL from the part of the paper that lists or explains experimental baseline methods (e.g., 'Baselines' or 'Experimental Setup' subsection).

decisions: How does the paper quantitatively measure the agreement between the queried data points selected by the proposed active learning agent and other active learning strategies?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper evaluates the agreement between queried data points selected by the proposed active learning (AL) agent and those selected by other AL strategies.
Must identify Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) as one of the metrics used to measure agreement of queried data points between the AL agent and other strategies.
Must identify accuracy (acc) as another metric used to measure agreement of queried data points between the AL agent and other strategies.
Must retrieve from the paper the explicit pairing of the two metrics (MRR and accuracy) as being used together for this agreement analysis, not as general performance metrics only.

Must locate and use the part of the paper (e.g., evaluation or experimental setup section) where the authors define or describe using MRR and accuracy specifically for comparing queried data points across AL strategies.

decisions: How does the paper define and use the parameter K as the size of a subset from the original unlabeled set in its analysis of sensitivity to K?

requirements.description: Must state that K is explicitly defined in the paper as the size of a subset sampled from the original unlabeled dataset (pool) used in active learning.

Must identify the section or methodological description where the authors introduce the sensitivity analysis with respect to K (e.g., an experimental setup or analysis subsection discussing varying K).

Must reference the specific figure or plot (e.g., 'Figure X') in which performance or behavior is analyzed as a function of K, indicating that K appears on an axis or in the legend as the size of the unlabeled subset.

Must retrieve any tabular or numerical description (e.g., in a table or in-text enumeration) that lists or specifies the concrete values of K used (such as K = 1000, 5000, etc.) as subset sizes from the original unlabeled set.

Must cover the experimental or analysis subsection where the authors describe how they construct the unlabeled subset of size K from the full unlabeled pool, including any sampling or selection procedure tied to K.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the key strands of related work (meta-learning, RL-based stream active learning, and imitation learning) that motivate the proposed imitation-learning-based active learning approach?

requirements.description: Must extract content specifically from the paper's related work discussion that contrasts heuristic-based active learning with learning-based approaches (meta-learning, reinforcement learning, and imitation learning), rather than from the abstract or experimental sections.

Must identify and state that prior meta-learning work is described as "learning to learn" (or equivalent phrasing) and that it involves learning without gradient descent by using gradient descent, as attributed to Chen et al. (2016).

Must retrieve the description that stream-based active learning has been formulated as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) and that the policy is learned with reinforcement learning, as referenced to Fang et al. (2017).

Must capture the specific limitation mentioned for the reinforcement-learning-based stream active learning approach, namely that it suffers from the credit assignment problem, and must attribute this issue to Bechman et al. (2017) or the equivalent citation used in the paper.

Must retrieve the characterization of imitation learning as learning from expert demonstrations and must associate this with the example citation to Schaal (or the exact imitation learning reference used in the related work section).

decisions: Does the system correctly summarize the paper’s main conclusions about learning active learning (AL) query strategies via imitation learning compared to heuristic- and RL-based methods?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper contrasts two options for AL query strategies: using fixed heuristics versus learning an agent to select queries.
Must describe that the agent-based active learning procedure is explicitly modeled as a Markov Decision Process (MDP).
Must explain that the learning of AL strategies or policies is formulated as an imitation learning problem, where a policy is learned from an expert’s actions.
Must state that the proposed imitation learning-based AL approach outperforms prior heuristic-based AL methods according to the paper’s experimental evaluation.
Must state that the proposed imitation learning-based AL approach also outperforms prior reinforcement learning (RL)-based AL methods according to the paper’s experimental evaluation.

decisions: Does the paper explicitly frame its research around the creativity of machine learning models and their ability to compose novel narrative, specifically in the context of sonnet generation?

requirements.description: Must identify that the paper explicitly investigates whether machine learning models can be creative, i.e., frames the work as exploring creativity in generative models.
Must extract that the paper questions whether such models can compose novel and interesting narrative (or text/poems), not just imitate existing data.

Must locate and use the part of the paper (e.g., introduction or motivation section) where the authors state the high-level research questions about creativity and narrative generation, rather than only technical model details.
Must state that the concrete application domain of the study is sonnet generation, i.e., that the work focuses specifically on generating sonnets rather than generic text or other poetic forms.
Must connect the creativity and narrative questions directly to the joint modeling of poetic language, meter, and rhyme for sonnets, as described in the paper's problem setup.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and present the paper’s treatment of poetic aesthetic forms, specifically rhyme, as illustrated through a Shakespearean sonnet example?

requirements.description: Must state that a key focus of the paper is on modelling aesthetic forms of poetry, explicitly including rhyme (and meter) as central properties of sonnets.
Must describe that the model includes a dedicated rhyme component or rhyme model, distinct from or in addition to the core language model, for capturing rhyme structure in sonnets.
Must cover the part of the paper where the authors discuss or exemplify rhyme patterns in sonnets (e.g., explanation of how line endings are paired or grouped to form rhymes).

Must explain that rhyme is operationalized in terms of relationships between line-final words (e.g., pairing words like 'day' and 'May', or 'temperate' and 'date') rather than general semantic similarity.
Must indicate that rhyme pairs can be represented explicitly as sets or pairs of words (e.g., {word1, word2}), mirroring the slide’s notation for rhyme groups.

decisions: How does the paper define and constrain the poem generation task in its modelling approach for sonnets?

requirements.description: Must state that poem generation is formulated as a constrained language modelling task, explicitly using the phrase 'constrained language modelling' or an equivalent clearly constrained language model description from the modelling approach section.
Must specify that the model is trained jointly on three components—language, rhyme, and meter—describing it as a single (joint or unified) model rather than separate independent models.

Must indicate that the approach conditions on a given rhyming scheme such that each line must follow a canonical meter and have a fixed length or structure, explicitly linking rhyming scheme to line-level metrical constraints.
Must identify that the modelling approach focuses specifically on sonnets as the target poetic form, including the rationale that sonnets are popular and provide sufficient data.
Must describe the formal constraints of sonnets used in the model: regular rhyming schemes (e.g., ABAB, AABB, or ABBA) and a regular stress pattern identified as iambic pentameter.

decisions: How is the sonnet corpus constructed from a generic poetry collection in the Deep-speare paper?

requirements.description: Must state that a generic poetry document collection is first created using the GutenTag tool, explicitly mentioning that its inbuilt poetry classifier is used.
Must state that word and character statistics are extracted specifically from Shakespeare's 154 sonnets.
Must state that the extracted word and character statistics are then used as criteria to filter out all non-sonnet poems from the generic poetry collection.
Must explicitly mention that the outcome of this filtering process is a dedicated 'sonnet corpus' used in the paper.
Must cover the paper's dataset or corpus construction description where the sonnet corpus is defined, rather than inferring from model or evaluation sections.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and label the three main components of the proposed joint model architecture for sonnet generation?

requirements.description: Must state that the overall architecture is a joint model specifically combining components for language, meter, and rhyme in sonnet modelling.
Must explicitly identify a 'Language model' component as one of the architecture modules, matching label (a) in the paper's model description or figure.
Must explicitly identify a 'Pentameter model' (i.e., meter/stress model) component as one of the architecture modules, matching label (b) in the paper's model description or figure.
Must explicitly identify a 'Rhyme model' component as one of the architecture modules, matching label (c) in the paper's model description or figure.

Must preserve the correspondence between component labels and names exactly as in the source (i.e., (a) Language model, (b) Pentameter model, (c) Rhyme model) when describing or recreating the architecture slide.

decisions: How is the language model (LM) component architected and configured in the Deep-speare system for generating a sonnet line from preceding context?

requirements.description: Must state that the LM is implemented as a variant of an LSTM encoder–decoder model with an attention mechanism, using the terminology 'LSTM encoder-decoder' (or 'LSTM encoderdecoder') and 'attention' as in the paper.
Must describe that the encoder processes the preceding context consisting of all sonnet lines before the current line (i.e., encodes all prior lines of the sonnet as context for the current line).
Must explain that the decoder generates the current line one word at a time while attending over the encoded preceding context (i.e., word-by-word decoding with attention to prior lines).

Must mention that the preceding context passed from encoder to decoder is filtered by a selective mechanism (a selective context mechanism or equivalent term explicitly indicating filtering of context).

Must specify both that character-level encodings are incorporated into the decoder input words and that the input and output word embeddings of the LM are tied (shared) as described in the model section.

decisions: Does the summary correctly describe the design and training objectives of the Pentameter Model (PM) for predicting stress patterns in sonnet lines?

requirements.description: Must state that the Pentameter Model (PM) is designed specifically to capture the alternating stress pattern in sonnet lines and to output 10 binary stress symbols for each line.
Must describe PM as an encoder–decoder model where the encoder processes the characters of a sonnet line and the decoder uses attention over these character encodings to predict stresses.
Must specify that decoder hidden states are not directly used in making the stress predictions, distinguishing this from standard encoder–decoder architectures.
Must explain that the attention mechanism in PM is constrained so that it focuses on character positions that are monotonically increasing along the input line.

Must mention that, in addition to the main cross-entropy loss for stress prediction, PM is regularized with two auxiliary objectives that penalize attention repetition and low coverage over the input characters.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize how the paper’s rhyme model is learned and applied in an unsupervised fashion for Shakespearean sonnets?

requirements.description: Must state that the rhyme model is learned in an unsupervised fashion and give both explicit motivations: (1) extendability to languages without pronunciation dictionaries, and (2) the sonnet language not being Modern English so contemporary pronunciation dictionaries may be inaccurate.
Must describe the core training assumption that rhyme exists within a quatrain and that sentence-ending word pairs from quatrains are used as input to the rhyme model.

Must explain that the model is trained to separate rhyming word pairs from non-rhyming ones by enforcing a margin where the best (most rhyming) pair is separated from all others, and the second-best pair is used to quantify this margin.
Must mention the use or definition of the function top(Q, k) as returning the k-th largest element in Q in the context of selecting or ranking rhyme candidates.
Must reference the illustrative Shakespearean quatrain example (beginning with 'Shall I compare thee to a summers day?') as being used to demonstrate sentence-ending word pairs for the rhyme model.

decisions: How does the paper describe the joint training setup for the language, meter, and rhyme components, and what happens if they are trained separately?

requirements.description: Must state that all three components (language model LM, meter/prosody model PM, and rhyme model RM) are trained jointly rather than independently.
Must describe that in the joint training scheme, each component (LM, PM, RM) is treated as a sub-task within a single training framework or objective.
Must explicitly mention that the components share parameters during training, enabling them to mutually influence or inform each other.
Must report that when each component is trained separately (i.e., without joint training), the prosody/meter model (PM) performs poorly compared to the joint training setup.
Must draw from the part of the paper that explains the training procedure or model architecture (e.g., the model or training section) rather than from evaluation or related work sections.

decisions: How does the paper define the crowdworker evaluation setup and the specific model variants (LM, LM+, LM+PM+RM) compared in that setup?

requirements.description: Must state that crowdworkers are shown pairs of poems where exactly one is machine-generated and one is human-written, and are asked to identify which poem is the human-written one.
Must retrieve the description of the crowdworker evaluation protocol from the evaluation or experiments section that explains how human judgments are collected for poem quality.
Must define the baseline 'LM' model explicitly as a vanilla LSTM language model, as described in the model or experimental setup section.
Must identify and describe the intermediate language model variant that extends the vanilla LSTM LM with character-level encodings (and any additional specified features) as used in the experiments.
Must define 'LM+PM+RM' as the full joint model that trains the language model together with the pentameter (meter) model and the rhyme model, as specified in the model description section.

decisions: How does the paper’s crowdworker evaluation demonstrate that lay annotators primarily rely on rhyme, rather than meter, when judging the quality of generated quatrains?

requirements.description: Must identify that the evaluation concerns crowdworkers (non-expert laypersons) judging the quality/authorhood of generated quatrains (four-line poem segments).

Must describe the comparison between at least two model variants used in the crowdworker study, including a baseline language model (LM) and a joint model that combines LM with both a meter/prosody model and a rhyme model (LM+PM+RM), in the context of evaluating poem quality or human vs. machine discrimination.

Must state that accuracy (of crowdworkers’ judgments) improves when moving from LM to LM+PM+RM, and that this improvement is interpreted as indicating that generated quatrains become harder to distinguish from human-written ones.

Must mention the specific experimental condition using a model with language and rhyme but without the meter component (LM+RM) as a diagnostic test to determine whether workers rely mainly on rhyme cues.

Must report the conclusion from the LM+RM condition that crowdworkers’ judgments are largely driven by rhyme and that meter/stress information is mostly ignored by laypersons in the evaluation, as evidenced by similar performance when meter is removed.

decisions: Does the summary correctly describe the expert evaluation of meter, rhyme, readability, and emotion for the different models compared to human poems?

requirements.description: Must state that a literature expert (or expert evaluator) is used to judge poems specifically on the quality of meter, rhyme, readability, and emotional impact.
Must report that the full joint model receives the highest ratings for meter and rhyme, and that these ratings are even higher than those of human-written poems.
Must explain that the higher meter and rhyme ratings for the full model compared to humans are interpreted as reflecting that human poets regularly break formal rules of meter and rhyme.
Must state that, despite strong performance on meter and rhyme, machine-generated poems are still easily distinguishable from human poems because they score lower on readability and emotional impact.
Must mention that a vanilla language model (LM) is found to capture meter implicitly or surprisingly well, based on the expert evaluation results.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the paper’s main contributions, evaluation setup, implications for future work, and code/data availability as presented in the summary slide?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper introduces a *joint neural model* that simultaneously learns or models *language*, *rhyme*, and *stress/meter* for sonnet or poetry generation, as described in the paper’s problem/method overview.

Must mention that the architecture explicitly *encodes assumptions about rhyme and stress/meter* (e.g., via dedicated rhyme and stress components or constraints), rather than treating them as purely implicit properties.
Must capture that the model is *adaptable to poetry in other languages*, as stated in the paper’s discussion or conclusion about generalization or applicability beyond English sonnets.

Must describe the *evaluation setup* in which poem quality is assessed using *both* crowdworker judgments and a *literature expert* (expert human) evaluation, as reported in the experiments or evaluation section.

Must identify that the paper provides *code and data* and give the *GitHub URL* exactly as in the paper (https://github.com/jhlau/deepspeare) or an equivalent explicit repository reference from the resources section.

decisions: Did the system correctly retrieve and reproduce the example machine-generated sonnet quatrain presented in the paper?

requirements.description: Must identify that the quoted text is an example of a machine-generated sonnet (not human-written) produced by the joint neural model of poetic language, meter, and rhyme.

Must retrieve the exact example quatrain from the section of the paper where sample generated poems or qualitative outputs of the model are presented (e.g., an examples, case study, or qualitative analysis section).

Must reproduce the full four-line quatrain exactly as in the paper, including line breaks and punctuation: 'in darkness to behold him, with a light' (line 1), 'and him was filled with terror on my breast' (line 2), 'and saw its brazen ruler of the night' (line 3), 'but, lo! it was a monarch of the rest' (line 4).

Must associate this example quatrain with the specific generation setting described in the paper (e.g., model configuration or decoding strategy) under which sample poems are produced, as indicated in the surrounding text of the examples section.
Must note that the example is used in the paper to illustrate the model's handling of meter and rhyme (e.g., sonnet-like structure), as described in the accompanying narrative around the example.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and restate the paper’s motivation that predicting stock movements is highly desirable but challenging?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper addresses the problem of stock movement prediction as its primary task, using wording that clearly indicates prediction of stock price movements or returns.

Must convey that stock movement prediction is described as challenging or difficult due to properties of the market (e.g., stochasticity, chaotic data, temporally dependent predictions) as mentioned in the abstract.

Must express the motivation that being able to predict stock movements is highly desirable or beneficial (e.g., that people would care about or be happy to predict stock movements), aligning with the slide’s statement that no one would be unhappy if they could predict stock movements.

Must derive the motivational content for the slide from the paper’s introductory or abstract-level discussion of the problem (e.g., the abstract or introduction), not from later technical or experimental sections.

Must avoid introducing specific methodological details (e.g., recurrent continuous latent variables, neural variational inference) on this slide, restricting content to the high-level problem and motivation only.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the paper’s background on analysis paradigms in finance and content resources in NLP, along with the brief historical timeline of NLP models relevant to stock movement prediction?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper distinguishes two mainstreams in finance, explicitly naming both 'technical analysis' and 'fundamental analysis' as separate approaches.
Must state that the paper identifies two main content resources for NLP in this domain, explicitly listing both 'public news' and 'social media'.

Must cover the background or related work discussion where the authors contrast financial analysis paradigms (technical vs. fundamental) and data sources (news vs. social media) as context for their model.
Must mention the historical use of 'feature engineering' for NLP models and explicitly associate it with a pre-2010 period (e.g., 'before 2010').
Must mention 'hierarchical attention' or 'hierarchical attention networks' as a later NLP modeling approach and explicitly associate it with around 2018.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and restate the paper’s description of the stock market prediction problem’s stochastic and temporally-dependent nature from the abstract?

requirements.description: Must state that the market is described as 'highly stochastic' using that exact phrase from the abstract.
Must state that predictions are 'temporally-dependent' using that exact phrase from the abstract.
Must mention that the data is characterized as 'chaotic' using that exact word from the abstract.
Must explicitly attribute the description of the market as highly stochastic and predictions as temporally-dependent from the abstract section of the paper.
Must convey that these three aspects (highly stochastic market, temporally-dependent predictions, chaotic data) are presented together as the core challenge of the stock movement prediction problem.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the paper’s explanation of how public information (e.g., major scandals) affects stock price movements over subsequent trading days and is shared across temporally-close predictions?

requirements.description: Must state that a major negative public event (e.g., a company scandal) occurring on a trading day is associated with a downtrend in that company’s stock price in the following trading days, as described in the paper’s motivation or problem description.
Must explain that public information requires time to be fully absorbed into stock price movements, explicitly linking information arrival to delayed price response over multiple future days.

Must identify that the model or problem setup assumes that information effects are shared across temporally-close predictions, i.e., that nearby time steps in the prediction horizon are correlated due to shared public information.

Must retrieve this temporal-information argument from the paper’s introductory or motivation-related discussion (e.g., early narrative or background section) rather than from experimental results or implementation details.
Must include the citation to Luss and d’Aspremont (2015) in connection with the claim that public information needs time to be absorbed into movements over time.

decisions: How does the paper decompose the challenges of stock movement prediction and map them to specific model components and temporal assumptions used in the proposed deep generative framework?

requirements.description: Must identify and pair each of the three core problem characteristics with its corresponding model component as stated in the paper: (1) 'chaotic market information' with a 'Market Information Encoder', (2) 'high market stochasticity' with a 'Variational Movement Decoder', and (3) 'temporally-dependent prediction' with an 'Attentive Temporal Auxiliary'.

Must describe that the model uses recurrent, continuous latent variables and neural variational inference (as mentioned in the abstract/method section) specifically in the context of the 'Variational Movement Decoder' to handle high market stochasticity.

Must retrieve and state the paper's reference to random walk theory, explicitly citing Malkiel (1999), and connect it to the discussion of market stochasticity or unpredictability in stock price movements.

Must retrieve the example scenario used in the paper where a company suffers a major scandal on a trading day and the stock price exhibits a downtrend in the following trading days, and use it to illustrate temporally-dependent prediction or delayed market reaction.

Must retrieve and state the claim that public information needs time to be absorbed into stock price movements over time, explicitly referencing Luss and d'Aspremont (2015), and link this to the idea that information is shared across temporally-close predictions (motivating the Attentive Temporal Auxiliary).

decisions: How does the paper formally define the stock movement prediction problem, including the target variable, prediction horizon, and input information window?

requirements.description: Must state that the prediction target is a binary stock movement variable, where 1 denotes a rise and 0 denotes a fall in price.
Must identify that the prediction is made for a specific target trading day denoted by the symbol d.
Must describe that the model uses market information from both relevant tweets and historical prices as input signals for prediction.

Must specify that the input information is taken over a fixed-length lag window ending at the target day d, i.e., over an interval [d - δ, d] or equivalent notation where δ (or d in the slide text) is a fixed lag size.

Must extract these elements (binary target definition, target day d, tweet and price inputs, and fixed lag window) from the paper's problem formulation or task definition portion, not inferred from abstract or results sections.

decisions: How does the paper define and structure the generative process for stock movement prediction over T eligible trading days in the d-lag window?

requirements.description: Must state that the generative process is defined over T eligible trading days within a d-lag window (i.e., explicitly mention both T trading days and the d-lag).

Must describe that observed market information for these T days is encoded as a random variable X composed of per-day observations, written as X = [x1; …; xT] or equivalent notation indicating a sequence of T elements.
Must identify that the generative process includes a step where a latent driving (or driven) factor is generated before generating stock movements.
Must explicitly include a separate generative step for stock movements that is conditioned on or follows from the latent factor and/or encoded market information.

Must extract these elements (T eligible trading days in d-lag, X = [x1; …; xT], latent factor generation, and stock movement generation) from the paper's section that formally defines the generative process or model formulation, rather than from unrelated narrative or results sections.

decisions: How does the paper factorize the joint probability distribution for multi-task stock movement prediction using tweets and historical prices?

requirements.description: Must state that for multi-task learning the model considers the joint distribution p(y, Z | X) rather than only the terminal prediction distribution p(y_T | X).

Must specify the factorization of the joint distribution over time as a product over t of p(y_t | x_t, z_t) and p(z_t | z_{<t}, x_t, y_t), i.e., p(y, Z | X) = ∏_t p(y_t | x_t, z_t) p(z_t | z_{<t}, x_t, y_t).
Must identify Z as recurrent, continuous latent variables introduced to model stochasticity in the temporal stock movement prediction process.

Must draw the factorization and probability expressions from the part of the paper that formally defines the generative model or probabilistic formulation for multi-task learning (e.g., the model or methodology section), not from the abstract or results sections.

Must indicate that X denotes the full observed input sequence (including tweets and historical prices) and that x_t represents the inputs at time step t used in the conditional terms p(y_t | x_t, z_t) and p(z_t | z_{<t}, x_t, y_t).

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the primary model components and their roles in the proposed deep generative framework for stock movement prediction?

requirements.description: Must state that the model is composed of three primary components named exactly as: Market Information Encoder (MIE), Variational Movement Decoder (VMD), and Z Attentive Temporal Auxiliary (ATA).

Must describe that the Variational Movement Decoder (VMD) performs variational inference by inferring the continuous latent variables Z using both input features X and stock movements y, and then decodes stock movements y from X and Z.

Must explain that the Market Information Encoder (MIE) is the component responsible for encoding market information (including text and/or price signals) into representations used by the generative model.

Must state that the Z Attentive Temporal Auxiliary (ATA) component is associated with a temporal auxiliary objective that integrates a temporal loss term into training, denoted in the paper by a quantity involving |D| (dataset size or sequence length).

Must draw from the paper's model/architecture description section (where the three components are first formally defined) rather than from abstract, introduction, or results-only passages when identifying MIE, VMD, and ATA and their functions.

decisions: What are the main architectural components and information flows in the StockNet model as depicted in the StockNet architecture figure?

requirements.description: Must identify that the architecture includes a variational encoder (henc) and a variational decoder (hdec) as core components of the model.
Must state that the variational encoder takes as prior or input a standard normal distribution denoted as N(0, I).
Must reference the 'Market Information Encoder (MIE)' block explicitly labeled as '(b) Market Information Encoder (MIE)' in the architecture figure.
Must describe that historical prices are processed through an input attention mechanism, with repeated 'Attention' operations applied to the historical prices input.
Must specify that the architecture includes a component labeled '(d) VAEs Bi-GRUs Message Embedding Layer', indicating the use of Bi-GRUs within a VAE-based message embedding layer.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the paper’s variational movement decoder, including its goal, inference challenge, and neural posterior approximation strategy?

requirements.description: Must state that the model’s goal is to recurrently infer continuous latent variables Z from inputs (historical prices and/or tweet-based features X and observed movements y) and then decode future or target stock movement y from (X, Z).

Must describe that posterior inference over the recurrent latent variables Z is intractable under the model’s factorized generative structure, explicitly mentioning intractable posterior or intractable inference in the factorized model.
Must explain that the paper uses a neural network–based variational posterior approximator (e.g., an inference network or recognition model) to approximate the true posterior over Z.

Must mention the use of the reparameterization trick (neural reparameterization) to enable gradient-based optimization of the variational objective with respect to the parameters of the posterior approximator.

Must attribute these points specifically to the part of the paper that introduces the variational movement decoder or the variational inference formulation for the recurrent latent variables (e.g., the model or inference section describing Z, the posterior, and its approximation).

decisions: How does the model interface between the variational market dynamics (VMD) component and the attention-based temporal aggregator (ATA) to decode stock movement hypotheses?

requirements.description: Must state that the interface combines a deterministic hidden feature h_t with a stochastic latent variable z_t to form a joint representation used for prediction.

Must describe the integration function g_t as a tanh nonlinearity applied to an affine transformation of the concatenated inputs [x_t, h_t, z_t], explicitly referencing a weight matrix W_g and bias term b_g (e.g., g_t = tanh(W_g [x_t, h_t, z_t] + b_g)).
Must explain that movement hypotheses are decoded in two stages: first predicting auxiliary temporal targets and then predicting the main stock movement target, explicitly noting this ordering.

Must identify that a temporal attention mechanism is applied over time steps, parameterized by a vector v (or equivalent notation), to weight the integrated representations when forming the final movement hypothesis.

Must draw from the section that defines the "Interface between VMD and ATA" (or the equivalent model-architecture subsection describing how latent variables and attention are connected), not from unrelated parts such as data description or experiments.

decisions: How does the paper define and use the attentive temporal auxiliary objective, including its decomposition of the approximated lower bound and the construction of the temporal weight vector?

requirements.description: Must state that the approximated variational lower bound (often denoted by L or a similar symbol) is explicitly broken down into a sequence of temporal objectives indexed over time steps t = 1,...,T.
Must specify that each temporal objective term has the form f_t = log p(y_t | x_t, z_t) or an equivalent conditional log-likelihood expression involving y_t, x_t, and z_t at time t.
Must identify that a vector v (introduced earlier in the model) is reused to construct a final temporal weight vector of dimension R^{1×T} (or R^{1T}), assigning a scalar weight to each time step.

Must mention that a scalar parameter (denoted in the paper, e.g., by a Greek letter such as lambda or similar) is used to control the overall effect or strength of the auxiliary temporal objective in the final loss.

Must reference the specific part of the paper where the 'attentive temporal auxiliary' or 'temporal auxiliary objective' is defined, including its mathematical formulation and how it augments the main training objective.

decisions: Does the system correctly extract and summarize the experimental setup for stock movement prediction, including datasets, time span, lag window, evaluation metrics, and comparative models?

requirements.description: Must state that the experiment uses two years of daily price movements for 88 stocks, matching the exact duration ('two-year') and stock count ('88 stocks') as reported in the experimental setup section.

Must identify that the experimental data consists of two components explicitly described as a Twitter dataset and a historical price dataset, and present both components together as the joint data source.

Must report the development (validation) period length as 2 months and the corresponding number of movements as 2,555, using both the correct time span ('2 months') and the exact count ('2,555 movements') from the experimental setup description or table.
Must specify the lag window used for modeling as 5 (i.e., a lag window of length 5), explicitly using the numeric value '5' as given in the experimental setup description.

Must list the evaluation metrics as accuracy and Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC), and must mention that the comparative study includes five baselines from different genres and five variations of the proposed StockNet model, matching these counts and categories.

decisions: Which baseline models and model variants does the paper define and compare against for stock movement prediction?

requirements.description: Must list the RAND baseline explicitly as a 'naive predictor' using the same naming (RAND) as in the paper's baselines section.
Must identify ARIMA as a baseline and expand the acronym as 'Autoregressive Integrated' consistent with the paper's description of this time-series model.
Must extract from the baselines/experimental setup section the three analyst-style variants named TECHNICALANALYST, FUNDAMENTALANALYST, and INDEPENDENTANALYST, preserving these exact variant names.
Must include TSLDA as a baseline and attribute it to 'Nguyen and Shirai, 2015' as written in the paper's baseline description.
Must distinguish DISCRIMINATIVEANALYST as a separate discriminative variant, using the exact name 'DISCRIMINATIVEANALYST' taken from the model variants/baselines section.

decisions: What experimental results and comparative baselines does the paper report to evaluate StockNet’s performance on stock movement prediction?

requirements.description: Must identify the specific table or section where baseline model performance is reported with both Accuracy (Acc.) and Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC), and state that these two metrics are used for comparison.
Must retrieve from the results table(s) that ARIMA is included as a baseline model and that its performance is characterized as not yielding satisfying results relative to other baselines.
Must retrieve from the results table(s) that TSLDA and HAN are among the baseline models and are identified as the two best-performing baselines prior to comparing with StockNet.

Must state that the evaluation compares two groups of models: (1) baseline models and (2) StockNet variations, each reported with Accuracy and MCC, reflecting two distinct sets of experimental results.

Must identify from the methodology or model description section that the proposed generative framework jointly incorporates two information sources—tweet text and historical price signals—for stock movement prediction.

decisions: How does the temporal auxiliary weight affect model behavior and the trade-off between main-target performance and generalization in the proposed stock movement prediction model?

requirements.description: Must identify that the paper introduces a temporal auxiliary component (or auxiliary objective) whose strength is controlled by a scalar 'auxiliary weight' hyperparameter.

Must state that the auxiliary weight directly controls the overall effect or influence of the temporal auxiliary objective on training, i.e., how strongly the auxiliary loss contributes relative to the main prediction loss.

Must report that model performance does not improve linearly or monotonically as the auxiliary weight increases (e.g., there is a non-linear or non-monotonic relationship between auxiliary weight and performance).

Must explain that adjusting (tweaking) the auxiliary weight creates a trade-off between focusing on the main prediction target (stock movement) and improving generalization through a denoising or regularization effect provided by the auxiliary objective.

Must reference the specific figure or table (e.g., an ablation or sensitivity analysis plot/table) where different values of the temporal auxiliary weight are compared and used to demonstrate the non-linear benefit and trade-off behavior.

decisions: Does the summary slide correctly capture the paper’s demonstrated effectiveness of deep generative approaches for stock movement prediction from social media, the proposed integration of fundamental and technical information with other market signals, the mention of investment simulation with modern portfolio theory, and the release location of the StockNet dataset?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper demonstrates the effectiveness of deep generative approaches for stock movement prediction using social media (tweet) information, as described in the main contribution/experiments section.

Must identify that the model provides a better way to integrate fundamental information and technical indicators, explicitly referencing the joint use of textual (social media) signals and historical price/technical features described in the methodology or model description sections.

Must mention that the paper discusses incorporating other market signals beyond tweets and prices, specifically including financial disclosures, periodic analyst reports, and company profiles as listed in the discussion or future work section.

Must reference that the paper includes or proposes an investment simulation based on modern portfolio theory, as described in the experimental setup or evaluation section where portfolio construction or backtesting is discussed.
Must provide the dataset availability information, including the explicit GitHub URL 'https://github.com/yumoxu/stocknet-dataset' as stated in the dataset or reproducibility section.

decisions: How does the paper define and parameterize the market information encoder’s temporal input and its components for combining tweet messages and price signals?

requirements.description: Must state that the temporal input at time t is defined as a concatenation xt = [ct, pt], where ct represents tweet-based corpus information and pt represents price-based signals.

Must describe that individual tweet messages are first embedded using a Bi-GRU (bidirectional GRU) to obtain message embeddings, which are then aggregated into a corpus-level embedding (ct) from the set of messages.

Must explain that price signals pt include the adjusted closing price and additional derived price features (e.g., pct, p_t^h, p_t^l or equivalent notation for percentage change, high, low, etc.) as specified in the market information encoder description.

Must identify the attention or weighting mechanism over messages defined as ut = softmax(w_u tanh(W_{m,u} M_t)), where M_t is the matrix of message embeddings, and ut provides weights used to form the corpus embedding.

Must mention the normalization step that combines the attention-weighted message representation and price information, including the use of ct, M_t, ut, pt, and a normalized ratio term such as pt/p_{t-1}^{c} (or equivalent notation for price normalization across time).

decisions: What are the exact likelihood and log-likelihood expressions used in the appendix variational inference derivation for stock movement prediction?

requirements.description: Must identify that the expressions concern the conditional likelihood of outputs given inputs and latent variables, specifically p(yt | xt, zt) and the sequence-level likelihood p(y | X).
Must retrieve the variational inference appendix section (or equivalent derivation section) where the log-likelihood log p(yt | xt, zt) and log p(y | X) are explicitly written and manipulated.
Must extract the definition of the likelihood term p(yt | xt, zt) as it appears in the derivation, including its role in the factorization of p(y | X) over time steps.

Must capture the time-indexed form of the likelihood with its conditional statement over t, i.e., the expression p(yt | xt, zt) together with the condition 'if t ≤ T' (or equivalent boundary condition on t and T).

Must restrict retrieval to the appendix (or dedicated 'Variational Inference' subsection) rather than using high-level model descriptions from the main text, ensuring the equations match the appendix notation for y, X, xt, zt, and T.

decisions: How does the paper formally define and parameterize the temporal attention mechanism used in the attentive temporal auxiliary module in the appendix?

requirements.description: Must identify that the 'Attentive Temporal Auxiliary' (or similarly named) component is an appendix module that applies a temporal attention mechanism over a sequence of vectors v_i.

Must retrieve the mathematical definition of the temporal attention weights w_i as functions of the input vectors v_i and a global/context vector g_T (or equivalent notation), showing that attention is computed per time step.

Must state that the context vector g_T is computed using a tanh nonlinearity applied to a linear transformation of a matrix G (or stacked v_i), specifically involving a parameter matrix denoted W_{g,d} (or Wg,d) in an expression of the form g_T = tanh(W_{g,d} G).

Must reproduce or describe the exact symbolic elements appearing in the appendix temporal attention formulae, including the variables v_i, w_i, g_T, v_d (if present), G, and the parameter matrix W_{g,d} (or Wg,d), preserving their roles and relationships.

Must explicitly reference that these temporal attention equations are located in the appendix section describing the 'Attentive Temporal Auxiliary' (or equivalent appendix subsection), not in the main model description.

decisions: How does the paper align tweet corpora and historical price data to trading days for predicting daily stock movement?

requirements.description: Must state that inputs (tweet corpora and historical prices) are reorganized by aligning them to the T trading days with a temporal lag structure.
Must specify that on the t-th trading day, the model uses a tweet corpus denoted as M_t (or equivalent notation) as the text signal source.
Must describe the temporal window for tweets as being collected from an interval [d_{t-1}, d_t] (or equivalent notation indicating tweets between the previous and current trading day).
Must state that the historical price input p_t (or equivalent notation) used for day t prediction corresponds to the price observed on d_{t-1}, i.e., the previous trading day.

Must explicitly link the aligned inputs (M_t in [d_{t-1}, d_t] and p_t on d_{t-1}) to the prediction target y_t on d_t, indicating that this alignment is used to predict the stock movement for trading day t.

decisions: How does the paper explain the role of objective-level temporal auxiliary tasks as a denoising regularizer for heterogeneous lagged market signals in the stock movement prediction model?

requirements.description: Must state that the objective-level auxiliary (temporal auxiliary tasks) is explicitly described as a "denoising regularizer" for the main stock movement prediction objective.
Must explain that the model deals with heterogeneous market sources in the lag (historical inputs) for a sample with a specific main movement target (e.g., rise/fall).
Must describe the concrete example where earlier-day tweets are negative due to bad news but later become positive because of timely crisis management, illustrating heterogeneity in lagged signals.

Must state that without temporal auxiliary tasks, the model incorrectly tries to identify positive signals on earlier days solely for the main target of rise movement, which is characterized in the paper as resulting in pure noise.

Must specify that temporal auxiliary tasks are used to (1) filter lagged market sources according to their aligned auxiliary movements and (2) encode more useful information into the latent driven factor Z.

decisions: What specific neural sequence-to-sequence semantic parsing model (including input/output representations and encoder–decoder architecture) is used in this work?

requirements.description: Must state that the model is a neural semantic parser implemented as a sequence-to-sequence architecture mapping natural language utterances to logical forms.
Must specify that both the encoder and decoder components of the model are LSTM-based (i.e., an LSTM encoder and an LSTM decoder).
Must describe the input side as an 'Utterance' or natural language input sequence that is fed into the encoder.
Must describe the output side as a 'Logical Form' sequence produced by the decoder, representing the semantic parse of the input utterance.

Must reference or reconstruct the example mapping from an Android/IFTTT-style utterance about missed phone calls (e.g., 'Android_phone_call, Any_phone_call_missed ... Archive your missed calls from Android to Google Drive') to its corresponding logical form with function-like arguments (e.g., Spreadsheet_name, Formatted_row, Drivefolder_path).

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the paper’s motivation that confidence modeling is important for neural semantic parsers built on sequence-to-sequence models?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper focuses on confidence modeling for neural semantic parsers built upon sequence-to-sequence models, as described in the abstract.
Must explicitly mention that models tend to always produce (or 'guess') some output even when uncertain, aligning with the slide text 'Most models always tend to guess some outputs'.
Must explicitly mention the need to know how confident the model is in its predictions, corresponding to the slide text 'We also want to know how confident they are'.

Must reference that the paper designs metrics to quantify uncertainty or causes of uncertainty in model predictions, as stated in the abstract ('three major causes of uncertainty' and 'design various metrics to quantify these factors').

Must extract or paraphrase the paper’s motivation for confidence estimation from the introductory or problem-statement discussion (e.g., the part of the abstract explaining that confidence scores indicate whether model predictions are likely to be correct and help users interpret/verify input).

decisions: What motivations for confidence modeling in neural semantic parsing does the paper identify, particularly regarding application needs and challenges specific to neural models?

requirements.description: Must state that any constrained distribution in the proposed framework is represented as a conjunctive logical expression (logical AND) of primitive constraints.
Must identify and name the two primitive constraints used to build logical expressions as 'ZeroPrim' and 'EqualPrim'.
Must explain that ZeroPrim(A) enforces a constraint that the probability of A, p(A), is zero (or effectively removed from the distribution).
Must explain that EqualPrim enforces equal frequency (or equal probability) between specified word pairs, as in EqualPrim(B, E) and EqualPrim(C, D).
Must describe the example configuration over items A, B, C, D, E, F, G where ZeroPrim(A) is applied to A and EqualPrim constraints are applied specifically to the pairs (B, E) and (C, D).

decisions: How does the paper formalize and represent the substitution of Must-links and Cannot-links with more primitive logical constraint components in the LDA-DF framework?

requirements.description: Must identify that the paper introduces a decomposition of pairwise constraints (Must-links and Cannot-links) into more primitive logical constraint units within the LDA-DF (Dirichlet forest prior) framework.

Must describe the formal substitution process where complex logical expressions over word links are rewritten or represented using a fixed set of primitive constraint constructs (e.g., basic link primitives or atomic logical forms) as defined in the paper.

Must cover the specific section or subsection where the authors define the logical constraint language and explicitly explain how Must-links and Cannot-links are mapped or reduced to primitive constraints.

Must state that the substitution with primitives is designed to generalize existing pairwise constraints and to enable the addition of new customized logical constraints beyond standard Must-links and Cannot-links.

Must explain how the primitive constraints, once substituted for the original links, are encoded or implemented in the Dirichlet forest prior structure (e.g., via modifications to tree/forest structure or prior parameters) as described by the authors.

decisions: How does the proposed algorithm in the paper construct topic-model distributions from logical expressions over must-link and cannot-link primitives using disjunctive normal form (DNF)?

requirements.description: Must state that the algorithm operates on logical expressions of pairwise constraints (Must-links and Cannot-Links) by first substituting each link in the expression with its corresponding primitive variables (e.g., A, B, C).

Must describe the second step of the algorithm as computing the minimum disjunctive normal form (DNF) of the logical expression over primitives, explicitly identifying DNF as a disjunction of conjunctions of primitives.

Must explain that for each conjunction (term) in the DNF, the method generates a separate distribution (e.g., over topics or word groups), corresponding one-to-one with each conjunction of primitives.

Must reference the figure or schematic in the paper that illustrates primitives labeled as A, B, C (and extended to A–G) and shows how these primitives are combined into conjunctions and then disjoined in DNF form.

Must cover the specific subsection that introduces the 'Proposed algorithm for logical expressions' (or equivalently titled algorithm section) and enumerate its three ordered steps: (1) substitute links with primitives, (2) compute minimum DNF, and (3) generate distributions for each conjunction.

decisions: Does the AI correctly identify and summarize the theorem stating the asymptotic equivalence between the proposed method and the existing constrained topic modeling method with respect to conjunctive expressions of links, including the associated distribution representations by primitives and by graphs?

requirements.description: Must state that there is a theorem claiming that the proposed method and the existing method are asymptotically equivalent with respect to conjunctive expressions of links (i.e., logical conjunctions of Must-links and Cannot-Links).

Must identify that the asymptotic equivalence is defined in terms of the distributions induced by the Dirichlet forest prior constructions used in both the proposed method and the existing constrained LDA (CL) method.
Must explicitly mention that the primitives (basic building blocks) used in the proposed method are the same as those used in the existing CL method when representing constraints.

Must describe that the paper includes a figure or schematic showing distributions constructed 'by primitives' (e.g., over items labeled A, B, C, D) and contrasting them with distributions constructed 'by a graph' (e.g., over items labeled A, B, C, D, E, F, G) to illustrate the equivalence.

Must locate and use the specific theorem or formal statement in the paper that is labeled or described as establishing the 'correctness' of the method via asymptotic behavior or asymptotic equivalence to the existing constrained method.

decisions: How does the paper define and formalize customizable new logical link types between words (such as exclusion and implication links) within the LDA-DF framework for topic models?

requirements.description: Must identify that the slide describes three specific logical link patterns between words in topics: (1) exclusion of a set of words X1, …, Xn from topics, (2) implication 'B appears if A appears', and (3) implication 'Y appears if X1, …, Xn appear'.
Must state that the exclusion of X1, …, Xn is implemented via a constraint of the form ISL(X1, …, Xn) = ∏_{i=1}^n ZeroPrim(Xi), or an equivalent product over i from 1 to n involving ZeroPrim(Xi).

Must state that the implication 'B appears if A appears' (A → B) is implemented via a constraint of the form IL(A, B) = EqualPrim(A, B) · ZeroPrim(A), or an equivalent expression explicitly combining EqualPrim(A, B) and ZeroPrim(A).

Must state that the implication 'Y appears if X1, …, Xn appear' (X1, …, Xn → Y) is implemented via a constraint of the form XIL(X1, …, Xn, Y) = (∏_{i=1}^n EqualPrim(Xi, Y)) · (∏_{i=1}^n ZeroPrim(Xi)), or an equivalent expression that clearly includes both EqualPrim(Xi, Y) and ZeroPrim(Xi) over i = 1…n.

Must attribute these link definitions to the part of the paper that discusses 'Customization of new links' or the equivalent subsection where new logical link types (ISL, IL, XIL) are introduced and formally defined.

decisions: How does the paper use logical word constraints to interactively refine topic models on a movie review corpus, specifically to isolate frequent but uninformative words and to separate Star Wars and Star Trek topics?

requirements.description: Must identify that the slide illustrates the use of logical word constraints (Isolate-Link and Cannot-Link) within the LDA-DF topic modeling framework to manipulate topic-word distributions on a movie review corpus.

Must describe the Isolate-Link constraint applied to the specific words {"have", "film", "movie", "not", "nt"}, including that these words are treated as a group to be isolated and removed along with related unnecessary words from topics.
Must state that the example corpus used in the slide is a movie review corpus consisting of 1000 reviews, as explicitly mentioned in the slide text.
