decisions: What example translations does the paper provide to illustrate document-level neural machine translation with memory networks, specifically for sentences about the Lisbon strategy and 'qimonda'?

requirements.description: Must identify that the example illustrates document-level translation consistency for sentences mentioning 'qimonda' and 'the lisbon strategy', not a generic translation example.
Must retrieve the exact example sentence 'qimonda meets the objectives of the lisbon strategy.' from the paper and include it in the slide content.
Must retrieve the exact example sentence '<UNK> is the objectives of the lisbon strategy.' from the paper and include it in the slide content, preserving the '<UNK>' token.

Must retrieve the full compound example line beginning with 'the millennium development goals are fulfilling the millennium goals of the lisbon strategy. in writing. - (ro) the lisbon strategy is fulfilling the objectives of the lisbon strategy. qimonda fulfils the aims of the lisbon strategy.' without omitting or rephrasing any of these clauses.

Must locate and use the specific example translation block in the paper that is attributed to '[Wang et al., 2017]' and includes the sentence '<UNK> fulfils the objectives of the lisbon strategy.' as shown on the slide.

decisions: Does the system correctly retrieve and present the example translation outputs illustrating document-level NMT behavior and comparative translations for the Lukashenko dictatorship sentence?

requirements.description: Must identify that the example illustrates multiple alternative English translations of the same Estonian source sentence about 'lukasenka diktatuur' to demonstrate document-level neural machine translation behavior.
Must reproduce the full Estonian source sentence exactly as shown: '... et riigis kehtib endiselt lukasenka diktatuur, mis rikub inim- ning etnilise vahemuse oigusi.'

Must retrieve and list the specific English translation variant containing the phrase 'this country is still under the dictatorship of lukashenko, breaching human rights and the rights of ethnic minorities.'

Must retrieve and list the specific English translation variant containing the token '<UNK>' in the phrase '... the country still keeps the <UNK> dictatorship that violates human rights and ethnic rights.'

Must include the final comparative translation line attributed to prior work, including the citation marker '[Wang et al., 2017]' and the following text: '... there is still a regime in the country that is violating the rights of human and ethnic minority in the country.'

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the main conclusion points of the paper about document-context neural machine translation with memory networks?

requirements.description: Must state that the proposed model explicitly incorporates both global source and global target document context (not just sentence-level context) as part of its core contribution.
Must mention that the authors propose specific training and decoding methodologies (or procedures/algorithms) tailored to the document-level NMT model with memory networks.
Must identify that the model is a document-context neural machine translation (NMT) model, not a generic NMT or other NLP model.

Must indicate that the work involves or motivates investigation of document-context NMT models that incorporate specific discourse-level phenomena (e.g., coherence, coreference, discourse relations), not just generic context.

Must draw these three points (global source/target context, training and decoding methodologies, and discourse-level document-context investigation) from the paper's conclusion or summary section rather than inferring them solely from the abstract.

decisions: How does the paper conceptually define 'fake news' for use in its analysis and presentation materials?

requirements.description: Must state that fake news is conceptualized as disinformation presented or displayed in the form of news articles (i.e., news-like content that is intentionally misleading).

Must retrieve the part of the paper where fake news is defined or operationalized (e.g., in the introduction, data description, or task definition), rather than inferring a definition from external knowledge.

Must reflect that the paper treats fake news as a category of articles within the collected corpus (i.e., as a label applied to full news articles), consistent with the notion of disinformation in article form.

Must identify that the slide’s image credit or conceptual framing is linked to Claire Wardle / First Draft and reproduce this attribution if it appears in the paper’s figures, captions, or referenced conceptual diagrams.

Must distinguish fake news from related categories discussed in the paper (e.g., hyperpartisan news, satire) by emphasizing that fake news is defined specifically as disinformation, not merely biased or humorous content.

decisions: How does the paper conceptualize and position hyperpartisan news publishers along the left-right political spectrum and distinguish them from partisan and mainstream actors?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper uses the left-right political spectrum as a system for classifying political positions, ideologies, parties, and related news media alignment (matching the definition drawn from Wikipedia).

Must define 'partisan' in line with the slide as someone with a psychological identification with one major party, explicitly indicating that this definition is sourced from Wikipedia or an equivalent definitional source referenced in the paper.

Must reproduce or describe the spectrum layout that orders political positions as 'Alt-left, Left, Center, Right, Alt-right' and maps them respectively to 'Hyperpartisan, Partisan, Partisan, Hyperpartisan' as shown in the slide.
Must indicate that news media reporting on politics can be aligned along the same left-right political spectrum used for political positions and ideologies.

Must report the observation from the paper that there is an increasing number of hyperpartisan news publishers, explicitly characterizing them as hyperpartisan rather than merely partisan or mainstream.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and explain how the paper relates hyperpartisan (alt-left and alt-right) news to mainstream news using the horseshoe theory concept?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper analyzes hyperpartisan news as consisting of both alt-left and alt-right publishers contrasted against mainstream (center/partisan) news.

Must explicitly mention that alt-left and alt-right, when considered separately, are difficult to distinguish from mainstream news by style, while hyperpartisan news as a combined category can be distinguished.

Must reconstruct or describe the political spectrum layout used in the slide with the ordered positions 'Alt-left', 'Left', 'Center', 'Right', 'Alt-right' and their corresponding labels 'Hyperpartisan', 'Partisan', 'Partisan', 'Partisan', 'Hyperpartisan'.
Must reference the horseshoe theory by name and explain that it claims the alt-left and alt-right resemble each other despite being at opposite ends of a linear political continuum.

Must identify and use the part of the paper where the authors conceptually discuss political positioning of publishers (left, center, right; alt-left/alt-right; hyperpartisan vs mainstream) rather than the sections focused solely on numerical F1 results.

decisions: Does the slide correctly identify and contextualize why fake news are predominantly published by hyperpartisan pages, as discussed in the paper?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper finds a very strong overlap between fake news and hyperpartisan content, specifically that 97% of the 299 fake news articles identified in the corpus are also hyperpartisan.

Must describe that the corpus is organized by publisher type, with three mainstream, three hyperpartisan left, and three hyperpartisan right political publishers, to ground the notion of 'hyperpartisan pages'.

Must retrieve and use the exact corpus size (1,627 articles) and the number of fake news articles (299) as reported in the abstract to support any quantitative claim about fake news on hyperpartisan pages.

Must report that style analysis can distinguish hyperpartisan news from mainstream news with an F1 score of 0.78, indicating that hyperpartisan pages have a distinct writing style relevant to understanding why they are associated with fake news.

Must report that style-based fake news detection does not work well (low F1 score as indicated in the abstract, truncated but explicitly mentioned as ineffective), to clarify that the association between fake news and hyperpartisan pages is empirical (overlap in the corpus) rather than due to a reliable stylometric fake-news detector.

decisions: How does the paper position style-based fake news detection within a broader taxonomy of fake news detection approaches, particularly in contrast to knowledge-based and semantic web/LOD methods and their practical limitations?

requirements.description: Must identify and name the 'knowledge-based (also called fact checking)' approach as a distinct category in the paper's taxonomy of fake news detection methods.
Must identify and name 'Semantic web / LOD' as a separate approach or sub-approach within the taxonomy of fake news detection methods.

Must state that knowledge-based/fact-checking approaches require a 'political knowledge base' and explicitly mention that such a knowledge base is 'unavailable ahead of time' and that 'we cannot trust the web' as a reliable source for it.

Must describe the deployment constraints of Semantic web / LOD or platform-based approaches by explicitly stating that they are 'limited to social media platforms' and that 'part of [the] damage [is] already done' by the time they act.

Must report the paper's explicit question or challenge about its own stylometric method by including the phrase or idea that 'style differences' may not be sufficient for fake news detection, e.g., by asking 'But are style differences sufficient?'.

decisions: How does the paper describe the annotation labels and source used to construct the fake and hyperpartisan news corpus?

requirements.description: Must identify that the corpus articles are annotated with discrete veracity labels including at least the categories 'true', 'false', and 'mix' (or equivalent wording indicating mixed truth).
Must state that there is an additional annotation category for articles that are not assigned a veracity label, referred to as 'n/a' or an equivalent 'not applicable' / 'not available' label.
Must explicitly mention that the annotations (the true/mix/false/n/a labels) were provided by professional journalists at BuzzFeed, as described in the corpus construction part of the paper.
Must draw the label set and annotation-source information from the corpus description or data/annotation section of the paper, not infer it from unrelated sections such as results or discussion.
Must correctly associate the BuzzFeed journalists' annotations with the political news articles in the constructed corpus (i.e., not misattribute the labels to another dataset or task).

decisions: What specific fake news detection annotations and publisher labels from the paper must be retrieved to recreate the 'Fake News and Hyperpartisan News Selected Results' slide?

requirements.description: Must identify that the slide content is about 'Fake News Detection' based on annotations provided by professional journalists at BuzzFeed, and explicitly link this to the paper's description of fact-checking by BuzzFeed journalists.
Must retrieve the categorical annotation labels used in the paper for article veracity as shown on the slide, specifically the four classes: 'true', 'mix', 'false', and 'n/a'.

Must retrieve from the paper the specific publisher names that appear on the slide, including 'Politico', 'Occupy Democrats', and 'Recall', and recognize them as part of the set of political publishers analyzed.

Must recognize and reproduce the tabular or matrix-like layout where the veracity labels ('true', 'mix', 'false', 'n/a') are presented together as column headers or category labels, matching the structure implied by the slide text.

Must draw from the part of the paper that describes the annotation process and dataset construction (including BuzzFeed journalist fact-checking and publisher list) rather than from sections on stylometric methods or classification results.

decisions: How does the horseshoe validation experiment with leave-out classification demonstrate the classifier’s behavior on right-wing articles when trained only on left-wing and center articles?

requirements.description: Must state that in the horseshoe validation (leave-out) experiment, the classifier is trained only on left-wing and center (mainstream) articles, explicitly excluding right-wing articles from the training set.
Must state that in this experiment right-wing articles are held out from training and used exclusively as the test set for evaluating the classifier.
Must report that, when tested on right-wing articles, the classifier assigns the majority of these right-wing articles to the left-wing class rather than to the center class.
Must identify that this setup is referred to as a 'horseshoe validation' or 'horseshoe' experiment in the paper, linking the described training/testing configuration to that specific term.

Must draw the above information from the specific experimental description section that details the horseshoe validation or leave-out classification experiment, not from unrelated experiments or overall corpus description.

decisions: Does the system correctly retrieve and summarize the paper’s description and use of the Unmasking (horseshoe validation) method to distinguish style genres (mainstream vs hyperpartisan left vs hyperpartisan right) and their normalized accuracies?

requirements.description: Must identify and explain that the paper uses the Unmasking method (originally from Koppel & Schler 2004) as a meta-learning approach to compare writing styles and make a "same author" vs "different author" style decision based on typical learning characteristics.

Must describe the horseshoe-style validation illustration showing two authors labeled "A" and "B" with sequences of feature removals (represented as repeated 'a' and 'b' symbols) that produce a characteristic learning curve used for the same-author decision.

Must state that Unmasking is repurposed in this paper to distinguish style genres (not individual authors), specifically applying the method to compare mainstream, hyperpartisan left, and hyperpartisan right news styles.

Must retrieve and report the normalized accuracy values associated with the Unmasking-based genre comparisons, including that mainstream vs left and mainstream vs right achieve higher normalized accuracies than left vs right, with explicit mention of the approximate values 0.4 and 0.2 as shown in the slide.

Must state the comparative outcome that, according to the Unmasking experiment, mainstream vs hyperpartisan (left or right) is stylistically more distinguishable than left vs right, as evidenced by the differing normalized accuracy scores for these three pairwise genre comparisons.

decisions: Does the system correctly summarize the paper’s main stylometric findings and implications about hyperpartisan and fake news as presented in the Summary and Outlook slide?

requirements.description: Must state that hyperpartisan news outlets (or pages/publishers) produce a disproportionately high or relatively large number of fake news articles, reflecting the corpus-level finding that most fake news items come from hyperpartisan sources.

Must describe that hyperpartisan news can be distinguished from mainstream news based on writing style alone, explicitly linking this to the stylometric or style-based analysis method used in the paper (e.g., classification by style features).

Must connect style-based detection to the possibility of real-time or near real-time detection of hyperpartisan content, i.e., explicitly stating that the style-based classifier can be applied without external fact-checking or long delays.

Must report that the style of hyperpartisan left (alt left) and hyperpartisan right (alt right) news is very similar according to the stylometric analysis, rather than being clearly separable by style.

Must capture the paper’s concluding implication that these stylometric findings provide linguistic evidence consistent with the horseshoe theory of the political spectrum and explicitly mention the need for larger-scale or future analysis as an outlook or limitation.

decisions: How does the paper define and implement the style-based classification model used to distinguish different types of news articles?

requirements.description: Must list all feature families used in the style model as given in the paper: character n-grams, stop-word n-grams, part-of-speech n-grams, 10 readability scores, General Inquirer dictionary-based features, and ratios of quoted words, external links, and number of paragraphs.
Must state the feature pruning criterion exactly as described, namely that word (n-gram) features occurring in less than 2.5% (10%) of the documents are discarded.
Must describe the class balancing procedure as oversampling, using the term 'balancing using oversampling' or an equivalent phrase explicitly tied to the training data preparation.
Must specify the train-test split constraint that publishers are not represented in both the training and test sets, i.e., that publisher identities are disjoint across splits.
Must identify the classifier as WEKA's random forest with default parameters, including explicit mention of both 'WEKA' and 'random forest'.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the paper’s motivation for automatic argument generation as presented in the Motivation slide?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper frames argumentation as crucial or essential for human communication or reasoning, matching the idea that 'Argumentation is crucial in communication.'
Must capture that the work is motivated by the need to avoid biased perception and uninformed decisions, explicitly linking argument generation to reducing bias or uninformed decision-making.
Must distinguish between being merely informative and being persuasive, explicitly indicating that being informative is already difficult and that being persuasive is even more challenging.
Must extract motivation content from the paper’s introductory or motivation-style discussion (e.g., abstract or introduction), not from method or results descriptions.

Must connect the motivation to the task of automatically generating arguments of a different stance for a given statement, indicating that the system’s goal is to support better, less biased decision-making through such arguments.

decisions: What overarching research question about automating human argumentation does the paper pose?

requirements.description: Must identify that the central problem studied is automatic generation of arguments, i.e., automating the human argumentation process.
Must recognize that the task involves generating arguments of a different stance for a given statement, as described in the abstract.
Must extract the paper’s high-level task description from the abstract (the novel task on automatically generating arguments) as the source for the research question.
Must note that the proposed solution involves an encoder-decoder neural network model, indicating that the research question is about automating argumentation via neural methods.

Must frame the research question in terms of 'how to automate' or 'how to automatically generate' human-like arguments, not in terms of related but different tasks such as classification or retrieval alone.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and describe the paper’s specific goal of generating counterarguments, including input/output format and required reasoning abilities?

requirements.description: Must state that the system generates a specific type of argument, namely a counterargument (an argument of the opposite/different stance) to a given statement.
Must describe the input as a statement of belief on a controversial topic and the output as a counterargument that refutes that statement.

Must include an example illustrating the input–output mapping for the task, specifically using the belief statement about humans not being designed to be vegan and a corresponding refuting counterargument.
Must identify that the task requires understanding both the topic and the stance of the given statement as an explicit capability of the system.
Must state that the task involves application of common sense knowledge and generating arguments in natural language text as explicit listed abilities or goals.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the specific strands of prior work on evidence detection, support classification, argument/evidence retrieval, and argument generation cited in the paper’s related work section?

requirements.description: Must cover the paper's prior work / related work discussion on evidence detection and support identification, including the works by Rinott et al. (2015) and Hua and Wang (2017) as distinct items.

Must identify that prior work is grouped into at least three conceptual areas: (1) evidence detection / support classification, (2) argument and evidence retrieval / search, and (3) argument generation approaches.

Must retrieve and correctly list the specific prior work references with author names and years exactly as in the paper for: Rinott et al. (2015), Hua and Wang (2017), Wachsmuth et al. (2017), Stab et al. (2018), Sato et al. (2015), and Zukerman et al. (2000).

Must distinguish between 'argument and evidence retrieval' work (e.g., argument search engines) and 'retrieval-based argument generation' work, reflecting the same separation of concepts as in the paper's prior work discussion.

Must capture that the paper situates itself relative to both retrieval-based argument generation (Sato et al., 2015) and argument strategy–based generation (Zukerman et al., 2000) as separate strands within the argument generation literature.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the dataset description used for argument generation, including the Reddit source, filtering criteria, topic selection, and basic statistics?

requirements.description: Must state that the dataset is collected from a subreddit dedicated to open discussion and debate (i.e., ChangeMyView or equivalent description as given in the paper).
Must cover the paper's data collection / dataset section where the example thread about government email surveillance is presented, including both the initial post and at least one reply.
Must describe the selection criterion that only politics and policy related topics are included in the study, as specified in the dataset description section.
Must specify the quality filtering rule that only high quality replies are kept, defined in the paper as those with a delta or at least a threshold number of upvotes ("delta or more upvotes").

Must retrieve and report the basic dataset statistics table or description that includes average number of sentences and average number of tokens for (a) the input statement and (b) the human argument, after removing non-root and low-quality replies.

decisions: What specific components of the proposed neural argument generation pipeline, as illustrated in the paper, must be retrieved to accurately describe the argument decoding stage with externally retrieved evidence and talking point phrases?

requirements.description: Must identify that the model generates arguments of an opposite or different stance for a given input statement, rather than supporting the same stance.
Must describe that the pipeline uses externally retrieved evidence sentences from Wikipedia (e.g., about 'Edward Snowden' and 'Political corruption') as inputs to the neural model.
Must state that the model first generates intermediate 'talking point phrases' (e.g., '<phz> right to privacy<phz>') before producing the final argument.
Must specify that the final argument is produced by an argument decoding component implemented as an LSTM decoder (e.g., labeled '5. Argument Decoding (LSTM)').

Must reference the pipeline-style illustration or description in the paper that shows the flow from input statement and retrieved evidence sentences, through talking point phrase generation, to the LSTM-based argument decoding stage.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and describe the paper’s Step 1 document retrieval process for extracting relevant evidence for counterarguments?

requirements.description: Must state that the goal of Step 1 (document retrieval) is to extract relevant evidence for counterarguments to a given statement or post.
Must explain that the retrieval step forms its query representation from topic signatures as defined by Lin and Hovy (2000), explicitly referencing them as the basis for topic signatures.
Must describe that topic signatures are representative of the text and that their representativeness is measured using a log-likelihood ratio (LLR) statistic.
Must provide example topic signature terms such as 'government', 'emails', and 'national security' as illustrative keywords extracted from a post.

Must reference the example input post used to illustrate Step 1, including the stance 'I believe the government should be allowed to view my emails for national security concerns. CMV.' and the follow-up sentence 'I have nothing to hide. I dont break the law.' as the source text from which topic signatures are derived.

decisions: How does the paper perform the second step of sentence reranking when selecting evidence sentences from retrieved Wikipedia articles for argument generation?

requirements.description: Must state that the retrieved Wikipedia articles are segmented into smaller units, specifically broken into paragraphs and then into individual sentences, before reranking.
Must specify that sentences are ranked using TF-IDF similarity, explicitly naming TF-IDF as the scoring method.
Must indicate that the TF-IDF similarity is computed against the original input post (the given statement) rather than against other sentences or documents.
Must identify that the sentences used as examples in this step are drawn from externally retrieved Wikipedia evidence, such as the Edward Snowden and political corruption sentences.
Must describe that the paper includes or implies example top-ranked sentences (e.g., one about Edward Snowden and one defining political corruption) to illustrate the sentence reranking step.

decisions: How does the model encode the input statement together with the retrieved evidence sentences in Step 3 of the argument generation process?

requirements.description: Must state that, in the encoding step, both the original input statement and the externally retrieved evidence sentences are encoded jointly as a single sequence.
Must specify that the joint sequence of input statement and evidence sentences is separated by a special delimiter token written exactly as '<evd>'.

Must describe the example encoding string shown in the paper/figure for this step, including the literal text fragment 'I believe the <evd> edward snowden' as the illustrative input-plus-evidence sequence.
Must indicate that the encoder processes two distinct components labeled or conceptualized as 'Input statement' and 'Evidence sentences' that are concatenated with the '<evd>' token between them.

Must reference the specific part of the paper that describes the encoding step of the model (e.g., the subsection detailing 'Step 3 Encoding' or the encoder input construction) rather than other stages like talking point generation or decoding.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and describe the paper’s keyphrase decoding step used as an intermediate representation for argument generation?

requirements.description: Must state that keyphrases are generated as an intermediate step to inform the model of the major talking points and to mimic keyphrases likely reused by humans, using wording equivalent to the slide’s first three bullet points.

Must describe that the model decodes keyphrases in a special format that includes an evidence marker and phrase markers, exemplified by a pattern equivalent to: 'I believe the <evd> edward snowden <phz> right to privacy<phz>'.
Must specify that keyphrases are extracted as noun phrases and verb phrases, matching the slide statement 'We extract noun phrases and verb phrases.'
Must report the explicit constraints on keyphrase length from the paper, namely that each keyphrase must be between 2 and 10 tokens.

Must indicate that keyphrases must contain non-stop words and illustrate their role using an example semantically equivalent to the slide’s sentence about civil rights and privacy groups opposing surveillance as a violation of the right to privacy.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and describe the argument decoding step that generates the final argument from encoder/keyphrase states with attention over input and keyphrases, including the use of <phz>, <evd>, and <arg> markers?

requirements.description: Must state that in the argument decoding step the argument decoder is initialized from either the encoder's last hidden state or the keyphrase decoder's last hidden state (or an explicit choice between them), as described in the model architecture section.

Must describe that the argument decoder uses an attention mechanism over both the original input statement representation and the generated keyphrase representations, as specified in the argument generation/decoding subsection.

Must explain that keyphrases are used as an intermediate representation ("talking points") between the input statement and the final argument, and that the argument decoder conditions on these keyphrases when generating the argument.

Must identify and explain the special markers/tags used in the model outputs, including <phz> for keyphrases, <evd> for externally retrieved evidence, and <arg> for the generated argument span, as defined in the paper's data format or model output description section.

Must draw from the section that details the multi-step generation process (talking point/keyphrase generation followed by argument decoding) rather than only from sections describing data collection, retrieval of Wikipedia evidence, or evaluation metrics.

decisions: How does the paper design and compare its experimental setups, including training configuration and the System vs. Oracle evidence retrieval conditions, for neural argument generation?

requirements.description: Must state that the first layers of both the encoders and the argument decoders are initialized (e.g., with pretrained parameters) as part of the experimental setup.
Must describe that the system is first "warmed up" using a good argumentation language model before full training, explicitly indicating a pretraining or warm-up phase for argument generation.

Must specify that the training data includes all training threads plus additional non-politics threads and non-root replies, matching the slide phrase "All training data + non-politics threads + non-root replies."
Must identify the baseline sequence-to-sequence model configuration that is trained without using evidence sentences or keyphrases, explicitly noting the absence of external evidence in this setup.

Must clearly distinguish between the "System" and "Oracle" retrieval conditions by stating that at test time the System can only retrieve evidence based on the input statement, whereas in the Oracle setup evidence is retrieved using human argument queries.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize all argument generation model variants and their configurations described in the experiments section for model comparison?

requirements.description: Must list and correctly name all baseline and proposed model variants as defined in the experiments section, including 'RETRIEVAL-BASED', 'SEQ2SEQ', 'SEQ2SEQ encode evidence', 'SEQ2SEQ encode keyphrase', 'DEC-SHARED', 'DEC-SEPARATE attend keyphrase', and 'DEC-SEPARATE'.

Must describe the input configuration for each SEQ2SEQ variant as stated in the paper: 'SEQ2SEQ' encoding only the input statement, 'SEQ2SEQ encode evidence' encoding both statement and evidence sentences, and 'SEQ2SEQ encode keyphrase' encoding statement and keyphrases.
Must state that the 'RETRIEVAL-BASED' model is defined in the experiments section as concatenating externally retrieved evidence sentences into a single input.

Must explain, using the experiments/model description text, that 'DEC-SHARED' initializes the argument decoder with the keyphrase decoder, while 'DEC-SEPARATE' initializes the argument decoder from the encoder, and 'DEC-SEPARATE attend keyphrase' adds attention over the keyphrase decoder.

Must explicitly mention the rationale from the experiments section that the 'SEQ2SEQ encode keyphrase' configuration is considered a stronger baseline because keyphrases are actually reused by human arguments.

decisions: How does the paper automatically evaluate the quality of generated arguments, and how do the proposed models compare to retrieval baselines under BLEU and METEOR metrics?

requirements.description: Must state that BLEU is used as an automatic evaluation metric and is defined as an n-gram precision-based measure for generated arguments.
Must state that METEOR is used as an automatic evaluation metric and is defined as a unigram precision-and-recall measure based on alignment between system and reference arguments.

Must describe that the gold-standard references for evaluation are user-generated (human-written) arguments and that a multi-reference setup is used where the best-aligned reference is selected, reflecting the existence of multiple plausible arguments.

Must report that higher BLEU and METEOR scores indicate better performance and that the proposed models achieve better precision (higher BLEU) such that their generated content is more likely to be found in human arguments.

Must retrieve from the relevant results table or section the comparison between system retrieval and oracle retrieval settings, explicitly mentioning BLEU-2, METEOR, and Length for both, and must note that the retrieval baseline generation attains better METEOR due to considering both precision and recall.

decisions: How does the paper automatically evaluate topic relevance of generated arguments, and why is this evaluation needed beyond BLEU?

requirements.description: Must state that the motivation for this evaluation is that generic, off-topic arguments can still obtain high BLEU scores, with examples such as short generic responses (e.g., "I dont agree with you.", "You are missing evidence.", "This is wrong.") being mentioned as problematic cases.

Must identify that the paper uses a semantic similarity model based on Huang et al. (2013) specifically for evaluating topic relevance between generated arguments and the input statement or reference.

Must explain that the semantic similarity model is used to represent or compute the semantic relatedness between two pieces of text (e.g., argument and topic/statement) as the core mechanism for topic relevance evaluation.
Must note that the semantic similarity model is tuned or trained on the paper's training set (or an explicitly named training split) rather than being used entirely off-the-shelf without adaptation.

Must report that the automatic topic relevance evaluation for the semantic similarity model is quantified using mean reciprocal ranking (MRR) and Precision at 1 (P@1), and must state that higher values of these metrics indicate better performance.

decisions: How does the paper conduct and report its human evaluation comparing RETRIEVAL-BASED, SEQ2SEQ, and OUR MODEL for argument generation quality?

requirements.description: Must identify and use the dedicated Human Evaluation section (or equivalent evaluation subsection) that describes manual assessment of generated arguments.
Must state that three trained human judges, fluent in English, are used to evaluate the generated arguments instead of relying solely on automatic evaluation metrics.
Must describe that three systems are compared in the human evaluation: a RETRIEVAL-BASED system, a SEQ2SEQ system, and the proposed model (OUR MODEL).
Must specify that human judges rate outputs on three aspects—Grammaticality, Informativeness, and Relevance—each on a 1 to 5 Likert scale where higher scores indicate better quality.
Must report the qualitative conclusion from the human evaluation that human judges favor the RETRIEVAL-BASED model over the other systems on all three aspects.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and extract the paper’s example of a generated counterargument to a political statement for use as a sample argument slide?

requirements.description: Must identify that the slide content is an illustrative example of the paper’s core task: generating an argument (counterargument) of a different stance given an original post/statement.

Must locate and extract the specific example pair from the paper’s examples/qualitative results section that contains the original post about Putin re-forming a Soviet Union and the corresponding generated counterargument.
Must retrieve the exact original post text beginning with "Putin is trying to re-form a Soviet Union with his past actions in Georgia and current actions in Ukraine." as it appears in the paper.

Must retrieve the full generated counterargument text associated with that original post, including the sentence starting "I firmly believe that Putin and the Russian Federation (RF) are trying to re-form a Soviet Union type regime" and the subsequent lines shown in the slide.

Must preserve the two-column layout structure used in the paper’s example (one column labeled or functioning as 'Original Post' and the other as 'Generated Counterargument') when mapping content into the slide.

decisions: What future work and limitations does the paper identify regarding evidence retrieval and the quality of generated arguments?

requirements.description: Must identify that the paper explicitly proposes improving or developing a 'better evidence retrieval system' as a future direction or limitation-related need.

Must extract this information from the paper's discussion of limitations or future work (e.g., a 'Future Work', 'Conclusion', or limitations paragraph), not from the abstract or method description alone.
Must state that the current system is prone to incoherence in generated arguments, as reported or discussed in the paper's evaluation or analysis sections.
Must state that the current system can generate inaccurate information (hallucinations or factually incorrect content) as a reported limitation in the paper.
Must state that the current system tends toward generic or overly general argument generation, as explicitly mentioned in the paper's error analysis, qualitative examples, or discussion.

decisions: Does the summary correctly capture the paper’s main contributions as stated in the conclusion, including the task definition, dataset creation, and proposed end-to-end system with Wikipedia evidence?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper studies a novel neural argument generation task, explicitly mentioning that it is an argument generation task and that it is characterized as novel and neural (model-based).
Must identify from the conclusion or contribution statements that the authors collect and release a new dataset specifically sourced from the r/ChangeMyView subreddit.
Must mention that the new dataset is accompanied by externally retrieved Wikipedia evidence (e.g., evidence sentences or passages) that are linked to the arguments or statements.
Must describe that the paper proposes an end-to-end argument generation system (or encoder-decoder model) rather than only a component or partial pipeline.
Must specify that the proposed end-to-end argument generation system is enhanced or augmented with Wikipedia retrieved evidence sentences, not just generic external knowledge.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and extract the example knowledge graph entities and relation used to illustrate a 'Football Team – Lionel Messi' triple from the paper?

requirements.description: Must identify that the paper uses a concrete example triple involving the entity 'Lionel Messi' and a 'Football Team' relation (or type) to illustrate knowledge graph structure or embeddings.
Must retrieve this example from the introductory or motivating example part of the paper where basic knowledge graph concepts (entities and relations) are first explained.
Must describe any figure or diagram (if present) that visually depicts a knowledge graph snippet including 'Lionel Messi' connected to a 'Football Team' node or label.
Must explain how this 'Football Team – Lionel Messi' example is used methodologically (e.g., as a running example to explain entity/relation embeddings or geometric arrangements).

Must extract the exact surface forms of the example entities/relations as written in the paper (specifically the tokens 'Football Team' and 'Lionel Messi') without paraphrasing them into different names.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify how knowledge graph embeddings represent entities and relations, and which foundational translational embedding method is cited?

requirements.description: Must state that knowledge graph embedding methods represent entities and relations as vectors in a (high-dimensional) vector space, matching the formulation in the abstract or introductory description.
Must explicitly mention that both entities and relations (not only entities) are embedded as vectors, as described in the paper's overview of KG embeddings.
Must extract from the background or related work section that translational embedding models are a key class of KG embedding methods used as reference in the paper.

Must correctly retrieve the full citation of the TransE paper: the title 'Translating Embeddings for Modeling Multi-relational Data' and the first author 'Bordes et al.' from the references or related work discussion.
Must correctly identify and state the venue and year for the TransE paper as 'NIPS 2013' (or 'NeurIPS 2013' if the paper uses the updated conference name) from the citation list.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the paper’s motivation for studying the geometry of knowledge graph embeddings, including the reference to prior work on the geometry of word embeddings?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper is concerned with the arrangement of entity and relation vectors (embeddings) in a high-dimensional/vector space, using wording equivalent to 'arrangement of vectors in the vector space'.
Must explicitly mention that the geometrical understanding of knowledge graph (KG) embeddings is limited or unexplored, despite their popularity or widespread use.
Must capture the paper’s motivation/introduction content that contrasts existing work on the geometry of word embeddings with the lack of such understanding for KG embeddings (i.e., a gap statement).
Must identify that the referenced prior work by Mimno and Thompson (2017) performs an analysis of the geometry of word embeddings and reports interesting or notable results about that geometry.
Must correctly retrieve and cite the specific prior work as 'The strange geometry of skip-gram with negative sampling' by Mimno and Thompson, EMNLP 2017, including both authors and year.

decisions: What specific research problems does the paper define regarding the geometry of knowledge graph embeddings?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper aims to study or analyze the geometrical behavior (or geometry) of KG embeddings learned by different embedding methods, as explicitly described in the problem/objective formulation in the introduction or abstract.

Must state that the paper aims to study the effect of various training hyper-parameters on the geometry of KG embeddings, using wording that clearly links hyper-parameters to geometric properties, as presented in the problem statement or goals section.

Must state that the paper aims to study or analyze the correlation between the geometry of KG embeddings and their performance on downstream tasks (e.g., link prediction), as explicitly framed in the paper's stated objectives.

Must identify and extract the explicit list or enumeration of research goals/problem statements where the three aims (geometry across methods, effect of hyper-parameters, correlation with performance) are jointly presented, typically in the introduction or a 'Problem'/'Objectives' subsection.

Must indicate that multiple KG embedding methods (e.g., different existing models) are compared specifically for their learned geometrical behavior, as described in the experimental design or methodology section that operationalizes the first problem statement.

decisions: What are the key components and operations of standard knowledge graph embedding methods as described in the paper?

requirements.description: Must state that KG embedding methods learn d-dimensional vector representations for both entities and relations in a knowledge graph.

Must describe the use of a score function that assigns higher scores to correct triples than to incorrect triples, including an explicit example contrasting (Messi, plays-for-team, Barcelona) with (Messi, plays-for-team, Liverpool).
Must specify that training uses a loss function and explicitly name at least one of the two types mentioned: logistic loss or margin-based ranking loss.
Must mention entry-wise (Hadamard) product as one of the operations used in the KG embedding methods described.
Must mention circular correlation as another operation used in the KG embedding methods described.

decisions: What experimental factors does the paper analyze to study the geometry of knowledge graph embeddings and its correlation with performance?

requirements.description: Must state that the experiments analyze the geometry of knowledge graph (KG) embeddings, not just general KG performance or training behavior.
Must identify the 'type of method' factor explicitly as comparing additive versus multiplicative KG embedding methods, using both terms 'additive' and 'multiplicative'.
Must specify that the 'number of negative samples' is treated as an experimental factor whose variation is studied for its effect on the geometry of KG embeddings.
Must specify that the 'dimension of vector space' (i.e., embedding dimensionality) is treated as an experimental factor whose variation is studied for its effect on the geometry of KG embeddings.
Must state that the experiments also study or analyze the correlation between model performance and the geometry of KG embeddings, using both terms 'performance' and 'geometry'.

decisions: How does the paper compare additive and multiplicative knowledge graph embedding models in terms of conicity and vector spread?

requirements.description: Must identify that 'conicity' is a geometric property defined and used in the paper to characterize the arrangement of knowledge graph embedding vectors.
Must identify that 'vector spread' is a geometric property defined and used in the paper to describe how embedding vectors are distributed in space.
Must distinguish between 'additive' and 'multiplicative' model types as two different classes of knowledge graph embedding methods analyzed in the paper.

Must retrieve the specific table or figure where conicity and vector spread are jointly reported or compared across additive and multiplicative model types (e.g., a table with columns for model type, conicity, and vector spread).

Must preserve the tabular structure that aligns 'Model Type' with the two geometric measures 'Conicity' and 'Vector Spread' as separate columns or labeled dimensions, matching the layout implied by the slide text.

decisions: How does introducing negative samples affect the conicity and AVL of entity and relation vectors across different knowledge graph embedding model types, including multiplicative relation models?

requirements.description: Must state that for the 'Entity' model type, both conicity and AVL of entity vectors show 'No Change' when negative samples are introduced.
Must state that for the 'Relation' model type, both conicity and AVL of relation vectors show 'No Change' when negative samples are introduced.
Must state that for the 'Multiplicative Relation' model type, conicity of the corresponding vectors 'Decreases' when negative samples are introduced.
Must state that for the 'Multiplicative Relation' model type, AVL shows 'No Change except HolE' when negative samples are introduced, explicitly mentioning HolE as the exception.

Must retrieve the tabular comparison that jointly lists 'Model Type', 'Vector Type', 'Conicity', and 'AVL' under the condition of adding negative samples, preserving the three model-type rows: 'Entity', 'Relation', and 'Multiplicative Relation'.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize how SGNS-based Word2Vec behaves as a multiplicative model and its relation to conicity with varying numbers of negative samples?

requirements.description: Must state that SGNS-based word embeddings exhibit higher conicity when the number of negative samples is increased, matching the phrasing 'higher #negatives resulted in higher conicity'.
Must state that Word2Vec (specifically SGNS) maximizes the dot product between word and context vectors for positive word–context pairs.

Must explicitly connect this dot-product-maximization behavior of Word2Vec/SGNS to being 'consistent with that of multiplicative models' or an equivalent statement that it behaves as a multiplicative model.
Must attribute the conicity observation to Mimno and Thompson (2017) as a prior work on 'the strange geometry of skip-gram with negative sampling'.

Must correctly retrieve and mention both cited references: (1) Mikolov et al., 'Distributed representations of words and phrases and their compositionality', NIPS 2013, and (2) Mimno and Thompson, 'The strange geometry of skip-gram with negative sampling', EMNLP 2017.

decisions: How does changing the embedding dimensionality affect the conicity and AVL of entity and relation vectors in the studied knowledge graph embedding models?

requirements.description: Must state that, according to the paper, varying the embedding dimension results in no change in conicity for entity vectors (i.e., conicity is reported as 'No Change' for entities).
Must state that, according to the paper, varying the embedding dimension results in no change in conicity for relation vectors (i.e., conicity is reported as 'No Change' for relations).
Must retrieve from the relevant table or figure the explicit entry that AVL for entity vectors under different dimensions is reported as 'No Change'.
Must retrieve from the relevant table or figure the explicit entry that AVL for relation vectors under different dimensions is reported as 'No Change'.
Must identify and use the specific section, table, or figure in the paper that analyzes the 'Effect of Dimensions' on geometric measures (conicity and AVL) for both entity and relation vectors.

decisions: Does the paper report how specific geometric measures (Conicity and AVL) correlate with model performance under a fixed number of negative samples?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper explicitly finds no overall correlation between geometry of knowledge graph embeddings and performance when considered in aggregate (i.e., without conditioning on number of negative samples).

Must identify that the correlation analysis is performed under the condition of a fixed number of negative samples used during training or evaluation, as specified in the experimental setup section describing negative sampling.

Must define or reference the geometric measure 'Conicity' as introduced in the paper (e.g., in the section where geometric properties of embeddings are formalized) and use that same term when describing its correlation with performance.

Must define or reference the geometric measure 'AVL' (Average Vector Length or the exact term used in the paper) as introduced in the geometry analysis section and use that same term when describing its correlation with performance.

Must report that, for a fixed number of negative samples, Conicity has a negative correlation with performance and AVL has a positive correlation with performance, as stated in the results text or shown in the corresponding correlation table or figure.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the paper’s main geometric contribution and the specific future work directions proposed in the conclusion?

requirements.description: Must explicitly draw from the paper's Conclusion (or Conclusion and Future Work) section to state that the work 'initiated the study' or 'initiated a study' of the geometrical behavior/geometry of KG (knowledge graph) embeddings and that it presented insights about this geometry.

Must state that the central contribution is analyzing the geometrical behavior/geometry of KG embeddings (i.e., arrangement of entity and relation vectors in high-dimensional space), not just generic KG embedding performance or link prediction.

Must mention that the future work includes exploring additional entity/relation features (specifically including 'entity category' as an example) to test whether they correlate with the geometry of the embeddings.
Must mention that the paper reports 'various insights' or 'several insights' about the geometry of KG embeddings as an outcome of the study, not only describing the setup or planned work.
Must state that future work includes exploring other geometrical metrics that have better correlation with performance and using such metrics to learn or design better KG embeddings.

decisions: How does the paper position dialogue within the spectrum of natural language generation tasks in terms of openness, neural LM success, need for control, and evaluation difficulty, and how does it define 'control' in this context?

requirements.description: Must identify and state the paper's definition of 'control' as the ability to specify desired attributes of the generated text at test time.

Must retrieve the conceptual spectrum that contrasts 'less open-ended' versus 'more open-ended' NLG tasks and explicitly link this to neural language models being 'more successful' on the less open-ended side and 'less successful' on the more open-ended side.
Must extract the claim that control is 'less important' for less open-ended, mostly word-level decision tasks and 'more important' for more open-ended tasks that require high-level decisions.

Must retrieve the specific error types attributed to neural language models in open-ended generation (e.g., repetition and generic responses under certain decoding algorithms) and the claim that control can be used to fix these errors and handle some high-level decisions.

Must capture the discussion that evaluation becomes harder as tasks become more open-ended, including the explicit contrast 'Eval is difficult' versus 'Eval is fiendish' and the added complexity of dialogue evaluation (single-turn vs multi-turn, interactive vs static conversation).

decisions: What specific research questions does the paper pose about controlling conversational attributes and their impact on chatbot quality?

requirements.description: Must identify that the paper investigates control over multiple conversational attributes of generated text, specifically including repetition, specificity, response-relatedness, and question-asking, as stated in the abstract or problem formulation.
Must extract that one explicit research question concerns how effectively the different attributes can be controlled (i.e., a question of control effectiveness over the attributes).

Must extract that another explicit research question concerns how the controllable attributes affect multiple aspects of conversational quality (i.e., the relationship between attribute control and human-judged quality).
Must extract that a third explicit research question concerns whether using attribute control can make a better chatbot overall (an overall quality improvement question).

Must identify that the paper uses human evaluation of conversational quality in conjunction with controllable neural text generation methods (conditional training and weighted decoding) as the basis for answering the three research questions.

decisions: Does the system correctly retrieve and summarize how the PersonaChat task and baseline model setup are described in the paper?

requirements.description: Must identify that the dialogue example is from the PersonaChat task, including both persona sentences (e.g., liking fancy tea, having a big library, being a museum tour guide, having two dogs, liking vintage cars, favorite music being country, owning two vintage Mustangs) and the subsequent conversational turns between the speakers.

Must capture that the slide illustrates persona-based chitchat by presenting explicit persona profile lines followed by a short multi-turn dialogue grounded in those personas (e.g., references to reading and the auto industry book).
Must state that the paper uses a baseline model described as a standard LSTM-based seq2seq architecture with attention for the PersonaChat task.
Must report that this baseline model is pretrained on 2.5 million Twitter message/response pairs and then finetuned on the PersonaChat dataset.

Must retrieve that, according to Dinan et al. 2019, most successful teams in the referenced PersonaChat competition built neural sequence generation systems and that the winning team, Lost in Conversation, used a finetuned version of GPT.

decisions: Which controllable dialogue attributes does the paper aim to manipulate to improve conversational quality?

requirements.description: Must identify that one controlled attribute is reduction of repetition, explicitly including both within-utterance and across-utterance repetition as described in the paper.
Must identify that one controlled attribute is reducing genericness of responses, using the paper's notion of generic chitchat replies (e.g., responses like "oh that's cool").
Must identify that one controlled attribute is response-relatedness, i.e., making system responses stay on-topic and not ignore the user's previous utterance.
Must identify that one controlled attribute is question-asking, specifically that the paper studies or optimizes the rate or frequency of asking questions in dialogue.

Must extract all four attributes (repetition, specificity/genericness, response-relatedness, and question-asking) from the same conceptual description in the paper where the authors enumerate the controllable attributes for chitchat dialogue.

decisions: Which specific human evaluation questions does the paper use to measure conversational quality aspects of the dialogue agent?

requirements.description: Must list all individual human judgment questions used to assess conversational quality, including repetition, interestingness, nonsensical content, natural English, attention to user, amount of questions asked, human-likeness, and overall enjoyment, without adding or omitting items.

Must extract these questions specifically from the paper's human evaluation or evaluation setup section where user study questions or rating prompts are defined, not infer them from abstract or introduction text.

Must preserve the interrogative form of each evaluation question as presented in the paper (e.g., starting with 'Does', 'Did', 'Is'), rather than paraphrasing them into statements or changing their polarity.

Must correctly associate each question with the underlying attribute it measures (repetition, interestingness, coherence/sense-making, fluency/natural English, context awareness/response-relatedness, question-asking frequency, perceived humanness, and enjoyment).
Must indicate that these questions are used as direct human rating prompts for evaluating dialogue quality, not as training labels, model inputs, or automatic metrics.

decisions: How does the paper define and distinguish the two controllable generation methods, Conditional Training and Weighted Decoding, used to control dialogue attributes?

requirements.description: Must state that Conditional Training (CT) is defined as training the model to generate a response y conditioned on both the input x and an additional desired output attribute variable z (i.e., p(y | x, z)).
Must explain that Conditional Training (CT) incorporates the attribute control at training time by adding the attribute signal z as part of the conditioning context for generation.
Must state that Weighted Decoding (WD) is defined as a decoding-time method that increases or decreases the probability of generating words w in proportion to feature functions f(w).
Must specify that in Weighted Decoding (WD), the modification of word probabilities is applied during the decoding process (not during training), based on the values of features f(w).

Must identify and draw from the section of the paper that introduces and formally defines the two control methods (Conditional Training and Weighted Decoding), rather than from results or discussion sections.

decisions: How effectively can the two controllable generation methods, Conditional Training and Weighted Decoding, control the four dialogue attributes in this paper?

requirements.description: Must list all four controllable dialogue attributes exactly as defined in the paper: repetition, specificity, question-asking, and response-relatedness.
Must identify Conditional Training (CT) as one of the two controllable neural text generation methods evaluated for attribute control.
Must identify Weighted Decoding (WD) as the second controllable neural text generation method evaluated for attribute control.
Must state that Conditional Training (CT) requires sufficient training examples for the target attribute in order to control it.

Must state that Weighted Decoding (WD) requires the attribute to be defined at the word level, is ineffective at learning complex relationships between input and output such as response-relatedness, and is reported as effective for controlling repetition, response-relatedness, and specificity.

decisions: How do conditional training (CT) and weighted decoding (WD) differ in their controllability range and output quality when controlling specificity in dialogue generation?

requirements.description: Must identify that the comparison is specifically about controlling the 'specificity' attribute of chitchat dialogue, not other attributes like repetition or question-asking.
Must describe weighted decoding (WD) as a controllable neural text generation method used in the paper, distinct from conditional training (CT).
Must describe conditional training (CT) as a controllable neural text generation method used in the paper, distinct from weighted decoding (WD).
Must state that for specificity control, weighted decoding (WD) provides a large controllable range over the attribute values but produces degenerate outputs at the extreme settings.
Must state that for specificity control, conditional training (CT) provides a smaller controllable range over the attribute values but generally yields well-formed outputs across that range.

decisions: According to the paper, what happens to dialogue system outputs when the weighted decoding (WD) weight for controlling response-relatedness is set too high?

requirements.description: Must identify that the discussed control mechanism is weighted decoding (WD) applied specifically to the response-relatedness attribute.
Must state that excessively increasing the WD weight for response-relatedness leads to degenerate or qualitatively poor outputs.
Must describe that the WD method modifies token selection scores during generation by adding a weighted response-relatedness feature, and that the 'weight' refers to this feature's coefficient.

Must reference the paper's empirical observation (in text, figure, or table) that higher response-relatedness WD weights correlate with degeneration effects (e.g., repetitive, unnatural, or collapsed outputs).

Must draw from the section or subsection that analyzes response-relatedness control via weighted decoding (e.g., the part comparing different WD weight settings for response-relatedness), not from sections on other attributes like repetition or question-asking.

decisions: According to the paper, which controllable dialogue attributes are adjusted, and in what direction, to study how control affects human evaluation quality?

requirements.description: Must identify that the paper explicitly treats 'n-gram repetition' as a controllable attribute in chitchat dialogue generation.
Must identify that 'genericness' (or lack of specificity) is treated as a controllable attribute distinct from repetition.
Must identify that 'response-relatedness' (similarity of the system response to the last user utterance) is a controllable attribute examined in the paper.
Must state that the target level for n-gram repetition is to match human-level repetition, not simply to minimize repetition arbitrarily.

Must state that the target level for genericness/specificity is to reduce genericness to human levels (i.e., adjust specificity toward human-like behavior), and to increase response-relatedness relative to an uncontrolled baseline.

decisions: According to the paper, does controlling specific dialogue attributes make the chatbot overall more engaging than baseline systems, and how does its performance compare to the ConvAI2 GPT-based competition winner and to humans on engagingness and humanness metrics?

requirements.description: Must identify that the improved overall chatbot quality is attributed specifically to controlling three dialogue attributes: repetition, specificity, and question-asking (and not include response-relatedness in this particular claim).
Must state that, when these attributes are controlled, the model achieves near-human engagingness (enjoyability) ratings as reported in the human evaluation section.
Must retrieve the comparison that the model's raw engagingness score matches that of the ConvAI2 competition winner's GPT-based model from the results tables or text where this benchmark is reported.

Must report the architectural and data-scale comparison that the proposed model is much smaller (2 layers vs 12 layers) and trained on approximately 12 times less data than the ConvAI2 GPT-based competition winner, as specified in the model description or experimental setup section.
Must explicitly state that on the humanness (Turing test-style) metric, the proposed models are far from human-level performance, as described in the paper's evaluation results.

decisions: How does the paper compare bots to humans in terms of engagingness and humanness, and what explanation is given for why human engagingness scores are easy for bots to match?

requirements.description: Must state the comparative finding that the dialogue bots are reported as almost as engaging as human interlocutors, while still being clearly identifiable as non-human, using the paper's explicit comparison between bots and humans on engagingness and humanness.
Must retrieve the result that human engagingness performance in the study is characterized as potentially or artificially low, as explicitly discussed in the paper's analysis of engagingness scores.

Must identify that the human conversational partners in the evaluation are crowd workers (Turkers) paid to chat, rather than people chatting voluntarily for fun, as described in the paper's data collection or evaluation setup.

Must explain the causal interpretation given in the paper that Turkers chatting for money are less engaging than people chatting for fun, and that this is proposed as the reason why human-level engagingness scores are relatively easy for the bots to match.

Must draw on the paper's evaluation or discussion section where engagingness and humanness judgments are analyzed, not solely on sections describing controllable attributes like repetition, specificity, response-relatedness, or question-asking.

decisions: What main conclusions does the paper draw about controllable attributes in neural dialogue systems and their evaluation?

requirements.description: Must state that applying simple controllable generation methods to neural sequence generation dialogue systems is beneficial and that such control can match the performance of a GPT-based contest-winning system, as concluded in the paper's discussion/conclusion section.

Must explicitly identify the recommended conversational behavior attributes: avoiding repetition, avoiding boring/overly generic responses (increasing specificity/engagingness), and increasing question-asking, as key controllable factors highlighted in the conclusions.

Must describe that multi-turn conversational phenomena (specifically repetition across turns and question-asking frequency) require multi-turn evaluation procedures, as stated in the conclusions or evaluation discussion, rather than relying only on single-turn metrics.

Must report the paper's conclusion that engagingness judgments are effectively equivalent to humanness judgments ("Engagingness = Humanness") and that this has implications for which human rating metric to choose in evaluation.

Must cover the paper's conclusion about annotator/source population, namely that paid Mechanical Turk workers are found to be poor conversational partners and unreliable judges of engaging conversation compared to humans chatting for fun, and that manually searching for the best combination of control settings is identified as a remaining practical problem.

decisions: Does the system correctly extract and summarize the paper’s basic definition and properties of word embeddings as presented in the introductory/background discussion?

requirements.description: Must state that word embeddings are represented as dense vectors of words, matching the paper’s introductory description of embeddings as dense, low-dimensional representations.
Must identify that the paper discusses unsupervised training methods for word embeddings and explicitly name at least GloVe and Word2Vec as example algorithms.
Must capture the distributional hypothesis from the paper’s background, namely that words appearing in similar contexts tend to have similar meanings.
Must state that in the embedding space, words with similar meanings are located close to each other (i.e., semantic similarity corresponds to geometric proximity in the vector space).

Must draw these points specifically from the paper’s introductory or background discussion of word embeddings (e.g., the section where standard embeddings like GloVe and Word2Vec are introduced), not from later sections on SentiVec or experimental analysis.

decisions: What example sentence does the paper use to illustrate training or learning word embeddings?

requirements.description: Must identify that the sentence "This camera is good for high quality" is used in the paper as an example in the context of explaining or illustrating word embeddings or their training.

Must retrieve this example sentence from the explanatory section where the authors introduce or motivate word embeddings (e.g., introductory or methodology explanation text), not from experimental results or discussion sections.

Must state that the example sentence "This camera is good for high quality" is tied to demonstrating how words in a sentence are represented or processed when learning word embeddings (e.g., context windows, input to the embedding model).

decisions: Does the system correctly retrieve and reproduce the definition of Wikipedia’s neutral point of view policy as used in the paper?

requirements.description: Must identify that the quoted text is Wikipedia’s definition of a 'neutral point of view' (NPOV), not a definition created by the paper’s authors.
Must locate the section or passage in the paper where Wikipedia’s NPOV policy is explicitly quoted or described as guidance for neutrality or objectivity in text.
Must capture that NPOV is defined in terms of representing 'all of the significant views that have been published by reliable sources on a topic.'
Must capture that NPOV requires representation that is 'fairly, proportionately, and, as far as possible, without editorial bias.'

Must reproduce the full NPOV sentence as it appears in the paper, including the clause structure (neutral point of view → which among other things means → representing fairly, proportionately, and, as far as possible, without editorial bias → all of the significant views ...).

decisions: How does the paper define and operationalize a subjectivity scale ranging from more objective to more subjective corpora or texts?

requirements.description: Must identify that the paper explicitly distinguishes between 'objective' and 'subjective' text or corpora as a core dimension in its analysis of word embeddings.
Must state that the paper conceptualizes subjectivity as a continuum or scale (e.g., ranging from more objective to more subjective), not as a purely binary label.
Must retrieve the section or subsection where the authors introduce or define the notion of corpus subjectivity and describe how it varies across different datasets or text sources.

Must describe how the authors operationalize different levels of subjectivity in practice (e.g., by selecting or constructing corpora with varying subjectivity levels, or by using a subjectivity lexicon or labels to quantify subjectivity).

Must reference any figure, diagram, or schematic (if present) that visually represents the subjectivity dimension or contrasts more objective vs. more subjective data, and map it to the 'More Objective � More Subjective' axis used on the slide.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the three binary classification tasks (sentiment, subjectivity, topic) and their associated datasets and example sentences used in the paper?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper evaluates three distinct binary classification tasks: sentiment classification (positive vs. negative), subjectivity classification (subjective vs. objective), and topic classification (in-topic vs. out-of-topic).
Must identify that the sentiment classification task uses Amazon Reviews spanning 24 categories together with Rotten Tomatoes Reviews as the datasets.
Must identify that the topic classification task uses a Newsgroups dataset with 6 categories as the source corpus.

Must describe that the sentiment classification task is framed as a binary decision between positive and negative sentiment, the subjectivity classification task as subjective vs. objective, and the topic classification task as in-topic vs. out-of-topic.

Must reproduce or clearly reference the example sentence pairs used to illustrate the tasks: 'A very funny movie' vs. 'One lousy movie' for sentiment, and 'The story needs more dramatic meat' vs. 'She's an artist' for subjectivity.

decisions: How did the authors design and control their experimental setup when using word embeddings for sentence-level classification tasks?

requirements.description: Must state that model evaluation used cross-validation, explicitly mentioning that it was performed on balanced samples (i.e., class-balanced datasets).
Must identify the classifier as a binary logistic regression model used for the sentence-level classification experiments.
Must describe the sentence representation method as computing sentence embeddings by averaging the word embeddings of all tokens in the sentence.
Must state that, when training different word embeddings for comparison, the experiments controlled for corpus size by using the same number of sentences across conditions.
Must state that, when training different word embeddings for comparison, the experiments controlled for lexical coverage by using the same vocabulary across conditions.

decisions: What empirical findings does the paper report about the comparative performance of SE, OE, and SentiVec embeddings on objective versus subjectivity/sentiment classification tasks?

requirements.description: Must state that SE (subjective embeddings) and OE (objective embeddings) perform very similarly on objective tasks, explicitly referencing both subjectivity classification and topic classification as the objective-style evaluation tasks used in the paper.

Must identify that SE and OE are compared specifically on sentiment-related tasks using sentiment words, and that the analysis is framed as testing whether SE 'understand' sentiment words better than OE on Amazon Sentiment and Rotten Tomatoes Sentiment datasets.

Must report the empirical conclusion that SentiVec does not affect objective classification tasks, explicitly tying this claim to the same objective-style tasks used for SE/OE comparison (subjectivity classification and topic classification).

Must retrieve that Amazon Sentiment results are aggregated as an average over 24 categories, and explicitly mention this 'average over 24 categories' phrasing as part of the description of the Amazon Sentiment evaluation.

Must draw from the empirical results/experiments section that reports performance on both Amazon Sentiment and Rotten Tomatoes Sentiment, and must mention both datasets by name when summarizing the findings about SE/OE and SentiVec.

decisions: What information from the paper is needed to construct the slide listing the top words most similar to the target word 'good' and their similarity scores?

requirements.description: Must identify that the paper computes word similarity lists for a target word (e.g., 'good') based on cosine similarity in the learned word embedding space.
Must retrieve the specific table or figure that lists the top-N most similar words to 'good' along with their numerical similarity scores (e.g., a table with columns 'Word' and 'Similarity').
Must preserve the two-column layout structure from the source (e.g., 'Word  Similarity  Word  Similarity') when generating the slide content.

Must state which embedding variant (e.g., SentiVec vs. baseline embeddings) is used to compute the similarity list for 'good' when that is specified in the caption or surrounding text of the table/figure.

Must locate and use the part of the paper (e.g., an analysis or case-study subsection) where qualitative examples of nearest neighbors for sentiment words like 'good' are presented, rather than quantitative task results or unrelated tables.

decisions: How does the paper empirically demonstrate that sentiment words can lead to problematic word similarities in standard word embeddings?

requirements.description: Must identify that the slide refers to an analysis of word pair similarities involving sentiment words that reveal problematic behavior in word embeddings (e.g., sentiment words being overly similar or dominating similarity structure).
Must locate and reference the specific table or figure in the paper that presents a three-column layout with headers equivalent to 'Word A', 'Word B', and a numeric similarity score between them.
